Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CRYPTREC
chunks.content:
Term: CRYPTREC (CRYPTREC)
Definition: Cryptography Research and Evaluation Committees, Japan's organization for evaluating and recommending cryptographic algorithms for government use.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: KpqC
chunks.content:
Term: KpqC (KpqC)
Definition: Korean Post-Quantum Cryptography project, South Korea's national initiative to develop and standardize its own PQC algorithms including HAETAE, AIMer, SMAUG-T, and NTRU+.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ITU-T
chunks.content:
Term: ITU-T (ITU-T)
Definition: International Telecommunication Union — Telecommunication Standardization Sector. Study Group 17 (SG17) is developing PQC standards for telecommunications infrastructure.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NCCoE
chunks.content:
Term: NCCoE (NCCoE)
Definition: NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, collaborating with industry to develop practical PQC migration guidance and reference architectures.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: BIS
chunks.content:
Term: BIS (BIS)
Definition: Bank for International Settlements, the international financial institution that published the quantum-readiness roadmap (Paper 158) for the global financial system.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CACR
chunks.content:
Term: CACR (CACR)
Definition: Chinese Association for Cryptologic Research, the organization that ran China's independent PQC competition and is shaping the NGCC (Next-Generation Commercial Cryptographic) standards program.
Category: organization | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: IETF PLANTS Working Group
chunks.content:
Term: IETF PLANTS Working Group (PLANTS)
Definition: The IETF working group responsible for standardizing Merkle Tree Certificates and related post-quantum PKI infrastructure. Adopted draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs in January 2026.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CMVP
chunks.content:
Term: CMVP (CMVP)
Definition: Cryptographic Module Validation Program — a joint NIST and CCCS program that tests cryptographic modules against FIPS 140-3 requirements. Validated modules appear on the NIST CMVP Active Validations list with a certificate number, providing formal assurance of implementation correctness.
Technical Note: PQC FIPS 140-3 validation for ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) modules began in 2024. Validation cycles take 12–18 months; procurement requiring FIPS 140-3 validated PQC must account for this lag. Check: csrc.nist.gov/projects/cmvp.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ACVP
chunks.content:
Term: ACVP (Automated Cryptographic Validation Program)
Definition: NIST-managed automated testing program for individual cryptographic algorithm implementations. Distinct from CMVP (which validates whole modules); ACVP grants per-algorithm validation IDs that CMVP submissions reference.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CC
chunks.content:
Term: CC (Common Criteria)
Definition: International standard (ISO/IEC 15408) for security-product evaluation. Country-specific schemes (BSI Germany, ANSSI France, NIAP US, CCS Canada, etc.) run evaluations; results mutually recognised through the CCRA. EUCC succeeds the SOG-IS MRA in the EU.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CSA
chunks.content:
Term: CSA (Cyber Security Agency of Singapore)
Definition: Singapore's national cybersecurity authority. Publishes the Cybersecurity Code of Practice and PQC readiness guidance for critical-information-infrastructure operators. Note: also used for Cloud Security Alliance (separate org).
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: ITSM (CCCS)
chunks.content:
Term: ITSM (CCCS) (Information Technology Security Management series)
Definition: CCCS Canada's technical-guidance document series (ITSM.40.xxx, ITSAP.xx.xxx). The PQC-relevant entry today is ITSAP.00.017 — Preparing your organization for the quantum threat to cryptography.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: MAS
chunks.content:
Term: MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore)
Definition: Singapore's central bank and integrated financial regulator. Publishes Technology Risk Management Guidelines and circulars that cover cryptographic-control expectations for financial institutions.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: KISA
chunks.content:
Term: KISA (Korea Internet & Security Agency)
Definition: South Korea's national agency for cybersecurity and internet governance. Operates the K-CMVP cryptographic-module validation programme and co-administers the KpqC competition with academic partners.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: MSIT (Korea)
chunks.content:
Term: MSIT (Korea) (Ministry of Science and ICT)
Definition: South Korea's policy ministry for science, ICT, and broadcasting. Co-sponsors the KpqC standardization competition with KISA and the National Intelligence Service.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: DISA
chunks.content:
Term: DISA (Defense Information Systems Agency)
Definition: US Department of Defense combat-support agency that runs IT infrastructure for the joint warfighter. Maintains the STIG library that locks down DoD system configurations, including cryptographic-suite controls.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TCG
chunks.content:
Term: TCG (Trusted Computing Group)
Definition: Industry consortium that publishes the TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and DICE (Device Identifier Composition Engine) specifications. PQC-relevant work covers TPM 2.0 PQC algorithm additions and attestation-quote signing.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

Title: Recommendation for Key Derivation Using Pseudorandom Functions (Revision 1)

chunks.content:
Reference: NIST-SP-800-56C-R2
Title: Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes (Revision 2)
Description: NIST SP 800-56C Rev.2 specifies one-step and extraction-then-expansion (EtE) key derivation methods for key-establishment schemes. chunks.content:
Reference: PKCS11-V3-OASIS
Title: PKCS #11 Cryptographic Token Interface Standard Version 3.0
Description: PKCS#11 v3.0 is the HSM programming interface standard. It adds CKM_HKDF_DERIVE and CKM_HKDF_KEY_GEN mechanisms for TLS 1.3 and CKM_SP800_108_COUNTER_KDF / FEEDBACK_KDF / DOUBLE_PIPELINE_KDF for NIST SP 800-108 derivation. Essential for HSM-based QKD integration workflows where QKD secrets are imported as non-extractable keys and used to derive session keys. Superseded by PKCS#11 v3.1 and v3.2.

Authors: OASIS PKCS11 Technical Committee
Algorithm Family: Symmetric; QKD
Security Levels: 
Migration Urgency: High

chunks.content:
Reference: PKCS11-V32-OASIS
Title: PKCS #11 Specification Version 3.2 (Committee Specification Draft)
Description: PKCS#11 v3.2 adds post-quantum cryptography mechanisms: ML-KEM (CKM_ML_KEM 0x00000017, CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000000f), ML-DSA (CKM_ML_DSA 0x0000001d, CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000001c, CKM_HASH_ML_DSA_*), and SLH-DSA (CKM_SLH_DSA, CKM_SLH_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN). Introduces C_EncapsulateKey() and C_DecapsulateKey() functions for KEM operations. New key types: CKK_ML_KEM (0x49), CKK_ML_DSA (0x4a), CKK_SLH_DSA (0x4b). New attributes: CKA_PARAMETER_SET, CKA_ENCAPSULATE, CKA_DECAPSULATE, CKA_SEED.

chunks.content:
Reference: Ethereum-EIP7702
Title: EIP-7702: Set Code for EOA
Description: Allows EOAs to set executable code via signed authorisation tuples (Pectra hard fork). chunks.title: OAuth Status List — draft-ietf-oauth-status-list
chunks.content:
Reference: IETF-Token-Status-List
Title: OAuth Status List — draft-ietf-oauth-status-list
Description: IETF specification for a compact bit-array status list to check validity states of credentials (valid revoked suspended). Provides privacy-preserving revocation: the verifier cannot determine which specific credential is being checked from the status list position alone. Used in EUDI Wallet ecosystem for credential revocation checking without revealing holder identity to the issuer.

chunks.content:
Reference: RFC 7517
Title: JSON Web Key (JWK)
Description: Defines the JWK format for representing cryptographic keys as JSON. JWKS endpoints publish public keys for JWT signature verification. PQC migration significantly increases JWKS response sizes: ML-DSA-65 public keys are 1952 bytes vs 65 bytes for P-256, challenging HTTP header limits and caching strategies.

chunks.content:
Reference: RFC 6749
Title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
Description: Defines the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework enabling secure delegated access using access tokens. Access tokens and ID tokens issued by authorization servers are typically JWTs signed with RSA or ECDSA. PQC migration requires updating JWT signing across all OAuth authorization servers and resource server token validation.

chunks.content:
Reference: RFC 9449
Title: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)
Description: Defines DPoP for binding OAuth 2.0 tokens to a client public key using signed proof-of-possession JWTs. DPoP proof JWTs use ECDSA signatures that are quantum-vulnerable. Migration to ML-DSA-signed DPoP proofs requires JOSE PQC standardization and results in significantly larger proof headers per request.

chunks.content:
Reference: RFC-9964
Title: RFC 9964 — ML-DSA for JOSE and COSE
Description: This document specifies JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) serializations for Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA) defined in NIST FIPS 204. Registers ML-DSA-44/65/87 with the new Algorithm Key Pair (AKP) key type (kty=AKP, COSE kty=7) and JOSE alg names matching the COSE registrations (-48/-49/-50). chunks.content:
Reference: EPC-342-08-Crypto-Guidelines-v16
Title: EPC 342-08 v16.0 — Guidelines on Cryptographic Algorithms Usage and Key Management (2026)
Description: European Payments Council v16.0 guidelines (73pp) on cryptographic algorithm selection and key management for SEPA payment schemes. Dedicated Chapter 4 on Post-Quantum Cryptography: CRQC impact on RSA/ECC, Harvest Now Decrypt Later (HNDL) and Harvest Now Forge Later (HNFL) threats, 3-step PQC transition (inventory → crypto agility → hybrid migration). Rec 4 mandates crypto agility integration and hybrid key establishment/digital signatures combining classical and PQC algorithms. Covers AES, SHA-2, RSA, ECC, TLS 1.3, key hierarchy, TRSM requirements, blockchain/DLT security, and 18 formal recommendations. chunks.content:
Reference: arXiv-2603-01091-HNDL-Rekeying
Title: Quantifying Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Threats: An Empirical Analysis of Rekeying Defences
Description: Empirical analysis of HNDL attack economics across TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, QUIC, and SSH. chunks.content:
Reference: NIST-SP-800-38D
Title: Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC
Description: NIST SP 800-38D specifies GCM and GMAC for AES. GCM provides authenticated encryption using a 96-bit (12-byte) nonce and a 16-byte authentication tag appended to ciphertext. Nonce uniqueness per key is mandatory — reuse lets an attacker recover the keystream and forge authentication tags (SP 800-38D §8). Used as CKM_AES_GCM in PKCS#11 v3.2.

Title: Divide and Surrender: Exploiting Variable Division Instruction Timing in HQC Key Recovery Attacks

Leaders: Robin Leander Schröder; Stefan Gast; Qian Guo

chunks.content:
Reference: IACR-2022-952-FrodoKEM-Rowhammer
Title: When Frodo Flips: End-to-End Key Recovery on FrodoKEM via Rowhammer
Description: Demonstrates end-to-end key recovery on FrodoKEM using Rowhammer DRAM bit flips. Forces key generation to produce high-error public keys, enabling decryption-failure attacks for full secret key recovery.

Authors: IACR ePrint
Algorithm Family: LWE-based
Security Levels: L1,L3,L5

Standardization Bodies: NIST
Leaders: Michael Fahr Jr.; Hunter Kippen; Andrew Kwong; Thinh Dang; Jacob Lichtinger; Dana Dachman-Soled; Daniel Genkin; Alexander Nelson; Ray Perlner; Arkady Yerukhimovich; Daniel Apon

chunks.title: SLasH-DSA: Breaking SLH-DSA Using an Extensible End-to-End Rowhammer Framework
chunks.content:
Reference: ArXiv-2025-SLH-DSA-Rowhammer
Title: SLasH-DSA: Breaking SLH-DSA Using an Extensible End-to-End Rowhammer Framework
Description: Demonstrates Rowhammer-based universal signature forgery on SLH-DSA. Induces DRAM bit flips during signature generation to produce valid signatures without knowledge of the private key. Emphasizes Rowhammer as a persistent remotely triggerable threat.
Type: Research Paper | Status: Preprint
Authors: arXiv
Algorithm Family: Hash-based
Security Levels: L1,L3,L5
Migration Urgency: High
Industries: Government;Defense;Cloud
Region: PQC-REGION-GLOBAL
Published: 2025-09-01 | Updated: 2025-09-01

Main Topic: The document presents a software-only universal forgery attack on SLH-DSA using Rowhammer-induced bit flips to corrupt internal states and forge signatures without private key knowledge.
PQC Algorithms: SLH-DSA
Standardization Bodies: NIST
PQC Products: Swage; OpenSSL 3.5.1
Leaders: Jeremy Boy; Antoon Purnal; Anna Pätschke; Luca Wilke; Thomas Eisenbarth

chunks.content:
Reference: Springer-MathFoundations-PQC-2026
Title: Mathematical Foundations for Post-Quantum Cryptography
Description: Open-access Springer volume (Mathematics for Industry 40) from the Crypto-Math CREST project. Covers mathematical foundations underlying NIST PQC standards: lattice theory (LWE, MLWE, NTRU, Module-LWE), code-based cryptography, hash-based signatures, isogeny-based cryptography, and multivariate schemes. Edited by leading Japanese cryptographers (Takagi, Wakayama, Kunihiro, Tanaka, Kimoto, Kudo). ISBN eBook 978-981-96-1218-5. CC BY 4.0.
Type: Book | Status: Published
Authors: Tsuyoshi Takagi; Masato Wakayama; Noboru Kunihiro; Keisuke Tanaka; Kazufumi Kimoto; Momonari Kudo (Eds.) — University of Tokyo; NTT Inc.; University of Tsukuba; Institute of Science Tokyo; University of the Ryukyus; Fukuoka Institute of Technology

Security Levels: L1; L3; L5
Migration Urgency: Medium
Industries: Cryptography Research; Government; Defense; Finance
Region: PQC-REGION-GLOBAL
Published: 2026-01-01 | Updated: 2026-01-01

chunks.title: SP 800-133 Rev. 3 (IPD): Recommendation for Cryptographic Key Generation
chunks.content:
Reference: NIST-SP-800-133r3-ipd
Title: SP 800-133 Rev. 3 (IPD): Recommendation for Cryptographic Key Generation
Description: NIST draft recommendation specifying methods for generating cryptographic keys. Rev. 3 adds ML-KEM-based symmetric key establishment, PQC signature algorithm support (ML-DSA), seed-expansion via SHAKE and DRBGs, and aligns randomness guidance with SP 800-90C. Public comment period closes June 16, 2026.
Type: NIST Special Publication | Status: Initial Public Draft
Authors: NIST; Quynh Dang; Dustin Moody; Andrew Regenscheid; Hamilton Silberg
Algorithm Family: Lattice-based; Hash-based; KEM
Security Levels: L1,L3,L5
Migration Urgency: High
Industries: All Industries
Region: US;PQC-REGION-GLOBAL
Published: 2026-04-17 | Updated: 2026-04-17

Main Topic: Guidance for generating cryptographic keys for use with approved algorithms. Rev. 3 integrates PQC key generation (ML-KEM, ML-DSA), introduces KEM-based symmetric key establishment, and expands seed-expansion methods via SHAKE and DRBGs. Aligns randomness guidance with SP 800-90C.
PQC Algorithms: ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204); seed-based deterministic key generation using SHAKE-128/256 and SP 800-90A DRBGs
Quantum Threats: Harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) risk mitigated by transitioning key generation to PQC algorithms; classical asymmetric key generation (RSA, ECDH) is quantum-vulnerable
Protocols: KEM-based key establishment; seed derivation for asymmetric key pairs; DRBG-based key generation
Infrastructure Layers: HSM firmware; cryptographic libraries; key management systems; PKCS#11 tokens
Standardization Bodies: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Compliance Frameworks: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM); FIPS 204 (ML-DSA); FIPS 186-5; SP 800-90A; SP 800-90B; SP 800-90C; SP 800-56C Rev. 2; SP 800-108 Rev. 1; FISMA 2014; OMB Circular A-130
Migration Timeline: Public comment period closes June 16, 2026; final publication expected late 2026; applicable to federal agencies under FISMA and OMB Circular A-130
Regions / Bodies: United States (federal); Global (advisory); NIST, U.S. Department of Commerce
Leaders: Quynh Dang (lead author); Dustin Moody (author); Andrew Regenscheid (author); Hamilton Silberg (author)
Related Algorithms: [ML-KEM-512](/algorithms?highlight=ml-kem-512), [ML-KEM-768](/algorithms?highlight=ml-kem-768), [ML-KEM-1024](/algorithms?highlight=ml-kem-1024)

chunks.content:
Reference: RFC-9155
Title: RFC 9155
Description: The MD5 and SHA-1 hashing algorithms are increasingly vulnerable to attack, and this document deprecates their use in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 digital signatures.  However, this document does not deprecate SHA-1 with Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC), as used in record protection.  This document updates RFC 5246.

Reference: RFC-6750
Title: RFC 6750
Description: This specification describes how to use bearer tokens in HTTP requests to access OAuth 2.0 protected resources.  Any party in possession of a bearer token (a "bearer") can use it to get access to the associated resources (without demonstrating possession of a cryptographic key).  To prevent misuse, bearer tokens need to be protected from disclosure in storage and in transport. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

chunks.title: RFC 9146
chunks.content:
Reference: RFC-9146
Title: RFC 9146

chunks.content:
Reference: FAEST-Round2-Spec
Title: FAEST: Fast AES-based Tight Signature (Round 2 Specification)
Description: AES-based MPC-in-the-Head signature using the VOLE-in-the-Head paradigm. Security reduces directly to AES — the most-studied symmetric cipher in existence — making FAEST the most conservative foundation among the MPCitH candidates. Smallest public and private keys in the contest (32 B each); signatures are kilobytes (FAEST-128f: 6,336 B). NIST selected it explicitly for the strength of its symmetric-primitive trust argument.

chunks.title: SDitH: Syndrome Decoding in the Head (Round 2 Specification)
chunks.content:
Reference: SDitH-Round2-Spec
Title: SDitH: Syndrome Decoding in the Head (Round 2 Specification)
Description: MPC-in-the-Head signature built on the syndrome decoding problem for random linear codes over finite fields — one of the most-studied hard problems in code-based cryptography, dating to McEliece (1978). Among the MPCitH candidates, only FAEST (AES-based) shares a comparably well-analysed security foundation. Tradeoff: typically slower than its MPCitH peers, though sizes are competitive when tuned.

chunks.title: UOV: Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (Round 2 Specification)
chunks.content:
Reference: UOV-Round2-Spec
Title: UOV: Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (Round 2 Specification)
Description: Original UOV construction by Kipnis-Patarin-Goubin (1999). Public key is a system of multivariate quadratic polynomials with the secret oil/vinegar partition hidden inside. Tiny 96 B signatures at NIST L1; large public key (~66 KB raw, ~1.2 KB compressed) and private key (~237 KB). 2025 Ran wedge attack pushed three of four parameter sets (uov-Ip, uov-III, uov-V) below their security targets; reparameterisation in odd-characteristic fields restores security.

chunks.content:
Reference: SNOVA-Round2-Spec
Title: SNOVA: Simple Noncommutative-ring UOV (Round 2 Specification)
Description: Most aggressive size optimisation in the multivariate family: combines a MAYO-like whipping structure with a noncommutative block-ring structure. SNOVA l=4 at NIST L1: pk=1,016 B, sk=48 B, sig=248 B. Hit hardest by the 2025 wedge attack — most original parameter sets broken, sometimes by a wide margin. Odd-characteristic reparameterisation proposed; resulting Category-1 sizes are smaller than FN-DSA. NIST IR 8528 notes SNOVA has 'not reached a stable form'.

Title: SQIsign: Compact Signatures from Quaternions and Isogenies (Round 2 v2.0 Specification)
Description: Isogeny-based signature scheme — the only post-quantum candidate built on supersingular elliptic-curve isogenies. Smallest combined public-key+signature of any PQC candidate by a wide margin: SQIsign-I (NIST L1) is pk=64 B, sig=177 B (up from 148 B in Round 1, traded for a 20× signing speedup). Round 2 redesign switched to higher-dimensional isogenies, simplifying the security analysis and dramatically improving performance. SQIsign avoids the auxiliary-torsion structure that enabled the 2022 SIKE break.

chunks.title: HAWK: Module Lattice Isomorphism Signature (Round 2 Specification)
chunks.content:
Reference: HAWK-Round2-Spec
Title: HAWK: Module Lattice Isomorphism Signature (Round 2 Specification)
Description: Lattice signature that eliminates FN-DSA's floating-point Gaussian-sampling pain — pure integer arithmetic on a rank-2 module lattice with a Gram matrix as the public key. Compact 555 B signatures at NIST L1 — smaller than both ML-DSA and FN-DSA — and dramatically easier to implement in constant time on constrained hardware. Security rests on newer assumptions: the Search Module Lattice Isomorphism Problem (smLIP) and the One-More-Shortest-Vector Problem (omSVP). NIST flagged these for further community analysis; Round 2 included a refined omSVP definition addressing a discrepancy found during evaluation.

chunks.content:
Reference: draft-reddy-lamps-x509-pq-commit
Title: X.509 Extensions for PQC Continuity
Description: Defines X.509 certificate extensions that allow a certificate authority or subscriber to embed a PQC Continuity commitment directly in a certificate. chunks.title: Circle's Post-Quantum Security Roadmap: Securing blockchains smart contracts and digital assets for the quantum era
chunks.content:
Reference: Circle-PQC-Roadmap-2026
Title: Circle's Post-Quantum Security Roadmap: Securing blockchains smart contracts and digital assets for the quantum era
Description: Three-phase PQC migration roadmap for Circle (USDC issuer) and the Arc blockchain. Catalogs seven quantum attack vectors on the full blockchain stack (at-rest forgery via EVM ecrecover; retroactive privacy loss; consensus disruption; history rewrite; P2P session compromise via libp2p/Noise; RPC interception; on-spend). Readiness phase: SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s on-chain precompile for smart-account signature verification; X-Wing hybrid KEM (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) for TLS 1.3 and encrypted memos; TEE-based private execution environment (AWS Nitro/SGX/TDX). Transition phase: dual-mode USDC smart contracts; post-quantum ecrecover override; multi-sig cold storage; encrypted mempool. Switch phase: full PQ validator signatures; account recovery (dual-key BIP-39 derivation; TEE-attested ZK proof; off-chain). Policy section covers quantum flag day regulatory implications for stranded USDC assets. Co-authored with Dan Boneh (Stanford).
Type: Research/Report | Status: Published
Authors: Circle; Stanford University (Dan Boneh)
Algorithm Family: Lattice; Hash-based; Hybrid
Security Levels: L1,L3
Migration Urgency: High
Industries: Finance; Blockchain; Digital Assets; DeFi

Published: 2026-05-30 | Updated: 2026-05-30

Protocols: TLS 1.3; HPKE; EVM; JSON-RPC; Noise; BIP 324; RLPx
Infrastructure Layers: Smart contracts; HSM; TEE; Cold storage; Backend infrastructure; Cloud service providers; Wallets
Standardization Bodies: NIST
Compliance Frameworks: NIST standards; AML/CFT; Sanctions; Unclaimed-property; Escheat; Estate; Court-order frameworks
Migration Timeline: Three-phase strategy: Readiness phase (assessing risk, SLH-DSA precompile, hybrid KEM); Transition phase (dual mode, hybrid signatures); Final phase (fully post-quantum switchover); 5-10 year window for regulatory guidance

chunks.title: Aerospace / Aviation — Satellite communication HNDL vulnerability: Military and commercial satellites h
chunks.content:
Industry: Aerospace / Aviation
Threat: Satellite communication HNDL vulnerability: Military and commercial satellites have 15-25 year operational lifespans. NSA CNSA 2.0 mandates PQC for all national security systems including satellite uplink/downlink — NSS equipment must phase out quantum-vulnerable algorithms by 2033 (CNSA 2.0 FAQ Dec 2024 sets December 31, 2030 for phasing out non-CNSA 2.0 equipment, mandatory CNSA 2.0 use by December 31, 2031, full NSS quantum resistance by 2033). Currently intercepted satellite communications are harvestable for future quantum decryption.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: Satellite uplink/downlink RSA/ECDSA, ground station TLS, inter-satellite link encryption
PQC Replacement: ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87 per CNSA 2.0, AES-256
Source: NSA CNSA 2.0 Cybersecurity Advisory

metadata.cryptoAtRisk: Satellite uplink/downlink RSA/ECDSA, ground station TLS, inter-satellite link encryption
metadata.pqcReplacement: ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87 per CNSA 2.0, AES-256

chunks.title: Aerospace / Aviation — While ICAO Assembly Resolution A41-19 addresses aviation cybersecurity, current
chunks.content:
Industry: Aerospace / Aviation
Threat: While ICAO Assembly Resolution A41-19 addresses aviation cybersecurity, current ADS-B transmissions remain unencrypted and unauthenticated, exposing the sector to immediate classical spoofing risks. The post-quantum threat emerges prospectively only if authenticated ADS-B is deployed using public-key cryptography. Consequently, migrating to post-quantum cryptography becomes essential to secure these future authenticated communications against quantum-enabled attacks.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: ADS-B (unencrypted), Mode S, ATC data links, ACARS messaging
PQC Replacement: Authenticated ADS-B with ML-DSA, quantum-safe ATC protocols
Source: ICAO Assembly Resolution A41-19

metadata.cryptoAtRisk: ADS-B (unencrypted), Mode S, ATC data links, ACARS messaging
metadata.pqcReplacement: Authenticated ADS-B with ML-DSA, quantum-safe ATC protocols

chunks.title: Automotive / Connected Vehicles — V2X PKI quantum transition: ISO/SAE 21434 (published August 2021) establishes cy
chunks.content:
Industry: Automotive / Connected Vehicles
Threat: V2X PKI quantum transition: ISO/SAE 21434 (published August 2021) establishes cybersecurity engineering requirements for road vehicles. V2X communications use ECDSA P-256 certificates per IEEE 1609.2. Vehicles have 12+ year lifecycles meaning 2026 production vehicles remain on roads through 2038+ when CRQCs may be operational.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: ECDSA P-256 V2X certificates, IEEE 1609.2 PKI, digital key infrastructure
PQC Replacement: ML-DSA V2X certificates, hybrid V2X authentication, FN-DSA for constrained ECUs
Source: ISO/SAE 21434 Road Vehicle Cybersecurity

metadata.cryptoAtRisk: ECDSA P-256 V2X certificates, IEEE 1609.2 PKI, digital key infrastructure
metadata.pqcReplacement: ML-DSA V2X certificates, hybrid V2X authentication, FN-DSA for constrained ECUs

chunks.title: Automotive / Connected Vehicles — Connected vehicle remote access quantum risk: SAE J3061 (2016, largely replaced
chunks.content:
Industry: Automotive / Connected Vehicles
Threat: Connected vehicle remote access quantum risk: SAE J3061 (2016, largely replaced in practice by ISO/SAE 21434) provided cybersecurity guidance for cyber-physical vehicle systems. Modern connected vehicles use TLS for OTA update channels, RSA for key management, and ECDSA for firmware signing. Vehicles must retain cryptographic agility for 15-20 year operational periods.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: RSA/ECDSA code signing, secure boot chains, ECU firmware verification
PQC Replacement: ML-DSA firmware signing, SLH-DSA for safety-critical ECUs, dual-signature verification
Source: SAE J3061 / ISO/SAE 21434 Vehicle Cybersecurity

chunks.title: Automotive / Connected Vehicles — UNECE WP.29 R155/R156 cybersecurity regulation gap: Mandatory for new vehicle ty
chunks.content:

Threat: UNECE WP.29 R155/R156 cybersecurity regulation gap: Mandatory for new vehicle type approvals in EU since July 2022 and extended to all new vehicles July 2024. Requires cybersecurity management systems and secure OTA updates but does not yet address post-quantum cryptography creating a future compliance gap.

Cryptography at Risk: TLS for telematics, RSA/ECDSA for OTA signing, connected car cloud API authentication

chunks.title: Automotive / Connected Vehicles — In-vehicle network security quantum exposure: ISO/SAE 21434 covers the full vehi
chunks.content:
Industry: Automotive / Connected Vehicles

chunks.title: Cloud Computing / Data Centers — FedRAMP High and Moderate authorized cloud services currently lack specific post
chunks.content:
Industry: Cloud Computing / Data Centers
Threat: FedRAMP High and Moderate authorized cloud services currently lack specific post-quantum cryptography requirements in their authorization packages. While OMB M-23-02 mandates federal agency CISOs to inventory cryptographic systems and develop migration plans, this compliance obligation flows to cloud providers through agency contracts rather than FedRAMP baseline controls. Consequently, certified providers processing government data face extended compliance runways without direct regulatory deadlines.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: Federal cloud TLS, FedRAMP-authorized encryption, cloud HSM FIPS modules
PQC Replacement: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) cloud implementations
Source: NIST IR 8547 / NIST SP 800-210

chunks.content:

Threat: Cloud HSM and key management PQC gap: NIST SP 800-210 defines access control for cloud systems but cloud-hosted HSMs and KMS services currently lack full PQC support. Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: Cloud HSM root keys, KMS key wrapping, tenant isolation keys, FIPS 140-3 modules

Quantum forgery of DNSSEC signatures enables DNS hijacking for any signed domain redirecting traffic to attacker-controlled servers. Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: RSASHA256 (RFC 6944), ECDSAP256SHA256/ECDSAP384SHA384 (RFC 6605), DNSSEC zone signing keys and key signing keys
PQC Replacement: ML-DSA or FN-DSA for compact DNSSEC signatures, hybrid DNS signing, TCP fallback for larger PQC signatures

As of 2025 54-59% of IPv4/IPv6 routes are covered by ROAs representing ~74% of global internet traffic. Quantum forgery of ROAs enables attackers to hijack arbitrary IP address prefixes globally redirecting internet traffic at scale. Post-quantum RPKI would increase data sizes from 1.2GB to 2.9-39.1GB depending on algorithm creating significant operational challenges.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: RSA-2048 ROA signatures, RPKI certificate hierarchy, BGP route validation
PQC Replacement: ML-DSA for ROA signing, hybrid RPKI certificates, bandwidth-optimized PQC for route validation
Source: APNIC / RIPE Labs RPKI Research

chunks.title: Cross-Industry — Quantum random number generation (QRNG) for PQC key security: PQC algorithm secu
chunks.content:
Industry: Cross-Industry
Threat: Quantum random number generation (QRNG) for PQC key security: PQC algorithm security depends on high-quality randomness for key generation. Classical PRNGs may contain algorithmic biases exploitable by sophisticated adversaries. QRNG uses quantum mechanical processes to generate theoretically unpredictable randomness. Quantinuum Quantum Origin was among the first software-delivered QRNGs to obtain NIST SP 800-90B entropy source validation. Commercial QRNG products from ID Quantique, Quside, and QNu Labs are available for HSM, IoT, and automotive integration. QRNG complements PQC by ensuring cryptographic keys are non-predictable from generation.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: Classical PRNGs with potential algorithmic bias, hardware RNG with insufficient entropy
PQC Replacement: NIST SP 800-90B validated QRNG, quantum entropy sources for HSM key generation, hybrid classical-quantum RNG
Source: NIST SP 800-90B / Quantinuum Quantum Origin

chunks.content:

Threat: Hydropower facilities face quantum exposure as many SCADA systems rely on TLS with RSA or ECDSA for remote management, supported by infrastructure lifespans of 20 to 30 years. Unlike the comprehensive NERC CIP standards for bulk electric systems, FERC’s cybersecurity mandate for hydropower is less codified, deriving primarily from Order 848 incident reporting requirements and general ratemaking authority rather than specific engineering guidelines. This regulatory gap leaves legacy cryptographic implementations vulnerable during the post-quantum transition.

chunks.content:

Threat: Wastewater treatment SCADA quantum vulnerability: Wastewater SCADA systems are architecturally distinct from drinking water treatment serving sewage pumping biosolids handling and effluent discharge control. EPA/CISA guidance (August 2024) classifies wastewater under essential services. Newer systems use OPC UA and DNP3 Secure Authentication with RSA/ECC key establishment. Quantum-enabled decryption of control commands could corrupt treatment processes releasing untreated sewage into waterways with environmental and public health catastrophe.

chunks.title: Critical Infrastructure — Critical infrastructure ICS/SCADA systems managing power grids, water treatment,
chunks.content:
Industry: Critical Infrastructure
Threat: Critical infrastructure ICS/SCADA systems managing power grids, water treatment, and pipelines rely on legacy protocols like Modbus and DNP3, often lacking native encryption. Where RSA or ECDSA is used for authentication, IEC 62443 defines security levels while delegating algorithm specifics to IEC 62351. This exposure matters because NERC CIP governs bulk electric systems, whereas pipeline cybersecurity falls under TSA Security Directives, creating distinct post-quantum migration challenges across sectors.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: All asymmetric cryptography across 16 CI sectors, sector-specific SCADA/ICS protocols, federal PKI
PQC Replacement: Sector-specific PQC migration roadmaps, FIPS 203/204/205 compliance, CISA ACDI deployment
Source: CISA Post-Quantum Cryptography Initiative / PPD-21

chunks.title: Critical Infrastructure — IEC 61850 substation automation relies on IEC 62351-6 symmetric HMAC-SHA-256 for
chunks.content:
Industry: Critical Infrastructure
Threat: IEC 61850 substation automation relies on IEC 62351-6 symmetric HMAC-SHA-256 for GOOSE and Sampled Values authentication, as sub-4ms latency requirements preclude per-message asymmetric signing. Consequently, RSA and ECDSA vulnerabilities are confined to IEC 62351-8 role-based access control and the station-level TLS/PKI hierarchy used for session establishment. This distinction isolates the quantum risk to certificate-based authentication rather than real-time protection relay messaging.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: IEC 62351-8 RBAC RSA/ECDSA, station TLS certificates, IEC 62351-6 HMAC keys (symmetric — distributed via quantum-vulnerable PKI), protection relay PKI
PQC Replacement: ML-KEM/ML-DSA per ECCG ACM v2.0, hybrid implementations, PQC-by-default for new systems by 2030

chunks.content:
Industry: Critical Infrastructure
Threat: Oil and gas pipeline operators rely on encrypted SCADA communications for remote monitoring and valve control, creating a critical dependency on current cryptographic standards. While TSA Security Directives and PHMSA regulations govern pipeline cybersecurity, the underlying Pipeline Management System security still utilizes TLS with RSA and ECDSA for operator authentication. This reliance on quantum-vulnerable algorithms poses a significant risk to infrastructure integrity during the post-quantum transition.

chunks.title: Cross-Industry — NIST IR 8547 establishes the deprecation trajectory for quantum-vulnerable publi
chunks.content:
Industry: Cross-Industry
Threat: NIST IR 8547 establishes the deprecation trajectory for quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms, with RSA-2048 and ECDSA/ECDH-P-256 expected to be disallowed for US federal use post-2030 or 2035. This timeline is distinct from NIST SP 800-131A Rev 2, which governs key-length transitions for currently approved algorithms. Organizations must complete post-quantum cryptography migration before these classical algorithms are prohibited.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: AES-128, 3DES (112-bit effective), RC4, DES, legacy symmetric ciphers with key sizes < 256 bits
PQC Replacement: AES-256, ChaCha20-Poly1305, migration to 256-bit symmetric keys for all long-term data confidentiality
Source: NIST IR 8547 (IPD Nov 2024) + SP 800-131A Rev 2

chunks.title: Cross-Industry — Hash function collision resistance halved by quantum algorithms: Grover's algori
chunks.content:
Industry: Cross-Industry
Threat: Hash function collision resistance halved by quantum algorithms: Grover's algorithm reduces the pre-image resistance of SHA-256 from 256-bit to ~128-bit effective security. Quantum collision attacks (Brassard-Høyer-Tapp / BHT) reduce SHA-256 collision resistance from 128-bit to ~85-bit effective security. SHA-1 (already classically broken) is fully negligible post-CRQC. Quantum security of a hash for collision/preimage is determined by output size: SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-384, and SHA3-512 (larger outputs) provide substantially improved quantum margins; SHA3-256 has the same 256-bit output as SHA-256 and therefore equivalent quantum resistance. HMAC-SHA-256 is less affected due to keying.
Criticality: Medium
Cryptography at Risk: SHA-1 (broken classically), SHA-256 collision resistance, MD5, RIPEMD-160, Merkle trees using SHA-256
PQC Replacement: SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-256, SHA3-512 for collision-sensitive applications; SLH-DSA hash chains use SHA-256/SHA-512 by design
Source: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 6 / NIST IR 8545

metadata.pqcReplacement: SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-256, SHA3-512 for collision-sensitive applications; SLH-DSA hash chains use SHA-256/SHA-512 by design

chunks.title: Cross-Industry — NIST SP 800-90A Rev 1 (2015) removed Dual_EC_DRBG, leaving CTR_DRBG and HMAC_DRB
chunks.content:
Industry: Cross-Industry
Threat: NIST SP 800-90A Rev 1 (2015) removed Dual_EC_DRBG, leaving CTR_DRBG and HMAC_DRBG as the approved standards. When configured with 256-bit security parameters, these DRBGs retain approximately 128-bit effective quantum security against Grover’s algorithm. This level of resistance exceeds practical CRQC thresholds, meaning the quantum risk for properly parameterized symmetric RNGs is largely mitigated.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: DRBG implementations using <256-bit symmetric parameters; entropy source quality (independent of quantum)
PQC Replacement: NIST SP 800-90A DRBG (CTR_DRBG with AES-256), NIST SP 800-90B validated hardware entropy, QRNG for HSM seeding
Source: NIST SP 800-90A Rev 1 / NIST SP 800-90B

metadata.pqcReplacement: NIST SP 800-90A DRBG (CTR_DRBG with AES-256), NIST SP 800-90B validated hardware entropy, QRNG for HSM seeding

chunks.title: Cross-Industry — Side-channel attacks on post-quantum implementations: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DS
chunks.content:
Industry: Cross-Industry
Threat: Side-channel attacks on post-quantum implementations: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA software implementations that are not constant-time are vulnerable to timing analysis, cache-timing attacks, and power side-channels that can expose private key material without breaking the underlying mathematical hardness assumption. FALCON (FN-DSA) requires Gaussian sampling with tight timing constraints especially vulnerable to FPA cache timing. FIPS 140-3 Derived Test Requirements require constant-time implementations for all sensitive cryptographic operations. Production deployments must use validated implementations (OpenSSL 3.5+, AWS-LC, BoringSSL) or hardware accelerators with demonstrated side-channel resistance.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: Naive ML-KEM/ML-DSA implementations without constant-time guarantees, FN-DSA Gaussian sampler timing leakage, SLH-DSA WOTS+ chain computation timing
PQC Replacement: Constant-time PQC implementations per FIPS 140-3 DTR, FIPS 140-3 Level 3+ HSMs, hardware accelerators (NPCM, Arm CryptoCell-713 with PQC extensions)
Source: NIST FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance / TCHES 2024

metadata.pqcReplacement: Constant-time PQC implementations per FIPS 140-3 DTR, FIPS 140-3 Level 3+ HSMs, hardware accelerators (NPCM, Arm CryptoCell-713 with PQC extensions)

chunks.title: Cross-Industry — Stateful hash-based signatures defined in NIST SP 800-208 offer quantum-resistan
chunks.content:
Industry: Cross-Industry
Threat: Stateful hash-based signatures defined in NIST SP 800-208 offer quantum-resistant security for IoT firmware updates where private key state can be maintained. LMS and HSS are preferred for one-time signing scenarios, representing a viable migration path for this specific subset of IoT use cases. This approach aligns with broader IoT cybersecurity guidance found in NIST SP 800-213 and the NISTIR 8259 series.
Criticality: Medium
Cryptography at Risk: ML-KEM-512 and ML-DSA-44 if classical BKZ preprocessing improves substantially; lattice-based schemes broadly under quantum sieving improvements
PQC Replacement: Use ML-KEM-1024/ML-DSA-87 for highest-value data; monitor NIST IR 8545 updates and NIST PQC standardization announcements; maintain cryptographic agility for algorithm migration
Source: NIST SP 800-208 + NIST SP 800-213

chunks.title: Hardware Security Modules — Fault injection attacks on PQC hardware implementations: Hardware Security Modul
chunks.content:
Industry: Hardware Security Modules
Threat: Fault injection attacks on PQC hardware implementations: Hardware Security Modules implementing ML-KEM and ML-DSA are susceptible to differential fault analysis (DFA) and laser fault injection (LFI) attacks that deliberately induce computation errors to leak secret key material. FN-DSA (FALCON) is particularly sensitive: a single fault during NTRU key generation can expose the secret polynomial. FIPS 140-3 Level 3 requires physical tamper resistance and active response mechanisms. Level 4 requires full environmental protection. Current production HSMs (Thales Luna, Entrust nShield, Utimaco) with PQC support must demonstrate fault countermeasures including redundant computation, error detection codes, and physical tamper response per FIPS 140-3 requirements.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: ML-KEM private key generation in HSMs without fault countermeasures, FN-DSA (FALCON) secret polynomial, ML-DSA private key during signing without redundant computation
PQC Replacement: FIPS 140-3 Level 3+ HSMs with validated PQC implementations, physical tamper response, redundant computation verification, and CMVP-validated algorithm testing
Source: NIST FIPS 140-3 Physical Security Requirements / IACR PQC fault attack research
Related Compliance: [PKCS#11 v3.2 (PQC HSM Interface)](/compliance?tab=standards&q=PKCS%2311%20v3.2%20(PQC%20HSM%20Interface))

metadata.pqcReplacement: FIPS 140-3 Level 3+ HSMs with validated PQC implementations, physical tamper response, redundant computation verification, and CMVP-validated algorithm testing

chunks.title: Internet of Things (IoT) — NIST SP 800-213 and NISTIR 8259A/B establish the cybersecurity feature catalog a
chunks.content:
Industry: Internet of Things (IoT)
Threat: NIST SP 800-213 and NISTIR 8259A/B establish the cybersecurity feature catalog and core cryptographic capabilities for IoT devices. However, current IoT guidance does not mandate post-quantum cryptography, creating a migration gap. Consequently, NIST IR 8547 serves as the applicable cross-cutting reference for planning IoT cryptographic transitions to address this vulnerability.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: TLS 1.3 with ML-KEM on Cortex-M0/M3 devices, SLH-DSA signature verification on 8-bit MCUs, code signing verification on embedded Class 1 devices, IKEv2 with PQC on constrained network equipment
PQC Replacement: NIST SP 800-232 Ascon (AEAD + hash) for symmetric operations, FN-DSA (FALCON-512) for constrained signatures, hardware PQC accelerators, device class upgrade strategy for Class 1 → Class 2+ migration
Source: NIST SP 800-213 + NISTIR 8259A

chunks.title: Telecommunications — Australian telecommunications providers operating national carrier-grade infrast
chunks.content:
Industry: Telecommunications
Threat: Australian telecommunications providers operating national carrier-grade infrastructure are regulated under the Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 and the Critical Infrastructure Risk Management Program Rules 2023, administered by the Department of Home Affairs. These entities must maintain robust risk management programs to protect communications secured by RSA and ECDSA certificates. This regulatory framework highlights the urgent need for post-quantum migration to safeguard critical infrastructure against emerging quantum threats.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: NBN backhaul TLS/IPsec, mobile network signalling (SS7/Diameter), carrier BGP authentication, lawful intercept systems
PQC Replacement: ML-KEM-1024 for IPsec/TLS key exchange, ML-DSA-87 for BGP route authentication; SOCI Act critical infrastructure obligations require 2030 compliance
Source: SOCI Act 2018 + CIRMP Rules 2023

chunks.title: IT Industry / Software — AI-assisted cryptanalysis acceleration: Research published 2024–2025 explores wh
chunks.content:
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Threat: AI-assisted cryptanalysis acceleration: Research published 2024–2025 explores whether machine learning heuristics can guide lattice reduction algorithms (BKZ block selection, basis pruning) and automate side-channel analysis against ML-KEM and ML-DSA implementations. No published peer-reviewed result has demonstrated a meaningful reduction in security against standardized ML-KEM/ML-DSA parameter sets, but the active research direction warrants ongoing monitoring of cryptanalytic frontier.
Criticality: High
Cryptography at Risk: ML-KEM-512 (NIST Level 1), ML-DSA-44, SLH-DSA-128
PQC Replacement: ML-KEM-768/1024 (higher security margins), constant-time implementations, hardware PQC accelerators
Source: IACR ePrint / NIST PQC Security Analysis

chunks.title: Hardware Security Modules — PKCS#11 v3.2 remains a Committee Specification Draft as of April 2025, with the
chunks.content:
Industry: Hardware Security Modules
Threat: PKCS#11 v3.2 remains a Committee Specification Draft as of April 2025, with the approved standard still being v3.1. Consequently, legacy v2.40 deployments cannot support post-quantum algorithms without middleware updates, and HSM vendors must certify new firmware implementing v3.2 mechanisms before customers can migrate. This gap delays the integration of ML-KEM and ML-DSA into existing cryptographic infrastructure.
Criticality: Critical
Cryptography at Risk: All RSA/ECDSA keys stored in HSMs with pre-2024 firmware; PKCS#11 v2.x buffer limits
PQC Replacement: HSM firmware upgrade to PKCS#11 v3.2 with PQC buffer support; hardware replacement if firmware upgrade not available
Source: PKCS#11 v3.2 Specification / NIST SP 800-227
Related Compliance: [PKCS#11 v3.2 (PQC HSM Interface)](/compliance?tab=standards&q=PKCS%2311%20v3.2%20(PQC%20HSM%20Interface))

chunks.title: NIST
chunks.content:
Framework: NIST
Description: National Institute of Standards and Technology — US federal agency that standardized the first PQC algorithms
Industries: 92;52;54;62;22
Countries: US
Requires PQC: yes
Deadline: Ongoing
Enforcement Body: NIST
Notes: NIST's PQC Standardization Project (launched 2016) selected ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) as the first post-quantum standards, published August 2024. FN-DSA (FIPS 206) published March 2025. NIST IR 8547 defines the transition timeline: deprecate 112-bit classical asymmetric by 2030, disallow by 2035. NIST also runs CMVP (module validation) and CAVP (algorithm validation) programs that enforce these standards globally.
