Q: What is the primary stated reason South Korea and China are developing national PQC standards independent of NIST's FIPS 203/204/205?
  A) NIST standards have known mathematical weaknesses that only Asian researchers discovered
  B) Domestic cryptographic sovereignty — ensuring national algorithms are not dependent on foreign standards for critical infrastructure
  C) NIST standards are not performance-optimized for Asian hardware architectures
  D) Both countries plan to replace NIST standards globally by 2030
Answer: B
Explanation: Both South Korea (KpqC) and China (NGCC/ICCS) frame their national PQC programs primarily around cryptographic sovereignty: ensuring that algorithms protecting national critical infrastructure are designed, analyzed, and standardized domestically, without reliance on US government processes. This mirrors longstanding patterns (China's SM2/SM3/SM4 replacing RSA/SHA/AES for domestic use; South Korea's ARIA/SEED). These national standards typically coexist with FIPS standards in international contexts but are mandated for government systems.

chunks.title: Quiz: compliance
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: compliance

Q: What is China's NGCC program (Next-Generation Commercial Cryptography), and which body oversees its PQC standardization?
  A) A NIST-aligned adoption program run by China's MIIT; standards mirror FIPS 203/204/205
  B) An independent national PQC standardization program run by OSCCA/ICCS; selecting domestic algorithms with a goal of 2030 national migration
  C) A joint research initiative between China and the EU for hybrid PQC standards
  D) A military-only cryptography program with no commercial implications
Answer: B
Explanation: China's Next-Generation Commercial Cryptography (NGCC) program is run by the Office of the State Commercial Cryptography Administration (OSCCA) in coordination with ICCS (Institute of Commercial Cryptography Standardization). The program issued a call for PQC algorithm proposals in 2024, targeting algorithms distinct from US NIST selections. China's existing commercial cryptography ecosystem (SM2/SM3/SM4) provides a template: separate domestic standards for government and regulated industries, with international standards permitted in some contexts. The NGCC targets national migration by approximately 2030.

chunks.title: Quiz: compliance
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: compliance

Q: By what date must Canadian federal government departments submit their initial PQC migration plans under CCCS guidance ITSM.40.001?
  A) January 2025
  B) April 2026
  C) December 2027
  D) October 2030
Answer: B
Explanation: The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS) published ITSM.40.001 (PQC Migration Roadmap) in June 2025, requiring federal departments to submit initial PQC migration plans by April 2026. The roadmap mandates that high-priority systems complete PQC migration by 2030 and all federal systems by 2033. This aligns with the broader Five Eyes coordination on PQC timelines, though Canada's April 2026 planning deadline is one of the most near-term compliance milestones globally.

Q: True or False: Canada's TBS Security Policy Implementation Notice (SPIN) on PQC became effective in October 2025, making PQC migration planning mandatory for federal institutions.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat (TBS) issued a Security Policy Implementation Notice (SPIN) on PQC that became effective October 9, 2025. This SPIN makes PQC migration planning a formal security policy requirement for all federal institutions — not merely guidance. Combined with ITSM.40.001's April 2026 planning deadline, Canadian federal agencies face both policy mandates and concrete milestones for PQC transition.

chunks.title: Quiz: compliance
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: compliance

Q: Australia's ASD Information Security Manual (ISM) December 2024 update sets requirements for critical systems. Which PQC algorithms are mandated for new systems by 2030?
  A) ML-KEM-512 and ML-DSA-44 (NIST Level 1)
  B) ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 (NIST Level 5)
  C) Only SLH-DSA-SHA2-256s for signatures; ML-KEM-768 for key exchange
  D) FrodoKEM-1344 and FN-DSA-1024 for maximum security
Answer: B
Explanation: Australia's ASD ISM December 2024 update mandates that new systems protecting sensitive information must use ML-KEM-1024 (key encapsulation) and ML-DSA-87 (digital signatures) — both at NIST Security Level 5 — by 2030. This is among the most conservative algorithm selections globally, requiring the highest security tier rather than Level 3. Existing systems have until 2030 for critical infrastructure and 2033 for all government systems, consistent with Five Eyes coordination.

chunks.title: Quiz: compliance
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: compliance

Q: Which Australian government body published the December 2024 ISM update mandating PQC requirements, and what is its relationship to the Five Eyes alliance?
  A) ASIO (Australian Security Intelligence Organisation); independent from Five Eyes
  B) ASD (Australian Signals Directorate); coordinates PQC guidance with NSA, GCHQ, NCSC-CA, and GCSB through Five Eyes
  C) ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre); operates independently of intelligence agencies
  D) AUSTRAC (financial intelligence); focused solely on financial sector PQC
Answer: B
Explanation: The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD), through its Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) arm, published the ISM update. ASD is Australia's national signals intelligence and cybersecurity agency and is a full member of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance (US NSA, UK GCHQ, Canadian CCCS/CSE, New Zealand GCSB, Australian ASD). Five Eyes members coordinate on PQC timelines and algorithm selections, which is why Australia's ML-KEM-1024/ML-DSA-87 mandate, Canada's ITSM.40.001, and US CNSA 2.0 are closely aligned in scope and timeline.

chunks.title: Quiz: compliance
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: compliance

Q: Which of the following statements about KpqC algorithm selection are correct? (Select all that apply)
  A) HAETAE is the primary signature algorithm — based on module lattices
  B) AIMer uses MPC-in-the-head (symmetric-key-based) design — different hardness from lattice
  C) SMAUG-T is the KEM winner — based on module lattices (MLWE/MLWR)
  D) NTRU+ replaces ML-KEM in all international contexts including TLS
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: Three statements are correct: (a) HAETAE is the KpqC signature winner, based on module lattices with distinct parameter choices from ML-DSA; (b) AIMer uses MPC-in-the-head design based on symmetric primitives — a mathematically distinct approach providing diversity; (c) SMAUG-T is the primary KpqC KEM, based on module learning with errors/rounding. Statement (d) is false: NTRU+ is a KpqC alternative KEM candidate, not a global replacement for ML-KEM. KpqC algorithms are mandated for Korean domestic systems, not international protocols.

chunks.title: Quiz: compliance
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: compliance

Q: An organization operates in both South Korea and the United States, handling government contracts in both countries. What PQC deployment strategy is most appropriate for 2025–2030?
  A) Deploy only NIST FIPS 203/204/205 globally — Korean KpqC standards can be ignored since they are not yet finalized
  B) Deploy only KpqC algorithms in Korea and FIPS 203/204/205 in the US — using separate cryptographic infrastructure
  C) Deploy FIPS 203/204/205 as the primary PQC layer globally with crypto-agile architecture ready to add KpqC algorithms for Korean government systems when mandated in 2029
  D) Wait until 2028 when both standards are finalized before beginning any PQC transition
Answer: C
Explanation: The correct approach is crypto-agile deployment: implement FIPS 203/204/205 now (already standardized, required by US federal contracts) while building the infrastructure to layer in KpqC algorithms for Korean government systems when mandated (~2029). A crypto-agile architecture (abstract key negotiation, algorithm registries, CBOM tracking) makes this addition straightforward. Deploying entirely separate infrastructure per country is operationally costly. Waiting until 2028 violates US CNSA 2.0 requirements and misses the NIST-mandated 2030 deadline for many system types.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: Which hybrid key exchange combination is already deployed in major web browsers?
  A) RSA-4096 + ML-KEM-512
  B) X25519 + ML-KEM-768 (X25519MLKEM768)
  C) P-521 + FrodoKEM-1344
  D) DH-2048 + HQC-256
Answer: B
Explanation: X25519MLKEM768 combines classical X25519 (ECDH) with ML-KEM-768 (NIST Level 3) for hybrid key exchange. It is already deployed in Chrome, Firefox, and other major browsers for TLS 1.3 connections.

Q: Which RFC defines the use of multiple key exchanges in IKEv2 (IPsec)?
  A) RFC 8446
  B) RFC 9370
  C) RFC 9629
  D) RFC 8391
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9370 defines support for multiple key exchanges in IKEv2, enabling hybrid PQC key exchange (e.g., ML-KEM combined with classical ECDH) for IPsec VPN tunnels.

Q: Which RFC defines the use of KEMs in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)?
  A) RFC 9370
  B) RFC 9629
  C) RFC 8391
  D) RFC 7748
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9629 defines the use of Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) in CMS, enabling PQC key exchange for S/MIME email encryption and other CMS-based applications.

Q: How is PQC being integrated into 5G authentication?
  A) By replacing the entire 5G protocol stack
  B) Through PQC upgrades to 5G-AKA authentication and SUCI subscriber identity protection
  C) 5G already uses PQC by default
  D) PQC is not applicable to 5G networks
Answer: B
Explanation: 5G security relies on 3GPP authentication protocols (5G-AKA) and SUCI (Subscriber Concealed Identifier) for subscriber identity protection. These protocols use RSA/ECDSA today and are being upgraded to support PQC algorithms, particularly for protecting the subscriber concealment mechanism.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: True or False: The Signal messaging protocol has already adopted post-quantum cryptography.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Signal upgraded its protocol to include PQXDH (Post-Quantum Extended Diffie-Hellman) using CRYSTALS-ML-KEM (now standardized as ML-KEM) for quantum-resistant key agreement, making it one of the first major messaging platforms to adopt PQC.

Q: Which RFC defines the use of ML-DSA signatures in CMS for email and document signing?
  A) RFC 9629
  B) RFC 9882
  C) RFC 9370
  D) RFC 8032
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9882 defines the use of ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) in Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) for S/MIME email signing and other document signature applications.

Q: What is the primary challenge of integrating PQC into TLS compared to classical algorithms?
  A) PQC algorithms are too slow for real-time connections
  B) Larger key and ciphertext sizes increase handshake overhead
  C) TLS does not support algorithm negotiation
  D) PQC requires a completely new protocol version
Answer: B
Explanation: PQC algorithms generally have larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures than classical algorithms. For example, ML-KEM-768 public keys are ~1.2KB vs ~32 bytes for X25519. This increases TLS handshake size and can cause issues with network MTU limits and packet fragmentation.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: Which protocols have published RFCs or drafts for PQC integration? (Select all that apply)
  A) IKEv2 / IPsec (RFC 9370)
  B) CMS / S/MIME (RFC 9629, 9882)
  C) DNS (DNSSEC)
  D) OpenPGP
Answer: A|B|D
Explanation: IKEv2 (RFC 9370), CMS/S/MIME (RFC 9629 for KEMs, RFC 9882 for ML-DSA), and OpenPGP all have published or draft specifications for PQC integration. DNSSEC PQC integration remains a significant challenge due to DNS packet size constraints.

Q: Which version of OpenSSL first included full PQC algorithm support (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)?
  A) OpenSSL 1.1.1
  B) OpenSSL 3.0
  C) OpenSSL 3.5
  D) OpenSSL 4.0
Answer: C
Explanation: OpenSSL 3.5, released in April 2025, was the first version with full PQC support including ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange. Earlier versions required external providers (like the OQS provider) for PQC support.

Q: In the context of PQC protocol integration, what is a "composite" certificate?
  A) A certificate signed by multiple certificate authorities
  B) A certificate containing both classical and PQC public keys and signatures
  C) A certificate that expires and renews automatically
  D) A certificate used exclusively for testing
Answer: B
Explanation: A composite certificate contains both classical (e.g., RSA/ECDSA) and PQC (e.g., ML-DSA) public keys and signatures. This enables hybrid trust during the transition period — verifiers that support PQC use the quantum-safe signature, while legacy systems fall back to the classical one.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: What does SUCI protect in 5G networks?
  A) Base station locations
  B) Subscriber identity — preventing IMSI-catching attacks
  C) Network bandwidth
  D) Billing records
Answer: B
Explanation: SUCI (Subscriber Concealed Identifier) protects subscriber identity in 5G networks by encrypting the SUPI (Subscriber Permanent Identifier). This prevents IMSI-catching attacks where adversaries track users by intercepting their identity. SUCI currently uses ECIES with P-256.

Q: In TLS 1.3, which message carries the server's public key share during the handshake?
  A) ClientHello
  B) ServerHello
  C) Certificate
  D) EncryptedExtensions
Answer: B
Explanation: In TLS 1.3, the ServerHello message carries the server's key share (public key for key exchange). With PQC hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768), this message is larger due to the ML-KEM-768 public key (~1.2KB).

Q: What is the GSMA Post-Quantum Telco Taskforce and when was it established?
  A) A 3GPP working group established in 2024
  B) An industry taskforce established September 2022 to guide telecom PQC migration
  C) A government mandate from the EU for telecom companies
  D) A quantum computing vendor consortium
Answer: B
Explanation: The GSMA Post-Quantum Telco Taskforce was established in September 2022 to guide the telecom industry's PQC migration. It published PQ.03 v2.0 (telecom use cases) in October 2024 and provides guidance for 5G/6G quantum-safe security.

Q: True or False: Chrome and Firefox have already shipped support for hybrid PQC key exchange (X25519+ML-KEM-768) in TLS.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Both Chrome and Firefox have shipped X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange for TLS 1.3 connections. This is one of the earliest large-scale PQC deployments, protecting billions of web connections.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: Why is DNSSEC PQC integration particularly challenging compared to other protocols?
  A) DNS servers cannot be upgraded
  B) PQC signatures are too large for DNS UDP packet size limits (512 bytes / 4096 bytes with EDNS)
  C) DNS does not use cryptography
  D) DNSSEC is being deprecated in favor of DNS-over-HTTPS
Answer: B
Explanation: DNSSEC PQC integration faces severe packet size constraints. DNS traditionally uses UDP with 512-byte limits (4096 with EDNS). PQC signatures (ML-DSA: 2.4-4.6KB, SLH-DSA: 7.8-16KB) can exceed these limits, requiring protocol-level solutions like DNS over TCP or signature compression.

Q: What protocol does RFC 9370 add PQC support to?
  A) TLS 1.3
  B) IKEv2 (IPsec VPN)
  C) SSH
  D) SMTP
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9370 defines support for multiple key exchanges in IKEv2, the key management protocol for IPsec VPN tunnels. This enables hybrid PQC key exchange combining classical ECDH with ML-KEM for quantum-safe VPN connections.

Q: Which 5G authentication protocol is being upgraded for PQC resistance?
  A) GSM A5 cipher
  B) 5G-AKA (Authentication and Key Agreement)
  C) SMS-based OTP
  D) Wi-Fi WPA3
Answer: B
Explanation: 5G-AKA (Authentication and Key Agreement) is the primary authentication protocol in 5G networks (3GPP TS 33.501). It currently uses ECDSA/RSA and is being upgraded to support PQC algorithms for quantum-resistant network authentication.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: Which of the following 5G security components use quantum-vulnerable cryptography? (Select all that apply)
  A) SUCI subscriber identity protection (ECIES P-256)
  B) N2/N3 interface IPsec tunnels
  C) Physical cell tower hardware
  D) SIM/eSIM PKI authentication (RSA-2048/ECDSA P-256)
Answer: A|B|D
Explanation: SUCI uses ECIES with P-256, N2/N3 interfaces use IPsec with quantum-vulnerable key exchange, and SIM/eSIM cards rely on RSA-2048/ECDSA P-256 PKI. Physical cell tower hardware itself is not a cryptographic component vulnerable to quantum attacks.

Q: What does OpenSSL 3.5 (released April 2025) include for PQC?
  A) Only ML-KEM support
  B) Full PQC support: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and X25519MLKEM768 hybrid
  C) Only experimental PQC via external providers
  D) No PQC support — PQC requires OpenSSL 4.0
Answer: B
Explanation: OpenSSL 3.5 was a landmark release with full built-in PQC support: ML-KEM for key exchange, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for signatures, and the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange as the default TLS negotiation option.

Q: What is the Samsung/Thales ML-KEM embedded secure element breakthrough from January 2026?
  A) A quantum computer chip for smartphones
  B) The first commercial PQC implementation for IoT embedded secure elements
  C) A new PQC algorithm proposal
  D) A quantum key distribution system for mobile devices
Answer: B
Explanation: Samsung and Thales achieved the first commercial PQC implementation using ML-KEM in an embedded secure element (January 2026). This breakthrough enables quantum-safe security for IoT devices, smart cards, and constrained environments.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: What does RFC 9882 standardize?
  A) ML-KEM key encapsulation in TLS 1.3
  B) ML-DSA signatures in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
  C) A new certificate format for PQC public keys
  D) SLH-DSA signatures for code signing
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9882 (published 2025) defines how to use ML-DSA (FIPS 204) digital signatures within CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax, RFC 5652). CMS is the underlying structure for S/MIME email signing, document signing (PDF, XML), timestamping responses, and PKCS#7/PKCS#12 containers. RFC 9882 enables these widely-deployed applications to use NIST's standardized lattice signature scheme, complementing RFC 9629 which covers ML-KEM in CMS for key encapsulation.

Q: An organization needs to send PQC-signed S/MIME emails. Which RFC combination provides the complete CMS-based PQC signing and encryption capability?
  A) RFC 9882 (ML-DSA signing) + RFC 9629 (ML-KEM encryption) in CMS
  B) RFC 9794 (hybrid terminology) + RFC 9802 (HSS/XMSS in X.509)
  C) FIPS 203 alone is sufficient for both signing and encryption in S/MIME
  D) RFC 9814 (SLH-DSA in CMS) is the only approved S/MIME PQC option
Answer: A
Explanation: Full PQC S/MIME capability requires two RFCs: RFC 9882 (ML-DSA in CMS) for digital signatures and RFC 9629 (ML-KEM in CMS) for key encapsulation/encryption. RFC 9629 was published in 2024 and covers ML-KEM-512/768/1024 in CMS EnvelopedData. RFC 9882 covers ML-DSA-44/65/87 in CMS SignedData. Together they enable PQC-protected email that can be signed (integrity/authentication) and encrypted (confidentiality) using NIST-standardized algorithms within existing S/MIME infrastructure.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: What does RFC 9794 standardize for PQC hybrid cryptography?
  A) A new hybrid encryption algorithm combining ML-KEM and ML-DSA
  B) Terminology and naming conventions for post-quantum/traditional (PQ/T) hybrid cryptographic schemes
  C) A key derivation function for combining classical and PQC shared secrets
  D) Certificate extensions for indicating hybrid algorithm support
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9794 (published 2025) standardizes the terminology for hybrid cryptographic schemes that combine post-quantum (PQ) algorithms with traditional (T) classical algorithms. It defines terms like 'PQ/T hybrid scheme,' 'composite,' 'parallel,' and 'non-composite' combinations. This shared vocabulary is essential for interoperability: when RFCs, FIPS documents, and vendor documentation use the same terms consistently, organizations can correctly evaluate whether they have deployed the hybrid approach their security policy requires.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: According to RFC 9794 terminology, what is the difference between a 'composite' PQ/T hybrid scheme and a 'non-composite parallel' scheme?
  A) Composite schemes use a single algorithm object containing both PQ and classical components; non-composite parallel schemes keep them as separate independent objects
  B) Composite schemes are slower; non-composite parallel schemes are always faster
  C) Composite schemes are only for KEMs; non-composite parallel schemes are only for signatures
  D) RFC 9794 does not distinguish between composite and parallel — these terms are synonymous
Answer: A
Explanation: RFC 9794 defines: a 'composite' scheme is one where the PQ and classical algorithms are bundled into a single cryptographic object (one key, one ciphertext/signature) that combines both — neither component is independently meaningful for security. A 'non-composite parallel' scheme transmits both components independently (e.g., separate PQ and classical signatures in a TLS extension) but requires both to verify. X25519MLKEM768 (used in TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange) is a non-composite parallel KEM: the classical X25519 shared secret and the ML-KEM-768 shared secret are combined via a KDF, but transmitted as separate values.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: What does RFC 9810 standardize for PQC key transport?
  A) ML-KEM in TLS 1.3 certificate-based key exchange
  B) Updates to CMP (Certificate Management Protocol) to support KEM-based key transport for certificate enrollment
  C) A new OID registry for all NIST PQC algorithms
  D) SLH-DSA signing of OCSP responses
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9810 (published 2025) updates the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP, RFC 4210) to support KEM-based key transport. CMP is widely used by enterprise PKI for automated certificate enrollment, renewal, and revocation (used by many CA software products). Before RFC 9810, CMP key transport assumed RSA or Diffie-Hellman; RFC 9810 adds support for ML-KEM to protect the key transport phase of certificate issuance — closing a critical gap in PQC-safe PKI automation.

Q: What does RFC 9814 standardize?
  A) ML-DSA signatures in TLS 1.3 certificate authentication
  B) SLH-DSA (FIPS 205 / SLH-DSA) signatures in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
  C) HQC key encapsulation in CMS
  D) FN-DSA (FALCON) signatures in S/MIME
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9814 (published 2025) defines how to use SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, FIPS 205) within CMS. SLH-DSA is the hash-based alternative to lattice signatures: its security relies only on hash function properties, providing a maximally conservative option where lattice assumptions are unacceptable. RFC 9814 enables SLH-DSA in document signing, timestamping, and S/MIME contexts — complementing RFC 9882 (ML-DSA in CMS) and giving implementers algorithm choice within the same CMS framework.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: True or False: RFC 9794 hybrid terminology applies exclusively to KEMs — PQC signature schemes do not have 'composite' or 'parallel' hybrid variants.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. RFC 9794 terminology applies to both KEMs and signature schemes. Hybrid signature schemes can be 'composite' (a single combined signature object verifiable only as a unit) or 'non-composite parallel' (two independent signatures — e.g., both ML-DSA and RSA — transmitted together, each independently verifiable). Composite signature OIDs are being standardized through IETF LAMPS working group drafts. Non-composite parallel signatures appear in protocols like TLS where the PQ and classical signatures are sent in separate extensions.

chunks.title: Quiz: protocol-integration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: protocol-integration

Q: A PKI engineer must design certificate enrollment for a new enterprise CA that will be PQC-safe. Which combination of RFCs covers the complete enrollment and signing stack?
  A) RFC 9882 (ML-DSA in CMS) + RFC 9794 (hybrid terminology)
  B) RFC 9810 (CMP KEM transport for enrollment) + RFC 9882 (ML-DSA in CMS for signed certificates) + RFC 9802 (HSS/XMSS in X.509 for long-lived CA keys)
  C) RFC 9629 (ML-KEM in CMS) + RFC 9814 (SLH-DSA in CMS) alone are sufficient
  D) Only FIPS 203/204/205 are required — no IETF RFCs are needed
Answer: B
Explanation: A complete PQC-safe PKI enrollment stack requires: RFC 9810 for CMP-based automated certificate enrollment using ML-KEM key transport (replacing RSA key transport); RFC 9882 for ML-DSA signatures on issued end-entity certificates and CA certificates; RFC 9802 for long-lived CA root/intermediate keys using HSS or XMSS (stateful hash-based, recommended by CNSA 2.0 for long-lived CA keys). FIPS documents define the algorithms but not the protocol integration — the RFCs are needed to specify interoperable use in PKI protocols. RFC 9794 terminology is useful for documentation but not a protocol specification.

chunks.title: Quiz: industry-threats
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: industry-threats

Q: Which industry is most vulnerable to HNDL attacks due to lifetime data sensitivity (e.g., genomic data)?
  A) Retail
  B) Healthcare
  C) Entertainment
  D) Hospitality
Answer: B
Explanation: Healthcare data — especially genomic data, mental health records, and patient histories — has lifetime sensitivity. This makes healthcare particularly vulnerable to HNDL attacks, where encrypted data intercepted today could be decrypted decades later.

Q: Approximately how many EMV payment cards worldwide use RSA-based offline authentication?
  A) ~500 million
  B) ~2 billion
  C) ~14.7 billion
  D) ~50 billion
Answer: C
Explanation: Approximately 14.7 billion EMV cards worldwide use RSA-based offline authentication (RSA-1024 or RSA-2048). Migrating this massive installed base to PQC represents one of the largest cryptographic transitions in history.

Q: Why are aviation and aerospace systems particularly challenging for PQC migration?
  A) They use quantum computers already
  B) They have 30-40 year service lives with limited crypto-agility
  C) They do not use any cryptography currently
  D) International aviation law prohibits cryptographic changes
Answer: B
Explanation: Aircraft and avionics systems have extremely long service lives (30-40 years) and are governed by strict certification standards (RTCA DO-326A). Updating cryptographic systems in certified avionics requires extensive re-certification, making rapid migration very difficult.

chunks.title: Quiz: industry-threats
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: industry-threats

Q: True or False: Bitcoin is vulnerable to quantum attacks because it uses ECDSA (secp256k1) for transaction signing.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Bitcoin uses ECDSA with the secp256k1 curve for transaction signing. Shor's Algorithm can break ECDSA, potentially allowing quantum attackers to forge transactions. Approximately $718 billion in quantum-vulnerable P2PK addresses exist, including ~1.1 million BTC attributed to Satoshi Nakamoto.

Q: What unique quantum threat does blockchain immutability create?
  A) Blockchains can be deleted by quantum computers
  B) On-chain encrypted data is permanently exposed — it cannot be re-encrypted after the fact
  C) Quantum computers can reverse blockchain consensus
  D) Mining becomes impossible with quantum hardware
Answer: B
Explanation: Blockchain immutability means encrypted data stored on-chain remains permanently accessible. Unlike centralized systems where archived data can be re-encrypted, blockchain data cannot be modified. Any HNDL-harvested on-chain encrypted data remains vulnerable indefinitely.

Q: Which critical infrastructure sector faces unique challenges due to 20-30 year equipment lifecycles and IEC 62443 standards?
  A) Retail
  B) Energy and utilities (SCADA systems)
  C) Media and entertainment
  D) Education
Answer: B
Explanation: Energy and utility systems (power grids, SCADA, nuclear facilities) have equipment lifecycles of 20-30 years governed by IEC 62443 standards. Nuclear plants are licensed for 60+ years (with 80-year extensions). These extremely long lifecycles make PQC migration particularly complex.

chunks.title: Quiz: industry-threats
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: industry-threats

Q: Why did the Ethereum Foundation establish a dedicated PQC team with $2M in research prizes in January 2026?
  A) To develop a quantum computer
  B) To research quantum-safe upgrades for Ethereum, as its secp256k1/BLS12-381 cryptography is vulnerable
  C) To create a competing PQC standard
  D) To build quantum mining hardware
Answer: B
Explanation: Ethereum uses secp256k1 ECDSA and BLS12-381 cryptography, both vulnerable to quantum attacks. The Foundation established a dedicated PQC team to research quantum-safe account abstraction, signature scheme upgrades, and consensus mechanism protections.

Q: Which automotive systems are vulnerable to quantum attacks? (Select all that apply)
  A) V2X (vehicle-to-everything) PKI communications
  B) OTA (over-the-air) firmware update code signing
  C) Windshield wiper controls
  D) In-vehicle network ECU authentication
Answer: A|B|D
Explanation: V2X communications use ECDSA P-256 certificates (IEEE 1609.2), OTA firmware updates use RSA/ECDSA code signing, and ECU authentication uses cryptographic protocols — all quantum-vulnerable. Windshield wipers do not involve cryptographic operations.

Q: According to Thales 2025 data, what percentage of healthcare operators have encrypted 80% or more of their cloud data?
  A) 4%
  B) 25%
  C) 57%
  D) 75%
Answer: A
Explanation: Only 4% of healthcare operators have encrypted 80% or more of their cloud data (Thales 2025). This is alarming given that 677 healthcare breaches in 2024 exposed over 182 million individuals and healthcare data has lifetime sensitivity.

chunks.title: Quiz: industry-threats
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: industry-threats

Q: How many healthcare breaches occurred in 2024, and how many individuals were affected?
  A) 200 breaches, 50 million individuals
  B) 677 breaches, 182+ million individuals
  C) 1000 breaches, 500 million individuals
  D) 50 breaches, 10 million individuals
Answer: B
Explanation: 677 healthcare breaches in 2024 exposed over 182 million individuals. Combined with only 4% of healthcare operators encrypting most cloud data, this represents a critical quantum vulnerability given the lifetime sensitivity of genomic and medical data.

Q: What percentage of global trade by volume is carried by maritime shipping, making maritime cryptography a critical concern?
  A) 30%
  B) 50%
  C) 80%
  D) 95%
Answer: C
Explanation: Maritime shipping carries approximately 80% of world trade by volume. Maritime systems use AIS (Automatic Identification System) and digital signatures (RSA/ECDSA) for vessel identification and electronic bills of lading, making them vulnerable to quantum-enabled forgery.

Q: What is the BIS Project Leap Phase 2 testing for quantum-safe financial infrastructure?
  A) Quantum computing for trading algorithms
  B) Hybrid PQC on the TARGET2 settlement system processing trillions daily
  C) Quantum key distribution for ATM networks
  D) Blockchain-based central bank digital currencies
Answer: B
Explanation: BIS Project Leap Phase 2 (July 2025) tests hybrid PQC implementations on the TARGET2 settlement system, which processes trillions of euros in daily interbank settlements. This is the first large-scale test of quantum-safe financial market infrastructure.

Q: True or False: Nuclear power plants have licensing periods of 60+ years with approved 80-year extensions.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Nuclear plants operate under NRC 10 CFR 73.54 with 60+ year licenses and approved 80-year extensions. These extremely long lifecycles make nuclear facilities some of the most challenging systems for PQC migration, as cryptographic systems must remain secure for decades.

Q: How many SIM cards globally use RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256, creating a massive quantum-vulnerable surface?
  A) Millions
  B) Hundreds of millions
  C) Billions
  D) Tens of thousands
Answer: C
Explanation: Billions of SIM cards globally use RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256 for authentication. The eSIM standard (SGP.22) also relies on quantum-vulnerable PKI. Replacing this massive installed base is one of the largest PQC migration challenges in the telecom industry.

Q: What does FS-ISAC warn about the financial sector's PQC readiness?
  A) The financial sector is well ahead of schedule
  B) Financial sector is unprepared and risks roadmap collapse by 2030 (September 2025 warning)
  C) PQC migration is unnecessary for financial institutions
  D) Only cryptocurrency firms are at risk
Answer: B
Explanation: FS-ISAC (Financial Services Information Sharing and Analysis Center) issued a September 2025 warning that the financial sector is unprepared for quantum threats and risks roadmap collapse by 2030 unless immediate action is taken.

chunks.title: Quiz: industry-threats

Quiz Category: industry-threats

Q: What is the quantum threat to global streaming DRM systems (Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay)?
  A) No threat — streaming is not encrypted
  B) RSA key hierarchies protecting content could be broken, exposing >$100B annual streaming revenue
  C) Only live streaming is affected
  D) DRM will be replaced by blockchain before quantum computers arrive
Answer: B
Explanation: Widevine, PlayReady, and FairPlay DRM systems rely on RSA key hierarchies. Quantum computers could break these hierarchies, potentially exposing the entire global streaming content catalog worth over $100 billion in annual revenue.

Q: Which of the following Ethereum cryptographic components are quantum-vulnerable? (Select all that apply)
  A) secp256k1 ECDSA (transaction signing)
  B) BLS12-381 (consensus signatures)
  C) SHA-256 (block hashing)
  D) Keccak-256 (address derivation)
Answer: A|B
Explanation: Ethereum's secp256k1 ECDSA (transaction signing) and BLS12-381 (consensus/beacon chain signatures) are both vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm. SHA-256 and Keccak-256 are hash functions only weakened (not broken) by Grover's Algorithm.

Q: What is the estimated value of quantum-vulnerable Bitcoin in P2PK addresses, according to blockchain analysis?
  A) ~$10 million
  B) ~$100 million
  C) ~$718 billion
  D) ~$5 trillion
Answer: C
Explanation: Approximately $718 billion in quantum-vulnerable P2PK (Pay-to-Public-Key) addresses exist on Bitcoin, including approximately 1.1 million BTC attributed to Satoshi Nakamoto. These addresses permanently expose their public keys, making them prime targets for future quantum attacks.

Q: According to Forescout 2025, by how much have average device risk scores increased across the top 10 countries year-over-year?
  A) 5%
  B) 15%
  C) 33%
  D) 50%
Answer: C
Explanation: Forescout 2025 reports average device risk scores across the top 10 countries increased 33% year-over-year (from 6.53 to 9.1), with overall device risk up 15%. Billions of IoT devices use ECDSA P-256 or RSA-2048 with no practical firmware update path, making IoT one of the most challenging sectors for PQC migration.

Q: What unique quantum threat do electronic bills of lading (eBL) in maritime shipping face?
  A) Data theft during transit
  B) Quantum forgery could enable cargo theft by forging digital proof of ownership
  C) Physical cargo damage
  D) Insurance fraud unrelated to cryptography
Answer: B
Explanation: DCSA electronic bills of lading (eBL) use digital signatures to prove cargo ownership. Quantum forgery of these signatures could enable cargo theft at a global scale, as forged eBLs would appear legitimate to all parties in the supply chain.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-operations
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-operations

Q: What is a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM)?
  A) A method for digitally signing documents
  B) A mechanism for securely establishing a shared secret key between two parties
  C) A technique for compressing encryption keys
  D) A hardware device for storing private keys
Answer: B
Explanation: A KEM securely establishes a shared secret key between two parties. Unlike Diffie-Hellman key exchange, a KEM works by having one party generate a shared secret and encapsulate it using the other party's public key. The recipient then decapsulates to recover the shared secret.

Q: What is the approximate public key size of ML-KEM-768 compared to X25519?
  A) About the same (~32 bytes each)
  B) ML-KEM-768 is ~37x larger (~1184 bytes vs ~32 bytes)
  C) ML-KEM-768 is ~1000x larger (~32KB vs ~32 bytes)
  D) X25519 is actually larger than ML-KEM-768
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-KEM-768 public keys are approximately 1184 bytes, compared to 32 bytes for X25519. While significantly larger, this is still manageable for most applications. The trade-off is worthwhile for quantum resistance, and ML-KEM-768 is still very fast (~80x faster keygen than RSA-2048).

Q: What are the three core operations of a KEM?
  A) Encrypt, Decrypt, Verify
  B) KeyGen, Encapsulate, Decapsulate
  C) Sign, Verify, Exchange
  D) Generate, Distribute, Revoke
Answer: B
Explanation: The three operations of a KEM are: KeyGen (generate a public/private key pair), Encapsulate (use the public key to produce a ciphertext and shared secret), and Decapsulate (use the private key to recover the shared secret from the ciphertext).

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-operations
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-operations

Q: True or False: ML-KEM key generation is approximately 80x faster than RSA-2048 key generation.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. ML-KEM key generation is dramatically faster than RSA-2048 because it uses simple linear algebra operations over polynomial rings, rather than RSA's computationally expensive prime number generation.

Q: How does ML-DSA signature size compare to RSA-2048 signature size?
  A) ML-DSA-65 signatures are smaller than RSA-2048 signatures
  B) They are approximately the same size (~256 bytes)
  C) ML-DSA-65 signatures are larger (~3.3KB vs ~256 bytes for RSA-2048)
  D) RSA-2048 does not produce signatures
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 produces signatures of approximately 3,309 bytes compared to RSA-2048's ~256 bytes. This larger size is a key trade-off for quantum resistance and impacts applications with bandwidth constraints, such as TLS handshakes and certificate chains.

Q: Why does FN-DSA require careful implementation to resist side-channel attacks?
  A) It uses extremely large key sizes
  B) Its signing algorithm relies on floating-point arithmetic that can leak timing information
  C) It requires internet connectivity during signing
  D) It stores private keys in plaintext
Answer: B
Explanation: FN-DSA (formerly FN-DSA) uses fast Fourier transforms over NTRU lattices, which require floating-point arithmetic. Variations in floating-point computation timing can leak information about the private key through side-channel attacks, requiring constant-time implementation techniques.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-operations
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-operations

Q: For multi-select questions about correctness: in ML-KEM, what does the encapsulation operation produce?
  A) A digital signature and verification key
  B) A ciphertext and a shared secret
  C) An encrypted message and decryption key
  D) A hash digest and salt
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-KEM encapsulation takes a public key and produces two outputs: a ciphertext (sent to the recipient) and a shared secret (kept by the sender). The recipient uses their private key to decapsulate the ciphertext and recover the same shared secret.

Q: Which of the following are valid hybrid key exchange combinations deployed or specified in standards? (Select all that apply)
  A) X25519MLKEM768
  B) SecP256r1MLKEM768
  C) SecP384r1MLKEM1024
  D) RSA2048MLKEM512
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 are all standardized or deployed hybrid key exchange combinations. RSA-based hybrid KEMs are not standard — hybrid approaches pair ECDH variants with ML-KEM variants.

Q: What is the fundamental difference between a KEM and a digital signature algorithm?
  A) KEMs are faster; signatures are slower
  B) KEMs establish shared secrets for encryption; signatures prove authenticity and integrity
  C) KEMs are quantum-safe; signatures are not
  D) There is no difference — they are interchangeable
Answer: B
Explanation: KEMs (like ML-KEM) establish a shared secret key between parties for subsequent encryption. Digital signature algorithms (like ML-DSA) prove that a message was created by a known sender (authenticity) and was not altered (integrity). They serve different cryptographic purposes.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-operations
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-operations

Q: Which SLH-DSA variant family does NIST prefer for long-term quantum resilience?
  A) SHA2 variants (SLH-DSA-SHA2-*)
  B) SHAKE variants (SLH-DSA-SHAKE-*)
  C) Both are equally preferred
  D) Neither — SLH-DSA is not recommended for long-term use
Answer: B
Explanation: NIST prefers SHAKE variants (SLH-DSA-SHAKE-*) over SHA2 variants for long-term quantum resilience. SHAKE (from the SHA-3/Keccak family) provides a different mathematical foundation from SHA-2, offering additional algorithm diversity for defense-in-depth.

Q: What is the shared secret size produced by all ML-KEM variants after decapsulation?
  A) 16 bytes
  B) 32 bytes
  C) 64 bytes
  D) 256 bytes
Answer: B
Explanation: All ML-KEM variants (512, 768, 1024) produce a 32-byte shared secret after decapsulation. This shared secret is then typically used as input to a Key Derivation Function (KDF) to produce symmetric encryption keys.

Q: How does ML-KEM key generation speed compare to RSA-2048?
  A) ML-KEM is about 2x faster
  B) ML-KEM is approximately 80x faster
  C) They are about the same speed
  D) RSA-2048 is faster
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-KEM key generation is approximately 80x faster than RSA-2048 because it uses efficient linear algebra operations over polynomial rings, while RSA requires finding large prime numbers — a computationally expensive process.

Q: What is the ML-DSA-44 signature size?
  A) 64 bytes (same as ECDSA)
  B) ~256 bytes (same as RSA-2048)
  C) ~2420 bytes
  D) ~7856 bytes
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-44 produces signatures of approximately 2,420 bytes. This is significantly larger than ECDSA P-256 (64 bytes) or RSA-2048 (~256 bytes) but much smaller than SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (~7,856 bytes).

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-operations
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-operations

Q: True or False: The TLS 1.3 handshake uses a key exchange to establish a shared secret before encrypting application data.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. In TLS 1.3, the client and server perform a key exchange (e.g., X25519 or X25519MLKEM768) during the handshake to establish a shared secret. This shared secret is then used to derive symmetric keys for encrypting all subsequent application data.

Q: What is the approximate ciphertext size of ML-KEM-768?
  A) 32 bytes
  B) ~1088 bytes
  C) ~3309 bytes
  D) ~16224 bytes
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-KEM-768 produces ciphertexts of approximately 1,088 bytes. Combined with the ~1,184-byte public key, the total data exchanged during hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) is around 2.3KB — larger than classical X25519 (64 bytes total) but still practical for TLS.

Q: Why is constant-time implementation critical for PQC algorithms in practice?
  A) To meet NIST performance benchmarks
  B) To prevent side-channel attacks that exploit timing variations to extract secret keys
  C) To ensure compatibility with older hardware
  D) To reduce memory usage
Answer: B
Explanation: Constant-time implementation prevents side-channel attacks where attackers measure execution timing to extract secret key information. FN-DSA is particularly susceptible due to its floating-point arithmetic, and all PQC implementations should be constant-time for production security.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-operations
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-operations

Q: In a TLS 1.3 handshake with X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange what happens if the PQC component fails?
  A) The entire handshake fails
  B) The connection falls back to X25519-only classical key exchange
  C) The server switches to RSA key exchange
  D) The client retries with a different PQC algorithm
Answer: A
Explanation: Once X25519MLKEM768 is negotiated and selected by both parties, both the X25519 and ML-KEM-768 components must succeed — there is no mid-handshake fallback. The handshake fails entirely. Note: during initial TLS negotiation (before selection), if one party does not support the hybrid group, a different mutually supported key exchange would be negotiated instead.

Q: Which of the following PQC operations are significantly slower than their classical counterparts? (Select all that apply)
  A) SLH-DSA signing (vs. RSA signing)
  B) ML-KEM key generation (vs. RSA key generation)
  C) ML-DSA verification (vs. ECDSA verification)
  D) FrodoKEM encapsulation (vs. ML-KEM encapsulation)
Answer: A|D
Explanation: SLH-DSA signing is 50-500x slower than RSA-2048 signing. FrodoKEM encapsulation is 10-20x slower than ML-KEM due to its use of unstructured LWE. ML-KEM key generation is actually 80x faster than RSA, and ML-DSA verification speed is comparable to ECDSA.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-operations
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-operations

Q: In a PQC key exchange, what is "encapsulation"?
  A) Wrapping a private key in a hardware module
  B) Using a recipient's public key to generate a ciphertext and shared secret
  C) Compressing a digital signature
  D) Encrypting a certificate for transmission
Answer: B
Explanation: Encapsulation is the process where one party uses the recipient's public key to generate two outputs: a ciphertext (sent to the recipient) and a shared secret (kept locally). The recipient decapsulates the ciphertext with their private key to recover the same shared secret.

Q: What is the approximate stack RAM requirement for ML-KEM-768 operations?
  A) ~300 bytes (similar to Ed25519)
  B) ~6KB
  C) ~180KB (similar to FrodoKEM)
  D) ~1MB
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-KEM-768 requires approximately 6KB of stack RAM — efficient enough for many embedded and constrained devices. Compare this to FrodoKEM-1344 at ~180KB (impractical for IoT) or Ed25519 at ~300 bytes (classical, extremely lightweight).

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: What are the three cryptographic pillars that secure blockchain systems?
  A) Firewalls + VPNs + passwords
  B) Keys & signatures, hash functions, and address derivation
  C) TLS certificates + OAuth + SAML
  D) Symmetric encryption + MAC + timestamps
Answer: B
Explanation: Blockchains are fundamentally cryptographic systems built on three pillars: (1) keys and digital signatures for transaction authorization, (2) hash functions for integrity and address derivation, and (3) address derivation pipelines that transform public keys into chain-specific addresses. There is no central authority — cryptography alone establishes ownership.

Q: Which elliptic curve is used by both Bitcoin and Ethereum for key generation and transaction signing?
  A) Ed25519
  B) Curve25519
  C) secp256k1
  D) P-256
Answer: C
Explanation: Both Bitcoin and Ethereum use the secp256k1 elliptic curve (defined in SEC 2 by Certicom, 2010) for key generation and ECDSA digital signatures. secp256k1 provides 128-bit security with 256-bit keys. Solana uses Ed25519 instead.

Q: True or False: Solana uses the same elliptic curve (secp256k1) as Bitcoin and Ethereum.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Solana uses Ed25519 (a twisted Edwards curve defined in RFC 8032), not secp256k1. Ed25519 provides 128-bit security with 32-byte public keys and uses EdDSA for signatures with deterministic nonces, unlike the random nonces used by secp256k1 ECDSA.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: What is the critical difference between ECDSA (used by Bitcoin/Ethereum) and EdDSA (used by Solana) in terms of nonce generation?
  A) ECDSA uses deterministic nonces; EdDSA uses random nonces
  B) ECDSA uses random nonces (nonce reuse leaks the private key); EdDSA derives nonces deterministically from the private key and message
  C) Both use random nonces but EdDSA adds a checksum
  D) Both use deterministic nonces but with different hash functions
Answer: B
Explanation: ECDSA requires a random nonce (k) for each signature. If the same nonce is ever reused with different messages, the private key can be algebraically recovered. EdDSA (Ed25519) eliminates this vulnerability entirely by deriving the nonce deterministically from the private key and the message being signed — no random number generator is needed.

Q: How does Bitcoin derive an address from a public key?
  A) Keccak-256 hash of the public key then take last 20 bytes
  B) SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160 then Base58Check encoding
  C) Direct Base58 encoding of the 32-byte public key
  D) SHA-3 hash followed by Bech32 encoding
Answer: B
Explanation: Bitcoin address derivation (P2PKH) follows a specific pipeline: compressed public key (33 bytes) is first hashed with SHA-256, then with RIPEMD-160 to produce a 20-byte hash, and finally encoded with Base58Check (which adds a version byte and 4-byte checksum) to produce the familiar "1..." address format.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: In Solana, what is the relationship between a public key and an address?
  A) The address is a Keccak-256 hash of the public key
  B) The address is derived from SHA-256 + RIPEMD-160 of the public key
  C) The 32-byte Ed25519 public key IS the address (Base58-encoded)
  D) The address is a truncated version of the public key
Answer: C
Explanation: Solana has the simplest address derivation of the three chains: the 32-byte Ed25519 public key is directly Base58-encoded to become the address. There is no hashing step. This means Solana addresses always expose the full public key, which has implications for quantum vulnerability.

Q: True or False: Ethereum uses NIST SHA3-256 (the standardized version) for address derivation.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Ethereum uses Keccak-256, which is the original Keccak submission to the SHA-3 competition. NIST SHA3-256 differs from Keccak-256 in its padding scheme. This distinction matters because using the wrong hash function would produce incorrect addresses.

Q: What does BIP-39 define?
  A) The hierarchical deterministic key derivation tree structure
  B) The conversion of random entropy into a 24-word mnemonic phrase for wallet backup
  C) The multi-account path structure (m/44'/coin'/...)
  D) The Ed25519 derivation standard for Solana
Answer: B
Explanation: BIP-39 (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39) defines how random entropy (128-256 bits) is converted into a human-readable mnemonic phrase (12-24 words) plus an optional passphrase. The mnemonic serves as a portable backup for HD wallets. The seed is derived from the mnemonic via PBKDF2 with 2048 rounds of HMAC-SHA512.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: What is the standard BIP-44 derivation path for the first Bitcoin address?
  A) m/44'/501'/0'/0'
  B) m/44'/60'/0'/0/0
  C) m/44'/0'/0'/0/0
  D) m/0'/0'/0'/0/0
Answer: C
Explanation: The BIP-44 derivation path for Bitcoin is m/44'/0'/0'/0/0, where: m = master key, 44' = BIP-44 purpose (hardened), 0' = Bitcoin coin type (hardened), 0' = account #0 (hardened), 0 = external chain (receiving), 0 = address index #0. Ethereum uses coin type 60, and Solana uses coin type 501.

Q: Which of the following are true about Solana's HD wallet derivation? (Select all that apply)
  A) Uses SLIP-0010 instead of BIP-32
  B) All path segments must be hardened
  C) Uses coin type 501
  D) Supports non-hardened child key derivation
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: Solana uses SLIP-0010 (not BIP-32) for HD wallet derivation because Ed25519 does not support non-hardened child key derivation. The path m/44'/501'/0'/0' has all segments hardened (denoted by the apostrophe). This is a fundamental difference from Bitcoin and Ethereum, which support both hardened and non-hardened derivation.

Q: What quantum algorithm threatens the security of blockchain digital signatures (both ECDSA and EdDSA)?
  A) Grover's Algorithm
  B) Shor's Algorithm
  C) Deutsch-Jozsa Algorithm
  D) Simon's Algorithm
Answer: B
Explanation: Shor's Algorithm can solve the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) in polynomial time, enabling a quantum computer to derive private keys from public keys. This breaks both secp256k1 ECDSA (Bitcoin/Ethereum) and Ed25519 EdDSA (Solana). Grover's Algorithm only provides a quadratic speedup against symmetric ciphers and hash functions.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: True or False: Bitcoin P2PKH addresses (starting with "1") keep the public key hidden until the first spending transaction.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. P2PKH (Pay-to-Public-Key-Hash) addresses only reveal the hash of the public key. The actual public key is not exposed until the owner signs a spending transaction. However, the older P2PK format and any address that has already transacted expose the public key permanently on the immutable blockchain.

Q: Why is the HNFL (Harvest Now, Forge Later) threat particularly severe for blockchains compared to traditional systems?
  A) Blockchain encryption is weaker than TLS
  B) On-chain data is immutable — exposed public keys cannot be retroactively protected by key rotation
  C) Blockchains use smaller key sizes
  D) Blockchain transactions are unencrypted
Answer: B
Explanation: Unlike traditional systems where keys can be rotated and old data re-encrypted, blockchain transaction history is permanent and immutable. Public keys exposed in past transactions remain harvestable indefinitely. When cryptographically relevant quantum computers arrive, every previously exposed public key becomes a target for private key recovery — and there is no retroactive fix.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: Which blockchain cryptographic components are vulnerable to quantum attacks via Shor's Algorithm? (Select all that apply)
  A) secp256k1 ECDSA signatures
  B) Ed25519 EdDSA signatures
  C) SHA-256 block hashing
  D) Ethereum BLS12-381 consensus signatures
Answer: A|B|D
Explanation: secp256k1 ECDSA (Bitcoin/Ethereum), Ed25519 EdDSA (Solana), and BLS12-381 (Ethereum beacon chain consensus) are all based on elliptic curve or pairing-based problems vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm. SHA-256 is a hash function that is only weakened (not broken) by Grover's Algorithm, which provides at most a quadratic speedup.

Q: What is the estimated value of quantum-vulnerable Bitcoin held in P2PK addresses with permanently exposed public keys?
  A) ~$10 million
  B) ~$1 billion
  C) ~$718 billion
  D) ~$5 trillion
Answer: C
Explanation: Approximately $718 billion in Bitcoin is held in P2PK (Pay-to-Public-Key) addresses where the public key is permanently exposed on-chain. This includes approximately 1.1 million BTC attributed to Satoshi Nakamoto. These addresses are prime targets for future quantum attacks because the public key is directly visible.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: Why does Ethereum include a recovery parameter (v) in its ECDSA signatures per EIP-155?
  A) To add quantum resistance to signatures
  B) To allow the signer's public key (and address) to be recovered from the signature itself
  C) To compress the signature for lower gas costs
  D) To prevent double-spending
Answer: B
Explanation: Ethereum's ECDSA signatures include a recovery parameter (v) as defined in EIP-155. This allows anyone to recover the signer's public key — and therefore their address — from just the signature and the signed message. This is why Ethereum transactions don't need to explicitly include the sender's public key, but it also means every transaction permanently exposes it.

Q: True or False: Solana accounts are always quantum-vulnerable because the Ed25519 public key IS the address meaning the public key is permanently exposed.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Unlike Bitcoin (where P2PKH hides the public key until spending) or Ethereum (where the address is a hash of the public key), Solana addresses are the Base58-encoded 32-byte Ed25519 public key itself. This means every Solana account permanently exposes its public key from creation, making all Solana accounts immediately targetable once a CRQC exists.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: What is the purpose of BIP-32 in the HD wallet standard?
  A) Converting entropy to a mnemonic word list
  B) Defining the hierarchical deterministic key derivation tree structure
  C) Assigning coin type numbers to different blockchains
  D) Specifying the Ed25519 derivation for Solana
Answer: B
Explanation: BIP-32 (Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets) defines how a single master seed can deterministically derive an unlimited tree of child keys. Parent keys can generate child keys using HMAC-SHA512, enabling a single backup (the seed/mnemonic) to recover all addresses across all chains. BIP-39 handles mnemonic generation, and BIP-44 standardizes the path structure.

Q: Which of the following correctly describe properties of blockchain addresses? (Select all that apply)
  A) Bitcoin P2PKH addresses use SHA-256 + RIPEMD-160 hashing
  B) Ethereum addresses are the last 20 bytes of a Keccak-256 hash
  C) Solana addresses are the public key encoded in Base58
  D) All three chains use the same address derivation pipeline
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: Each chain has a different address derivation pipeline. Bitcoin P2PKH: compressed pubkey is SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160 hashed, then Base58Check encoded. Ethereum: uncompressed pubkey (64 bytes) is Keccak-256 hashed, last 20 bytes taken, EIP-55 checksum applied. Solana: 32-byte Ed25519 public key is directly Base58-encoded as the address.

chunks.title: Quiz: Digital Assets
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: Digital Assets

Q: Which of the following are true about HD wallet mnemonic phrases (BIP-39)? (Select all that apply)
  A) A 24-word mnemonic encodes 256 bits of entropy
  B) The seed is derived using PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512
  C) The mnemonic words come from a standardized 2048-word list
  D) The mnemonic can only generate keys for one blockchain
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: BIP-39 mnemonics encode 256 bits of entropy (for 24 words) from a standardized 2048-word English wordlist. The mnemonic is converted to a 512-bit seed using PBKDF2 with 2048 iterations of HMAC-SHA512. This single seed can derive keys for any blockchain via BIP-32/BIP-44 derivation paths — Bitcoin (coin 0), Ethereum (coin 60), Solana (coin 501), and more.

chunks.title: Quiz: tls-basics
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: tls-basics

Q: Which RFC defines TLS 1.3?
  A) RFC 5246
  B) RFC 8446
  C) RFC 9370
  D) RFC 7748
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 8446 defines TLS 1.3, the latest version of the Transport Layer Security protocol. It was published in August 2018 and brought major security and performance improvements over TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246).

Q: True or False: TLS 1.3 removed support for RSA key exchange to enforce forward secrecy.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. TLS 1.3 eliminated static RSA key exchange because it does not provide forward secrecy — if the server's private key is compromised, all past sessions encrypted with it can be decrypted. TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral (EC)DHE key exchange, ensuring each session uses unique keys.

Q: How many cipher suites does TLS 1.3 support compared to TLS 1.2?
  A) 5 (vs hundreds in TLS 1.2)
  B) 37 (vs hundreds in TLS 1.2)
  C) 5 (vs 37 in TLS 1.2)
  D) Hundreds (same as TLS 1.2)
Answer: A
Explanation: TLS 1.3 dramatically simplified the cipher suite landscape from hundreds of options (many insecure) in TLS 1.2 down to just 5 well-vetted AEAD cipher suites. This simplification eliminates entire categories of attacks that exploited weak cipher suite negotiation.

Q: What is the first message sent in a TLS 1.3 handshake?
  A) ServerHello
  B) ClientHello
  C) Certificate
  D) EncryptedExtensions
Answer: B
Explanation: The TLS 1.3 handshake begins with the ClientHello message, where the client sends its supported cipher suites, key exchange groups, signature algorithms, and key_share (ephemeral public key). The server responds with ServerHello containing its choices and key_share.

chunks.title: Quiz: tls-basics
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: tls-basics

Q: True or False: In TLS 1.3, all handshake messages after ServerHello are encrypted.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Unlike TLS 1.2 where the entire handshake was plaintext, TLS 1.3 encrypts all messages after ServerHello using handshake traffic keys derived from the ECDHE/KEM shared secret via HKDF. This protects certificate information and other handshake data from passive observers.

Q: Which TLS 1.3 cipher suite is specifically optimized for mobile and ARM devices?
  A) TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  B) TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
  C) TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256
  D) TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256
Answer: C
Explanation: TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 uses the ChaCha20 stream cipher with Poly1305 MAC. ChaCha20 is designed to perform well in software without hardware AES acceleration, making it ideal for mobile and ARM devices that may lack AES-NI instructions.

Q: What does AEAD stand for in the context of TLS 1.3 cipher suites?
  A) Advanced Encryption Algorithm Design
  B) Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data
  C) Asymmetric Encryption and Decryption
  D) Automated Endpoint Authentication Digest
Answer: B
Explanation: AEAD stands for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data. TLS 1.3 requires all cipher suites to use AEAD algorithms (such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305), which provide both confidentiality and integrity in a single operation, eliminating vulnerabilities associated with separate MAC-then-encrypt schemes in TLS 1.2.

chunks.title: Quiz: tls-basics
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: tls-basics

Q: How many round trips does a full TLS 1.3 handshake require compared to TLS 1.2?
  A) 1-RTT (vs 2-RTT in TLS 1.2)
  B) 2-RTT (vs 3-RTT in TLS 1.2)
  C) 0-RTT (vs 1-RTT in TLS 1.2)
  D) 3-RTT (vs 4-RTT in TLS 1.2)
Answer: A
Explanation: TLS 1.3 completes a full handshake in just 1 round trip (1-RTT), compared to 2 round trips in TLS 1.2. This is achieved by the client sending its key_share in the ClientHello, allowing the server to compute the shared secret immediately. TLS 1.3 also supports 0-RTT for resumption.

Q: True or False: TLS 1.3 mandates forward secrecy for all connections.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. TLS 1.3 requires ephemeral (EC)DHE or KEM-based key exchange for every connection, ensuring forward secrecy. If a server's long-term private key is later compromised, past session keys cannot be recovered because each session used unique ephemeral keys that were discarded after the handshake.

Q: What key derivation function does TLS 1.3 use to derive handshake and application traffic keys?
  A) PBKDF2
  B) HKDF (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function)
  C) scrypt
  D) Argon2
Answer: B
Explanation: TLS 1.3 uses HKDF (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function) for its entire key schedule. HKDF operates in two stages: Extract (to derive a pseudorandom key from input keying material) and Expand (to derive output keys). The key schedule chains through Early Secret, Handshake Secret, and Master Secret.

chunks.title: Quiz: tls-basics
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: tls-basics

Q: What is the purpose of 0-RTT early data in TLS 1.3?
  A) To establish a connection without any encryption
  B) To send application data in the first flight during session resumption
  C) To bypass certificate verification for faster connections
  D) To downgrade to TLS 1.2 for compatibility
Answer: B
Explanation: 0-RTT (zero round trip time) allows clients to send encrypted application data in the very first message when resuming a previously established TLS 1.3 session, using a pre-shared key (PSK). This eliminates the round-trip latency for the initial data. However, 0-RTT data is vulnerable to replay attacks and lacks forward secrecy.

Q: Approximately how large is an ML-KEM-768 public key compared to an X25519 public key?
  A) ~1,184 bytes vs 32 bytes
  B) ~256 bytes vs 32 bytes
  C) ~64 bytes vs 32 bytes
  D) ~4,096 bytes vs 256 bytes
Answer: A
Explanation: ML-KEM-768 public keys are approximately 1,184 bytes, compared to just 32 bytes for X25519. This ~37x size increase is one of the main trade-offs of post-quantum key exchange in TLS — larger handshake messages mean more bandwidth and potentially slower connections, especially on constrained networks.

chunks.title: Quiz: tls-basics
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: tls-basics

Q: What is hybrid key exchange in TLS, and why is it used?
  A) Combining two classical algorithms for double security
  B) Combining a classical and a post-quantum algorithm for security against both classical and quantum attacks
  C) Using different key exchanges for client and server
  D) Switching between key exchange algorithms mid-handshake
Answer: B
Explanation: Hybrid key exchange combines a classical algorithm (e.g., X25519) with a post-quantum algorithm (e.g., ML-KEM-768) so that the connection is secure against both classical and future quantum attacks. Even if one algorithm is broken, the other still provides security. This is the recommended transition approach.

Q: Which hybrid key exchange group is already deployed in Chrome and Firefox for TLS 1.3?
  A) SecP384r1MLKEM1024
  B) X25519MLKEM768
  C) P256MLKEM512
  D) X448MLKEM1024
Answer: B
Explanation: X25519MLKEM768 combines the X25519 elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman with ML-KEM-768 (NIST Level 3). It is already deployed in production in Chrome, Firefox, and other major browsers, making it the first widely-deployed post-quantum key exchange mechanism in TLS 1.3.

Q: What does mutual TLS (mTLS) add compared to standard TLS?
  A) Encryption of application data
  B) Client certificate authentication in addition to server authentication
  C) Support for multiple cipher suites
  D) Compression of handshake messages
Answer: B
Explanation: Standard TLS only authenticates the server to the client via the server's certificate. Mutual TLS (mTLS) adds client certificate authentication, where the client also presents a certificate to prove its identity to the server. This is commonly used in zero-trust architectures, API security, and service-to-service communication.

chunks.title: Quiz: tls-basics
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: tls-basics

Q: Which of the following were removed in TLS 1.3 compared to TLS 1.2? (Select all that apply)
  A) Static RSA key exchange
  B) CBC cipher modes
  C) Renegotiation and compression
  D) Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange (no forward secrecy), CBC cipher modes (vulnerable to padding oracle attacks like POODLE and Lucky13), and renegotiation/compression (vulnerable to attacks like CRIME). Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman was kept and made mandatory to ensure forward secrecy.

Q: True or False: In TLS 1.3, cipher suites specify the key exchange algorithm.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. In TLS 1.3, cipher suites only specify the symmetric encryption algorithm and hash function (e.g., TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384). Key exchange and authentication are negotiated separately via the supported_groups and signature_algorithms extensions. This is a simplification from TLS 1.2 where cipher suites bundled all four components.

Q: What is the correct order of the three main secrets in the TLS 1.3 key schedule?
  A) Master Secret, Handshake Secret, Early Secret
  B) Early Secret, Master Secret, Handshake Secret
  C) Handshake Secret, Early Secret, Master Secret
  D) Early Secret, Handshake Secret, Master Secret
Answer: D
Explanation: The TLS 1.3 key schedule derives three main secrets in order: (1) Early Secret — from PSK or zero, used for 0-RTT; (2) Handshake Secret — incorporating the ECDHE/KEM shared secret, producing handshake traffic keys; (3) Master Secret — producing application traffic keys for the encrypted session data.

chunks.title: Quiz: tls-basics
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: tls-basics

Q: Which post-quantum signature algorithm is used for quantum-resistant TLS server certificates?
  A) ML-KEM-768
  B) ML-DSA (e.g. ML-DSA-44 or ML-DSA-87)
  C) X25519
  D) HKDF-SHA256
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-DSA (Module-Lattice Digital Signature Algorithm, formerly CRYSTALS-ML-DSA) is the NIST-standardized post-quantum signature algorithm used for TLS certificates. ML-KEM is for key encapsulation (key exchange), not signatures. ML-DSA-44 provides NIST Level 2 security and ML-DSA-87 provides Level 5.

Q: What is the purpose of the CertificateVerify message in the TLS 1.3 handshake?
  A) To check if the certificate has expired
  B) To prove the sender possesses the private key corresponding to the certificate's public key
  C) To verify the certificate chain up to a trusted root CA
  D) To negotiate which signature algorithm to use
Answer: B
Explanation: The CertificateVerify message contains a digital signature over a hash of the handshake transcript, proving that the sender possesses the private key corresponding to the public key in their certificate. This prevents an attacker from replaying a stolen certificate without the associated private key.

chunks.title: Quiz: digital-id
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: digital-id

Q: When was the eIDAS 2.0 regulation (EU 2024/1183) adopted?
  A) January 2023
  B) May 2024
  C) December 2025
  D) June 2026
Answer: B
Explanation: eIDAS 2.0 (EU Regulation 2024/1183) was adopted in May 2024, replacing the original eIDAS regulation from 2014. It mandates EUDI Wallets for all 27 EU member states and creates a pan-European trust framework for identity, attestations, and qualified electronic signatures.

Q: By when must all 27 EU member states provide citizens with at least one EUDI Wallet?
  A) December 2024
  B) June 2025
  C) December 2026
  D) December 2028
Answer: C
Explanation: eIDAS 2.0 mandates that all 27 EU member states must provide citizens and residents with at least one EUDI Wallet by December 2026. The first implementing acts were due by December 2024, with private sector acceptance required by late 2027.

Q: What is the key difference between eIDAS 1.0 and eIDAS 2.0?
  A) eIDAS 2.0 removes trust services entirely
  B) eIDAS 2.0 makes digital identity wallets mandatory, whereas eIDAS 1.0 had voluntary national eID notification
  C) eIDAS 2.0 only applies to government services
  D) eIDAS 2.0 eliminates cross-border recognition
Answer: B
Explanation: eIDAS 1.0 (2014) made national eID notification voluntary and had no wallet framework. eIDAS 2.0 (2024) makes EUDI Wallets mandatory for all member states, adds attribute attestations (EAA, QEAA), requires full cross-border mutual recognition, and mandates private sector acceptance.

chunks.title: Quiz: digital-id
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: digital-id

Q: True or False: eIDAS 2.0 currently mandates post-quantum cryptography (PQC) for EUDI Wallet implementations.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. eIDAS 2.0 does NOT yet mandate post-quantum cryptography. Current EUDI implementations use classical ECDSA (P-256, P-384). However, ENISA has identified wallet providers as high-impact entities for early PQC adoption, and future ARF versions are expected to require PQC-safe algorithms such as ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.

Q: What encoding format does the mso_mdoc (ISO 18013-5) credential use?
  A) JSON
  B) XML
  C) CBOR
  D) ASN.1
Answer: C
Explanation: mso_mdoc uses CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation), a binary encoding format defined in ISO 18013-5. It is optimized for proximity verification scenarios using NFC and BLE, making it ideal for in-person identity verification.

Q: What type of verification is the vc+sd-jwt (SD-JWT VC) credential format optimized for?
  A) Proximity verification via NFC and BLE
  B) Remote/online verification via APIs
  C) Offline-only air-gapped environments
  D) Blockchain-based attestation
Answer: B
Explanation: vc+sd-jwt (IETF SD-JWT VC) uses JSON text-based encoding optimized for remote/online presentation via APIs and web services. In contrast, mso_mdoc uses CBOR binary encoding optimized for proximity verification via NFC and BLE.

chunks.title: Quiz: digital-id
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: digital-id

Q: What does PID stand for in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem?
  A) Private Identity Document
  B) Person Identification Data
  C) Public Identity Descriptor
  D) Protected Identity Device
Answer: B
Explanation: PID (Person Identification Data) is the core identity credential issued by national authorities in the EUDI ecosystem. It contains mandatory attributes such as name, birth date, nationality, and document number. A valid PID is required before most other operations in the wallet.

Q: What role does a Qualified Trust Service Provider (QTSP) play in the eIDAS 2.0 framework?
  A) Stores user wallet data on a public blockchain
  B) Issues qualified attestations (QEAA) and provides qualified electronic signatures (QES)
  C) Manages DNS records for identity providers
  D) Operates the EU's central identity database
Answer: B
Explanation: A QTSP is a certified organization that issues qualified attestations (QEAA) and provides qualified electronic signatures (QES). QTSPs operate under strict compliance requirements and are listed in National Trusted Lists published by each EU member state.

Q: True or False: A Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) has the same legal effect as a handwritten signature across all EU member states.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Under eIDAS, a Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) has the equivalent legal effect of a handwritten signature and is recognized across all EU member states. QES requires identity verification (PID) and uses keys stored in a secure device, with signatures created via a QTSP.

chunks.title: Quiz: digital-id
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: digital-id

Q: What is the primary purpose of a Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD)?
  A) Displaying credentials on the device screen
  B) Storing private keys securely in tamper-resistant hardware
  C) Connecting the wallet to the internet
  D) Translating credentials between mso_mdoc and SD-JWT formats
Answer: B
Explanation: A WSCD (Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device) stores private keys securely in tamper-resistant hardware. It can be local (device secure element, eSE, TEE) or remote (cloud HSM). The WSCA (Wallet Secure Cryptographic Application) is the firmware managing cryptographic operations within the WSCD.

Q: What does the OpenID4VCI protocol handle in the EUDI ecosystem?
  A) Presenting credentials to a relying party for verification
  B) Issuing verifiable credentials from an issuer to the wallet
  C) Creating qualified electronic signatures remotely
  D) Managing wallet backup and recovery operations
Answer: B
Explanation: OpenID4VCI (OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance) handles the protocol flow for issuing verifiable credentials from an issuer (such as a PID Provider or university) to the EUDI Wallet. The flow includes discovery, authorization, access token exchange, proof of possession, and credential issuance.

chunks.title: Quiz: digital-id
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: digital-id

Q: What does the OpenID4VP protocol handle in the EUDI ecosystem?
  A) Issuing new credentials to the wallet
  B) Revoking expired or compromised credentials
  C) Presenting verifiable credentials to relying parties for verification
  D) Generating new cryptographic key pairs
Answer: C
Explanation: OpenID4VP (OpenID for Verifiable Presentation) handles the presentation of verifiable credentials to relying parties. It defines how credentials are selected, how selective disclosure is applied, and how device binding proofs are created. For example, a bank uses OpenID4VP to verify identity during account opening.

Q: Which of the following are privacy features of the EUDI Wallet framework? (Select all that apply)
  A) Selective disclosure — only requested attributes are revealed
  B) Unlinkability — presentations to different relying parties cannot be correlated
  C) Data minimization aligned with GDPR Art. 5(1)(c)
  D) Automatic sharing of all credential attributes with every relying party
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: The EUDI Wallet framework implements three key privacy features: selective disclosure (only requested attributes are revealed while others remain cryptographically hidden), unlinkability (presentations to different relying parties should not be correlatable via batch-issued credentials and pseudonymous identifiers), and data minimization (GDPR compliance — only the minimum data necessary for a specific purpose is shared). Automatic sharing of all attributes would violate these principles.

chunks.title: Quiz: digital-id
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: digital-id

Q: By when must private sector entities accept EUDI Wallet credentials under eIDAS 2.0?
  A) December 2025
  B) May 2026
  C) Late 2027
  D) January 2030
Answer: C
Explanation: Under eIDAS 2.0, private sector entities are required to accept EUDI Wallet credentials by late 2027. This follows the December 2026 deadline for member states to make wallets available, giving the private sector approximately one year to integrate wallet-based identity verification.

Q: What is the correct structure of an SD-JWT Verifiable Credential?
  A) <Disclosure1>~<Disclosure2>~<IssuerJWT>
  B) <IssuerJWT>~<Disclosure1>~<Disclosure2>...~<KB-JWT>
  C) <KB-JWT>~<IssuerJWT>~<Disclosures>
  D) Header.Claims.Disclosures.Signature
Answer: B
Explanation: An SD-JWT VC has the structure: <IssuerJWT>~<Disclosure1>~<Disclosure2>...~<KB-JWT>. The Issuer JWT contains the signed claims (Header.Payload.Signature in Base64URL). Each Disclosure is a Base64URL-encoded [salt, key, value] array. The Key Binding JWT (KB-JWT) at the end is signed by the holder and contains iat, aud, nonce, and sd_hash.

chunks.title: Quiz: digital-id
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: digital-id

Q: Which of the following are components of the eIDAS 2.0 trust framework? (Select all that apply)
  A) National Trusted Lists of certified QTSPs published by each member state
