Explanation: Gateway-mediated PQC at ground stations (ATC centers, airline ops centers, airport facilities) allows PQC protection on the ground side while maintaining classical crypto compatibility with legacy aircraft. This is the practical approach since legacy aircraft will operate for decades.

chunks.title: Quiz: ai-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ai-security-pqc

Q: What is the primary quantum threat to AI training data pipelines?
  A) Quantum computers can generate better training data
  B) Adversaries can harvest encrypted training data now and decrypt it later (HNDL)
  C) Quantum noise degrades model accuracy
  D) Quantum computers make all encryption unnecessary
Answer: B
Explanation: The Harvest Now Decrypt Later (HNDL) threat means adversaries can intercept and store encrypted proprietary training data today, then decrypt it once cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs) arrive. For organizations with 10+ years of valuable training data, this is the highest-priority quantum threat to AI pipelines.

Q: What is model collapse in the context of AI training?
  A) A model that runs out of GPU memory during training
  B) Progressive quality degradation when models are trained on AI-generated data
  C) A neural network that fails to converge during optimization
  D) A model that produces identical outputs for all inputs
Answer: B
Explanation: Model collapse is a degenerative process where AI models trained on AI-generated (synthetic) data progressively lose quality, diversity, and accuracy over successive generations. Without cryptographic provenance verification to distinguish human-created from AI-generated data, training corpora become contaminated and model quality spirals downward.

chunks.title: Quiz: ai-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ai-security-pqc

Q: Which cryptographic standard provides content provenance to help combat synthetic data contamination?
  A) FIPS 203 (ML-KEM)
  B) C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity)
  C) FIPS 204 (ML-DSA)
  D) RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3)
Answer: B
Explanation: C2PA (Content Credentials) embeds cryptographically signed metadata into digital content to verify its origin, creation method, and edit history. This helps AI training pipelines distinguish human-created from AI-generated data, combating model collapse from synthetic data contamination.

Q: ML-KEM key wrapping for model weight encryption is actually faster than RSA-2048 for the same operation.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) key encapsulation is computationally faster than RSA-2048 key wrapping. While ML-KEM produces larger ciphertexts, the speed advantage makes it practical for protecting model weights. For a 140 GB model file, the key wrapping overhead is negligible regardless of algorithm choice.

Q: What is the primary purpose of ML-DSA model signing for AI model weights?
  A) Encrypting model weights to prevent unauthorized access
  B) Providing tamper-evident integrity verification analogous to code signing
  C) Compressing model weights for faster distribution
  D) Authenticating users who download the model
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) model signing provides cryptographic integrity verification — proving that model weights have not been modified since the creator signed them. This is analogous to code signing for software packages. The signature does not encrypt the weights; it provides non-repudiation and tamper detection.

chunks.title: Quiz: ai-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ai-security-pqc

Q: In an AI agent delegation chain (Human → Agent → Sub-Agent → Service) what is the primary PQC concern?
  A) Delegation tokens are too large for network transmission
  B) All classical signing schemes used for delegation tokens are quantum-vulnerable
  C) Agents cannot use PQC algorithms
  D) Sub-agents always have more permissions than parent agents
Answer: B
Explanation: Every link in a delegation chain — from human to agent to sub-agent to service — is typically signed with ECDSA or RSA. These classical schemes are vulnerable to quantum attack for the entire credential validity period. ML-DSA delegation tokens provide quantum-safe authority chaining with larger but acceptable signature sizes.

Q: What distinguishes agentic commerce from traditional e-commerce in terms of cryptographic requirements?
  A) Agentic commerce does not need encryption
  B) Autonomous agents must sign transactions with machine identity credentials rather than human credentials
  C) Agentic commerce only uses symmetric encryption
  D) Payment amounts in agentic commerce are always smaller
Answer: B
Explanation: In agentic commerce, AI agents autonomously negotiate, sign purchase orders, and execute payments on behalf of users. Unlike traditional e-commerce where humans authenticate directly, agents need machine identity credentials (X.509 certs or JWT tokens) for signing and non-repudiation. All classical signing is quantum-vulnerable.

chunks.title: Quiz: ai-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ai-security-pqc

Q: Lattice-based homomorphic encryption (FHE) schemes like BGV and CKKS are inherently quantum-resistant because they share the same mathematical foundation as ML-KEM.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: Most practical fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) schemes — BGV, CKKS, and TFHE — are based on the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem or Ring-LWE, the same lattice problems underlying ML-KEM (FIPS 203). This makes them inherently resistant to quantum attacks, unlike RSA or ECC-based approaches.

Q: When designing agent-to-agent (A2A) PQC communication at 10K messages/second what is the primary operational challenge?
  A) ML-KEM handshakes are too slow
  B) ML-DSA per-message signature size creates significant bandwidth overhead
  C) PQC algorithms cannot operate at that throughput
  D) Agents cannot use TLS 1.3
Answer: B
Explanation: At high message rates, ML-DSA-65 signatures (~3.3 KB each) create significant bandwidth overhead compared to ECDSA (~72 bytes). At 10K messages/second, this means ~33 MB/s of signature data alone versus ~720 KB/s for ECDSA. This requires careful bandwidth planning and protocol design, though the security benefit justifies the cost.

chunks.title: Quiz: ai-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ai-security-pqc

Q: For enterprise-scale AI infrastructure with 7-year data retention what HNDL risk level applies?
  A) No risk — data will be obsolete before quantum computers arrive
  B) Low — quantum computers are decades away
  C) High — retained data exceeds most CRQC timeline estimates
  D) Critical — quantum computers can already decrypt this data
Answer: C
Explanation: With 7-year data retention, the HNDL risk is High because the retention period overlaps with many credible CRQC timeline estimates (2030-2035). Data encrypted today and retained for 7 years may still be valuable when quantum computers capable of breaking current encryption become available.

Q: Which of the following are valid privacy-preserving ML techniques that have quantum-resistant properties? (Select all that apply)
  A) Lattice-based FHE (BGV/CKKS)
  B) Garbled circuits with AES-256
  C) Differential privacy with Laplace noise
  D) RSA-based secure aggregation
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: Lattice-based FHE (a) is quantum-resistant by design (LWE hardness). Garbled circuits (b) rely on symmetric crypto (AES), which is Grover-resistant with sufficient key sizes. Differential privacy (c) adds statistical noise independent of cryptographic assumptions. RSA-based secure aggregation (d) is quantum-vulnerable since RSA can be broken by Shor's algorithm.

chunks.title: Quiz: ai-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ai-security-pqc

Q: What is the recommended first phase in a phased PQC migration for AI infrastructure?
  A) Replace all model signing with ML-DSA immediately
  B) Upgrade to hybrid TLS and ML-KEM key wrapping for data in transit
  C) Perform a cryptographic inventory of all AI pipeline components
  D) Deploy FHE for all inference workloads
Answer: C
Explanation: The recommended first phase is always a cryptographic inventory — identifying all cryptographic operations across the AI pipeline (data ingestion, storage, training, inference, API endpoints). Without understanding what crypto is used where, migration efforts are unfocused and may miss critical quantum-vulnerable touchpoints.

Q: C2PA content credentials currently use ECDSA/RSA signatures which are quantum-vulnerable and will need PQC migration to remain trustworthy beyond Q-Day.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: C2PA content credentials use X.509 certificates with CMS signatures, currently based on ECDSA or RSA. These are quantum-vulnerable — a quantum computer could forge provenance signatures, undermining the entire content authenticity framework. Migration to ML-DSA signatures is needed to ensure provenance claims remain trustworthy.

chunks.title: Quiz: ai-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ai-security-pqc

Q: In a hierarchical KMS for AI infrastructure at petabyte scale what is the primary benefit of ML-KEM envelope encryption?
  A) It eliminates the need for key rotation
  B) It allows encrypting each data object with a unique DEK while wrapping DEKs with a smaller number of KEKs
  C) It makes data smaller through compression
  D) It provides faster encryption than AES-256-GCM
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-KEM envelope encryption separates data encryption (AES-256-GCM with unique DEKs per object) from key protection (ML-KEM wrapping of DEKs with KEKs). This scales to petabytes because only the KEKs need HSM-level protection — millions of DEKs can be managed efficiently without each requiring direct HSM operations.

Q: Why is the HNDL threat particularly concerning for proprietary AI training datasets?
  A) Training data is always public information
  B) Proprietary training datasets often retain commercial value for 10+ years overlapping with CRQC timelines
  C) AI models cannot be retrained with new data
  D) Encrypted training data cannot be harvested
Answer: B
Explanation: Proprietary training datasets — customer transaction data, medical records, research corpora — often retain enormous commercial value for a decade or more. This long value lifetime overlaps with credible CRQC timelines, making encrypted training data a prime HNDL target. Adversaries harvesting this data today could reconstruct proprietary model capabilities once quantum decryption becomes possible.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-dev-apis
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-dev-apis

Q: Which Java API provides a pluggable provider architecture for cryptographic operations?
  A) JCA/JCE
  B) PKCS#11
  C) CNG
  D) EVP API
Answer: A
Explanation: The Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA) and its extension (JCE) define a pluggable provider model. Engine classes like KeyPairGenerator, Cipher, and Signature delegate to registered Provider implementations. Bouncy Castle is the most widely used JCA provider for PQC algorithms.

Q: Which open-source crypto library (Java/.NET) has supported all NIST PQC algorithms — ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and FN-DSA — since early 2024?
  A) OpenSSL
  B) PQClean
  C) Bouncy Castle
  D) wolfSSL
Answer: C
Explanation: Bouncy Castle 1.78 (January 2024) added full support for all four NIST PQC finalists. It works as a JCA provider (register with Security.addProvider(new BouncyCastleProvider())) or as a standalone API. The C# port provides equivalent coverage for .NET.

Q: True or False: In PKCS#11, all cryptographic operations (key generation, signing, encryption) must be performed within an open session.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: PKCS#11 requires an open session (C_OpenSession) for every operation. This is a key difference from JCA and OpenSSL, where sessions are implicit. Session management — including handling session limits on HSMs — is the #1 source of bugs in PKCS#11 implementations.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-dev-apis
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-dev-apis

Q: Which programming language feature prevents use-after-free vulnerabilities on cryptographic key material at compile time?
  A) Python's garbage collector
  B) Rust's ownership and borrow checker
  C) Java's JVM memory model
  D) Go's goroutine scheduler
Answer: B
Explanation: Rust's ownership model makes it impossible to access memory after it has been freed or to have two mutable references simultaneously. This prevents use-after-free bugs on key buffers at compile time — a critical property for cryptographic key management services where leaked key material is a catastrophic failure.

Q: What does the oqsprovider add to OpenSSL 3.x?
  A) Post-quantum cryptography algorithm support via liboqs
  B) FIPS 140-3 validation for classical algorithms
  C) A PKCS#11 interface for HSM integration
  D) TLS 1.3 session resumption optimizations
Answer: A
Explanation: The oqsprovider is an OpenSSL 3.x provider plugin that exposes all liboqs PQC algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, FN-DSA, and more) through the standard OpenSSL EVP API. Once loaded via OSSL_PROVIDER_load(NULL, "oqsprovider"), any existing OpenSSL-based application can use PQC algorithms without code changes.

Q: Which Java method registers Bouncy Castle as a JCA provider so that ML-DSA-65 signing works via standard JCA calls?
  A) BouncyCastleProvider.install()
  B) Security.addProvider(new BouncyCastleProvider())
  C) JCE.registerProvider("BC")
  D) KeyFactory.setProvider(BouncyCastle.INSTANCE)
Answer: B
Explanation: Security.addProvider(new BouncyCastleProvider()) registers Bouncy Castle in the JCA provider registry. After registration, standard JCA calls like Signature.getInstance("ML-DSA-65", "BC") route to BC's implementation. This is called once at application startup.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-dev-apis
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-dev-apis

Q: For a regulated fintech company needing immediate PQC support, which crypto library sourcing strategy offers the best balance of algorithm availability, community auditing, and zero licensing cost?
  A) Build Your Own
  B) Open Source (Bouncy Castle or OpenSSL + oqsprovider)
  C) Commercial (Thales Luna HSM SDK only)
  D) None — wait for OS vendors to add native PQC support
Answer: B
Explanation: Open-source libraries like Bouncy Castle and OpenSSL+oqsprovider already have production-ready PQC support, are community-audited, and are free. "Build Your Own" is only justified at Google/Amazon scale due to the engineering and certification costs. Commercial HSM SDKs are complementary but not sufficient alone for application-layer PQC.

Q: In OpenSSL 3.x, which function enables the provider pattern by loading a named provider at runtime?
  A) EVP_load_provider()
  B) SSL_CTX_set_provider()
  C) OSSL_PROVIDER_load()
  D) ENGINE_by_id()
Answer: C
Explanation: OSSL_PROVIDER_load(NULL, "oqsprovider") loads a named provider into the default library context. After this call, all EVP operations can use algorithms from that provider. ENGINE_by_id() is the deprecated OpenSSL 1.x engine API — never use it in new code.

Q: Which PQC crypto library is a FIPS 140-3 validated fork of BoringSSL used in AWS infrastructure?
  A) AWS-LC
  B) liboqs
  C) PQClean
  D) wolfSSL
Answer: A
Explanation: AWS-LC (Amazon's Libcrypto) is Amazon's FIPS 140-3 validated fork of BoringSSL. It includes ML-KEM-768 in the FIPS module as of 2024. The aws-lc-rs Rust crate provides safe bindings. It is used internally across all AWS services for TLS.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-dev-apis
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-dev-apis

Q: True or False: Windows CNG (Cryptography Next Generation) currently supports ML-DSA digital signatures in production as of early 2026.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: Windows CNG does not yet support ML-DSA in production. ML-KEM appeared in Windows 11 Insider builds in 2024, and ML-DSA is on the roadmap for Windows Server 2026+. Organizations needing PQC signing on Windows today must use OpenSSL, Bouncy Castle, or another library alongside CNG.

Q: In PKCS#11 v3.2, which mechanism family is used for ML-DSA digital signature operations?
  A) CKM_RSA_PKCS_*
  B) CKM_ECDSA_*
  C) CKM_SHA3_*
  D) CKM_ML_DSA_*
Answer: D
Explanation: PKCS#11 v3.2 (2023) introduced CKM_ML_DSA_* mechanisms for ML-DSA signing and CKM_ML_KEM_* for ML-KEM encapsulation. The mechanism structure is: CK_MECHANISM mech = { CKM_ML_DSA_44, NULL, 0 } for the ML-DSA-44 parameter set. HSM vendors (Thales Luna 10.x, Utimaco) are beginning to implement these mechanisms.

Q: Which crypto agility pattern enables A/B testing and gradual rollout between classical and PQC algorithms without redeploying application code?
  A) Provider Abstraction
  B) Configuration-Driven Algorithm Selection
  C) Hybrid/Composite Operations
  D) Algorithm Negotiation
Answer: B
Explanation: Configuration-Driven Selection externalizes the algorithm name (e.g., crypto.algorithm=ML-DSA-65 in a config file or environment variable). This enables runtime algorithm changes without code deploys, A/B testing between algorithm variants, and FIPS/non-FIPS environment differentiation from the same binary.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-dev-apis
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-dev-apis

Q: What is the correct dependency chain between PQClean, liboqs, and OpenSSL oqsprovider?
  A) PQClean → liboqs → oqsprovider → OpenSSL
  B) liboqs → PQClean → oqsprovider → OpenSSL
  C) oqsprovider → liboqs → PQClean → OpenSSL
  D) OpenSSL → oqsprovider → liboqs → PQClean
Answer: A
Explanation: PQClean provides audited reference C implementations. liboqs integrates PQClean implementations (plus optimized variants) into a unified C library with a common API. oqsprovider wraps liboqs as an OpenSSL 3.x provider. OpenSSL applications then consume PQC algorithms via the standard EVP API through this chain.

Q: A team is building a key management service that handles ML-KEM key generation and wrapping. They prioritize compile-time prevention of key material exposure over ecosystem maturity. Which language is the best fit?
  A) Rust
  B) Java
  C) Python
  D) Go
Answer: A
Explanation: Rust's ownership/borrow checker prevents use-after-free on key buffers at compile time — not at runtime. The aws-lc-rs and pqcrypto crates provide production-ready PQC support. Java is a strong second (Bouncy Castle, zero-copy APIs) but GC non-determinism means key material may persist in memory longer. Python is unsuitable for production key handling.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-dev-apis
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-dev-apis

Q: JCProv is primarily used to bridge which two technologies in an enterprise Java application?
  A) JCA/JCE and PKCS#11 hardware security modules
  B) Bouncy Castle and Windows CNG
  C) OpenSSL and Java KeyStore
  D) JSSE and FIPS 140-3 certified modules
Answer: A
Explanation: JCProv (from Thales/SafeNet) is a JCA provider that wraps PKCS#11. Once registered via Security.addProvider(), standard JCA calls like Signature.getInstance('ML-DSA-65', 'JCProv') route through PKCS#11 to the Luna or SafeNet HSM. Private key material never enters JVM heap memory — the HSM handles all key operations with opaque handles.

chunks.title: Quiz: platform-eng-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: platform-eng-pqc

Q: What does HNDL stand for in the context of CI/CD pipeline security?
  A) High-Node Dependency Layer
  B) Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later
  C) Hash-Node-Deploy-Link
  D) Hybrid-Network-Data-Layer
Answer: B
Explanation: Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) describes the adversary strategy of capturing encrypted data today — before a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) exists — and storing it for decryption once a CRQC becomes available. CI/CD pipelines are high-value targets because they produce long-lived signed artifacts (container images, SBOMs, build attestations) that an adversary can harvest now and decrypt later when they gain a CRQC.

Q: Which CI/CD pipeline assets have the HIGHEST HNDL exposure because they are captured and stored for long periods?
  A) Build logs and unit test results
  B) Ephemeral build container filesystems
  C) Container image signatures and SBOM attestations
  D) CI runner session tokens
Answer: C
Explanation: Container image signatures and SBOM attestations are stored in registries for years — the asset is both high-value (proves software provenance) and long-lived (retained across product lifecycle). An adversary who captures a signed SBOM today can forge provenance attestations once a CRQC breaks ECDSA. Ephemeral containers and session tokens expire quickly, reducing HNDL risk. Build logs lack cryptographic signatures that could be exploited.

chunks.content:

Q: ML-DSA-65 produces a signature of what approximate size, compared to ECDSA P-256's 64 bytes?
  A) 256 bytes (4×)
  B) 1,024 bytes (16×)
  C) 3,309 bytes (52×)
  D) 17,088 bytes (267×)
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, formerly CRYSTALS-ML-DSA level 3) produces 3,309-byte signatures — approximately 52× larger than ECDSA P-256's 64-byte signatures. This size increase matters significantly for OCI artifact signing because every container image pull verifies signatures, and TLS handshakes carry certificate chains. Planning for storage and bandwidth expansion is a core part of PQC platform migration.

Q: Which PQC algorithm is preferred for long-lived SBOM attestations (20+ year validity) instead of ML-DSA?
  A) ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203)
  B) SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, hash-based stateless signatures)
  C) X-Wing hybrid KEM
  D) FN-DSA-512 (FN-DSA)
Answer: B
Explanation: SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, formerly SLH-DSA) is preferred for SBOMs and long-lived build attestations because it is stateless — no per-key state management required — and its security is based purely on well-studied hash function assumptions. ML-DSA is faster but relies on module lattice hardness, making SLH-DSA preferable for signatures that must remain trustworthy for 20+ years. ML-KEM is a KEM (not a signature scheme) and X-Wing is for key exchange.

Q: Docker Content Trust (DCT) is based on which protocol that has no PQC migration roadmap?
  A) cosign with Rekor transparency log
  B) Notary v1 (The Update Framework)
  C) OCI image manifest signing (RFC 9052)
  D) Notation with AWS Crypto plugin
Answer: B
Explanation: Docker Content Trust uses Notary v1 (based on The Update Framework — TUF). Notary v1 is in maintenance mode and has no PQC migration roadmap. Docker has not announced plans to extend DCT with ML-DSA or any NIST PQC algorithm. Teams should migrate immediately to Notation (Notary v2) or cosign, both of which have PQC support on their roadmaps. Staying on DCT/Notary v1 beyond 2027 creates a HNDL risk for container image provenance.

Q: In an OPA Gatekeeper deployment, what does a ConstraintTemplate provide in a PQC enforcement context?
  A) A Kubernetes RBAC role granting crypto operations to platform engineers
  B) A Prometheus scrape configuration for certificate algorithm metrics
  C) A Rego policy schema that defines rules to block quantum-vulnerable algorithm OIDs in Kubernetes resources
  D) A cert-manager Certificate resource template for ML-DSA issuance
Answer: C
Explanation: An OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate defines a reusable Rego policy schema that describes what violation conditions to check. For PQC enforcement, a ConstraintTemplate would inspect incoming Kubernetes manifests (e.g., cert-manager Certificate resources or Helm values) for quantum-vulnerable algorithm identifiers (OIDs for RSA-2048, ECDSA, Ed25519) and block them at admission time. Concrete Constraint objects instantiate the template to target specific resource types.

Q: Which SLSA supply chain security level first requires ML-DSA or SLH-DSA for provenance attestations?
  A) Level 1 — basic provenance
  B) Level 2 — hosted build platform
  C) Level 3 — hardened build platform
  D) Level 4 — two-party review with HSM-backed signing
Answer: C
Explanation: SLSA Level 3 (hardened build platform) requires that provenance attestations use ML-DSA or SLH-DSA signatures, ensuring the build provenance is quantum-resistant. Level 4 further strengthens requirements by mandating ML-DSA-87 or SLH-DSA-256 (higher security parameters) and HSM-backed key storage. Levels 1 and 2 do not yet impose PQC signature requirements, though they are expected to align with NIST standards as adoption matures.

Q: The cert-manager Prometheus exporter exposes which metric that is central to PQC migration monitoring?
  A) CPU usage of the cert-manager controller pod
  B) Number of Kubernetes namespaces with active certificate issuers
  C) Certificate algorithm type, key size, and expiry date for all managed certificates
  D) TLS session resumption rate per ingress controller
Answer: C
Explanation: The cert-manager Prometheus exporter (certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds and certmanager_certificate_ready_status) tracks certificate metadata including algorithm type (RSA, ECDSA, ML-DSA), key size, issuer, and expiry. A PQC posture alert fires when a certificate using a quantum-vulnerable algorithm has an expiry date beyond the CRQC harvest horizon (e.g., after 2030). This enables automated detection of non-compliant certificates before they become a migration risk.

Q: To generate an ML-DSA-44 key via cert-manager v1.17+, which field in the Certificate resource must be configured?
  A) spec.acme.solvers[0].algorithm set to MLDSA44
  B) spec.issuerRef.kind set to MLDSAClusterIssuer
  C) spec.privateKey.algorithm set to MLDSA44
  D) spec.keystores.pkcs12.create set to true with algorithm: MLDSA44
Answer: C
Explanation: cert-manager v1.17+ added support for ML-DSA key generation via the Certificate resource's spec.privateKey.algorithm field. Setting algorithm: MLDSA44 (or MLDSA65, MLDSA87) instructs cert-manager to generate an ML-DSA key pair. The issuer (Vault PKI, EJBCA, or an internal CA) must also support ML-DSA certificate issuance — ACME issuers (Let's Encrypt) do not yet support PQC until 2026/2027. The spec.acme and spec.issuerRef fields control issuer selection, not key type.

Q: Rekor is the Sigstore transparency log used with cosign. What type of record does it store for a container signing event?
  A) The container image layers in encrypted form for supply chain verification
  B) An immutable, signed log entry recording the signing event: public key, artifact hash, and timestamp
  C) The signing private key in a hardware-secured append-only vault
  D) An OPA policy bundle describing which keys are authorized to sign which image repositories
Answer: B
Explanation: Rekor stores an append-only, cryptographically signed log entry for each signing event. The entry includes the public key (or certificate), the artifact hash being signed, the signature, and a timestamp — but never the private key. This enables anyone to verify that a container image was signed by a specific key at a specific time, and that the log has not been tampered with (Merkle tree root). Rekor is preparing for ML-DSA transparency log entries as cosign migrates to PQC signatures.

Q: As of 2025-2026, which container image signing tool offers the BEST production-ready ML-DSA support?
  A) Docker Content Trust (DCT / Notary v1)
  B) cosign v2 (Sigstore)
  C) Notation with AWS Signer or a compatible ML-DSA crypto plugin
  D) GPG/OpenPGP with ML-DSA patch
Answer: C
Explanation: Notation (Notary v2) reached beta PQC support in 2025 and, when combined with a crypto plugin such as AWS Signer or a compatible PKCS#11 plugin, enables ML-DSA-65 OCI artifact signing today. cosign has ML-DSA on its roadmap for 2026 but has not yet shipped it. Docker Content Trust (Notary v1) has no PQC roadmap. GPG/OpenPGP PQC drafts are in progress (RFC 9580) but OCI ecosystem integrations are not yet production-ready.

Q: A TLS 1.3 handshake using ML-DSA-65 certificates increases the handshake payload from approximately 4KB to what size?
  A) 6KB (1.5× increase)
  B) 10KB (2.5× increase)
  C) 18KB (4.5× increase)
  D) 50KB (12.5× increase)
Answer: C
Explanation: A classical TLS 1.3 handshake is approximately 4,096 bytes. With ML-DSA-65 certificate chains (each cert ~5,800B vs 800B for ECDSA P-256), the same handshake grows to approximately 18,432 bytes — a 4.5× increase. This affects not just bandwidth but also TLS handshake latency (P99 grows from ~12ms to ~28ms, a +133% increase). Capacity planning for etcd storage is also required: 1,000 certificates grow from 3MB to 14MB when migrating to ML-DSA.

Q: In an nginx-ingress Helm values file, which directive enables preference for ML-KEM key exchange (X25519MLKEM768)?
  A) proxy-ssl-protocols: "TLSv1.3 PQC"
  B) ssl-ecdh-curve: "X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256"
  C) ssl-prefer-server-ciphers: "on"
  D) proxy-ssl-ciphers: "TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_MLKEM_768"
Answer: B
Explanation: The nginx-ingress controller exposes ssl-ecdh-curve as a ConfigMap annotation that maps to OpenSSL's SSL_CTX_set1_groups(). Setting it to X25519MLKEM768:X25519:P-256 tells nginx to prefer the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid KEM (classical X25519 + ML-KEM-768) for TLS 1.3 key exchange, falling back to X25519 and P-256 for clients that do not yet support PQC. This is one of the lowest-risk IaC changes in a PQC migration because it is a pure cipher preference with backward compatibility.

Q: When deploying Kyverno policies that block quantum-vulnerable algorithm OIDs in Kubernetes, which rollout strategy minimises service disruption?
  A) Deploy in Enforce mode immediately and monitor for blocked resources in logs
  B) Deploy in Audit mode first for 2 weeks to build a baseline, then switch to Enforce mode
  C) Deploy both OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno simultaneously in Enforce mode to maximise coverage
  D) Enable Dry-Run flag permanently to avoid ever blocking legitimate workloads
Answer: B
Explanation: The recommended pattern for admission control policy rollouts is: (1) Deploy in Audit mode, which logs violations without blocking resources. (2) Run for approximately 2 weeks to capture a realistic baseline of existing quantum-vulnerable algorithm usage. (3) Review and triage violations — create exceptions for legacy systems that cannot migrate immediately. (4) Switch to Enforce mode with exceptions in place. Deploying directly in Enforce mode risks blocking CI/CD pipelines and production workloads that have not yet migrated signing keys.

Q: A platform engineering team plans a full Kubernetes cluster PQC migration. What is the correct dependency-respecting phase order?
  A) Artifact Signing → Root CA → TLS Key Exchange → Policy Enforcement → CI Identity
  B) Root CA (ML-DSA-65) → X-Wing TLS KEX → Artifact Signing → CI Identity → Policy Cut-Over
  C) Policy Enforcement → Root CA → TLS KEX → Artifact Signing → Inventory
  D) TLS Key Exchange → Policy Enforcement → Root CA → Artifact Signing → Inventory
Answer: B
Explanation: The correct phase order follows trust chain dependencies: (1) Inventory — understand blast radius before any change; (2) Root CA migration to ML-DSA-65 — everything downstream depends on a PQC-capable trust anchor; (3) X-Wing TLS KEX — protects in-flight data from HNDL once the CA can issue PQC certificates; (4) Artifact Signing — container and SBOM signatures now use ML-DSA-backed trust chain; (5) CI Identity — service accounts, build credentials; (6) Policy Cut-Over — enforce that all new resources use PQC. Starting with Policy Cut-Over before the Root CA breaks all existing certificate issuance.

Q: What is the 'Secret Zero' problem in secrets management?
  A) The first secret stored in a vault is always unencrypted by default
  B) The bootstrapping challenge of securely authenticating to a secrets manager before any secrets have been provisioned
  C) A vulnerability in HashiCorp Vault version 0.x affecting seal/unseal operations
  D) The master encryption key that encrypts all other keys in a KMS hierarchy
Answer: B
Explanation: Secret Zero is the bootstrapping dilemma: to retrieve secrets from a vault, a service needs a credential, but that credential must itself be stored somewhere securely. Solutions include platform identity (AWS IAM roles, Kubernetes service accounts), HSM-backed tokens, and vault agent auto-auth. PQC does not change the Secret Zero problem but introduces larger key material for the authentication credential.

Q: In HashiCorp Vault's Transit Secrets Engine, what is the primary purpose?
  A) Storing and retrieving static API keys and credentials for applications
  B) Providing encryption-as-a-service: encrypting/decrypting data without storing the plaintext in Vault
  C) Managing TLS certificates for Kubernetes ingress controllers
  D) Automatically rotating database passwords on a schedule
Answer: B
Explanation: The Transit Secrets Engine is Vault's 'encryption-as-a-service' offering. Applications send plaintext to Vault via API; Vault encrypts it with a named key and returns ciphertext. The plaintext never persists in Vault. This is the component most directly impacted by PQC: the transit key wrapping algorithm (currently AES-256-GCM for DEKs, protected by ECDH or RSA KEKs) must be upgraded to ML-KEM-768 for quantum safety.

Q: Which category of secret has the HIGHEST HNDL (Harvest Now Decrypt Later) risk?
  A) Session tokens valid for 15 minutes
  B) API keys that are automatically rotated every 24 hours
  C) Long-term signing keys protecting code repositories expected to remain valid for 10+ years
  D) Temporary AWS STS credentials with a 1-hour lifetime
Answer: C
Explanation: HNDL risk is a function of (1) sensitivity of the protected data and (2) how long the secret must remain valid. Long-term code-signing keys protecting firmware or software that may be verified for decades represent the highest HNDL risk. An adversary who harvests the encrypted key material today and decrypts it in 10 years gains the ability to forge software signatures retroactively.

Q: HashiCorp Vault uses envelope encryption: a Data Encryption Key (DEK) encrypts the data, and a Key Encryption Key (KEK) wraps the DEK. For post-quantum safety, which component MUST be upgraded first?
  A) The DEK algorithm (AES-256-GCM) -- upgrade to AES-512
  B) The KEK wrapping mechanism -- replace RSA-OAEP or ECDH wrapping with ML-KEM-768
  C) The Vault audit log encryption algorithm
  D) The Vault TLS certificate used for API connections
Answer: B
Explanation: AES-256-GCM (the DEK) is already quantum-resistant: Grover's algorithm reduces its effective security from 256 bits to 128 bits, which remains computationally infeasible. The vulnerability is in the KEK wrapping layer: RSA-OAEP and ECDH are both broken by Shor's algorithm. The critical PQC change is replacing KEK wrapping with ML-KEM-768 (or the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid for backward compatibility during transition).

Q: AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets encrypted at rest using AWS KMS data keys. The data key itself is protected by a KMS key. Which AWS KMS change provides the STRONGEST quantum protection for secrets at rest?
  A) Enable automatic rotation for all secrets (90-day rotation)
  B) Migrate KMS keys to ML-KEM-768-protected key material (using AWS CloudHSM PQC HSM backing)
  C) Enable multi-region KMS key replication for all secrets
  D) Switch from symmetric KMS keys to asymmetric KMS key pairs
Answer: B
Explanation: AWS Secrets Manager uses envelope encryption: AES-256-GCM for the secret value, protected by a KMS data key, which is in turn protected by the KMS key's backing material. The AES-256 layer is quantum-resistant. The vulnerability is the KMS key protection mechanism. Migrating KMS key wrapping to ML-KEM-768 (when available) eliminates the HNDL attack surface on the key hierarchy. Automatic rotation addresses compromise detection but not quantum harvesting of key material.

Q: What are 'dynamic secrets' in HashiCorp Vault and how do they reduce HNDL risk?
  A) Secrets that change their encryption algorithm based on the client's quantum readiness
  B) Short-lived credentials generated on-demand for each request, reducing HNDL exposure by minimizing credential lifetime
  C) Secrets stored in RAM only, never written to disk, ensuring forward secrecy
  D) Vault secrets with automatic quantum-random number generation for key material
Answer: B
Explanation: Dynamic secrets are generated by Vault on-demand for each request and have a defined TTL (lease duration). For example, Vault's database secrets engine creates a unique database user with a random password for each client request, then revokes it when the TTL expires. This dramatically reduces HNDL risk: an adversary who harvests a dynamic secret in transit can only use it for its TTL window (typically minutes to hours) rather than years.

Q: A CI/CD pipeline uses GitHub Actions OIDC to authenticate to HashiCorp Vault and retrieve deployment secrets. The OIDC token is signed with RS256 (RSA-2048). For PQC migration, what change is REQUIRED to harden the authentication path?
  A) Enable Vault's PKI secrets engine and issue ML-KEM-768 certificates to GitHub runners
  B) Migrate GitHub's OIDC token signing from RS256 to ML-DSA-65 (when GitHub adds PQC OIDC support)
  C) Switch from OIDC to AppRole authentication with a 4096-bit RSA wrapped secret_id
  D) Enable Vault Agent's auto-auth with AWS IAM instead of GitHub OIDC
Answer: B
Explanation: OIDC-based authentication relies on JWT token signatures for identity proof. RS256 (RSA-2048) is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. An adversary who captures OIDC tokens could later forge authentication tokens if they can derive the private key. The migration path is for GitHub (or any OIDC provider) to adopt ML-DSA-65 for token signing per the JOSE/JWT PQC draft (draft-ietf-jose-dilithium).

Q: In Kubernetes, the External Secrets Operator (ESO) syncs secrets from external providers (Vault, AWS SM, Azure KV) into Kubernetes Secrets. What is the PRIMARY quantum vulnerability in this architecture?
  A) The ESO pod communicates with backends over mTLS using ECDSA certificates
  B) Kubernetes Secrets are stored in etcd encrypted with AES-CBC, which is quantum-vulnerable
  C) The ExternalSecret resource exposes secret metadata in plaintext in the Kubernetes API
  D) Both A and B represent quantum vulnerabilities in the ESO architecture
Answer: D
Explanation: ESO has two PQC-relevant surfaces: (1) The transport layer between ESO and external backends uses mTLS with ECDSA/RSA certificates vulnerable to quantum key recovery. (2) Kubernetes Secrets stored in etcd use AES-CBC (or AES-GCM in newer versions) for encryption at rest, but the etcd encryption key is typically wrapped with an RSA or ECDH master key. Both require PQC upgrades: ML-KEM for transport KEX and ML-DSA for mTLS certificates.

Q: BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) allows organizations to use their own HSM-generated keys in cloud secrets managers. In a PQC context, what does a quantum-safe BYOK implementation require?
  A) An HSM with ML-KEM-768 key generation capability for the BYOK key transport wrapping
  B) Cloud provider support for importing ML-KEM-768 public keys as BYOK transport keys
  C) A hybrid key transport protocol (ML-KEM + classical) for backward-compatible BYOK during transition
  D) All of the above are required for a complete PQC BYOK implementation
Answer: D
Explanation: Quantum-safe BYOK requires the entire key import ceremony to use PQC-resistant cryptography: (1) The HSM must generate ML-KEM-768 keys for the key transport wrapping operation. (2) The cloud provider must accept ML-KEM-768 public keys for the BYOK import endpoint. (3) During transition, hybrid key transport (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) provides backward compatibility while protecting against HNDL attacks on the import ceremony.

Q: Secret Sprawl describes the proliferation of secrets across systems without centralized management. How does PQC migration potentially worsen secret sprawl?
  A) PQC migration forces secrets to be replicated across all geographic regions simultaneously
  B) PQC migration requires larger key material storage, increasing memory and disk pressure that incentivizes teams to store keys in non-standard locations
  C) Each team may independently migrate to different PQC algorithms, creating a heterogeneous secret ecosystem with inconsistent algorithm policies across services
  D) PQC migration automatically triggers secret rotation, exposing previously unknown secret locations
Answer: C
Explanation: PQC migration often reveals secret sprawl because each team may implement their own PQC approach: Team A uses ML-KEM-768, Team B uses X25519MLKEM768 hybrid, Team C delays migration entirely. The result is algorithm heterogeneity that defeats centralized key management policies. A centralized secrets manager (Vault, AWS SM) with a unified PQC algorithm policy is the solution, but requires discovery of all secret locations first -- which is exactly the problem that secret sprawl creates.

Q: HashiCorp Vault Enterprise uses AWS KMS as an Auto Unseal provider. The unseal key is wrapped with the KMS key using RSA-OAEP or AES-256-GCM (depending on key type). What is the most complete post-quantum hardening of the Vault unseal path?
  A) Switch from AWS KMS Auto Unseal to Shamir Secret Sharing with 5-of-7 physical key holders
  B) Upgrade the AWS KMS key backing to ML-KEM-768 key wrapping once AWS adds PQC KMS key types
  C) Configure Vault Enterprise HSM Integration (PKCS#11) pointing to an ML-KEM-capable HSM for unseal key wrapping
  D) Rotate the Vault master key monthly to reduce the HNDL window
Answer: C
Explanation: HSM Integration via PKCS#11 provides the most direct path: an ML-KEM-768 capable HSM (using CKM_ML_KEM_ENCAPSULATE for unseal key wrapping) keeps the root of trust in validated hardware with PQC capabilities. AWS KMS PQC key types are on the roadmap but not yet generally available. Monthly rotation reduces the HNDL window but doesn't eliminate the fundamental vulnerability of RSA-wrapped unseal keys that may have been harvested.

Q: A rotation policy designer must set TTLs for ML-DSA-65 signing keys used in a firmware authentication system. Which rotation trigger is MOST appropriate for high-security firmware signing keys?
  A) Time-based: rotate every 90 days (NIST SP 800-57 recommendation)
  B) Use-based: rotate after each firmware release, generating a new ML-DSA-65 key per product version
  C) Volume-based: rotate after signing 1000 firmware images
  D) Risk-based: rotate only when threat intelligence indicates key compromise risk
Answer: B
Explanation: For firmware signing keys, use-based rotation is superior to time-based rotation. Each firmware release should be signed by a unique key, limiting blast radius: if signing key K was compromised, only firmware signed with K is affected, not all firmware. ML-DSA-65's stateless nature (unlike LMS/XMSS) makes per-release key rotation operationally practical. The corresponding public key is embedded in the root of trust or certificate chain for each release.

Q: A pipeline integration lab deploys GitHub Actions OIDC with Vault for a microservices platform. 47 services each have unique AppRole credentials stored in a centralized secrets manager. When migrating all AppRole credentials to ML-KEM-protected storage, what is the SAFEST migration sequence?
  A) Rotate all 47 AppRole secret_ids simultaneously in a maintenance window to minimize the migration window
  B) Migrate one service at a time: update secret_id wrapped with ML-KEM in Vault, update the service's retrieval path, verify, then proceed to the next
  C) Back up all AppRole credentials to a separate encrypted store, then perform batch rotation
  D) Enable Vault's namespace feature to create a parallel PQC namespace and gradually migrate services
Answer: B
Explanation: Sequential per-service migration minimizes blast radius. Each service is individually migrated, verified, and monitored before the next service begins. This approach catches issues early (e.g., a service that cannot handle the larger ML-KEM-wrapped credential) without affecting all 47 services. The batch approach (A) risks a simultaneous failure across all services if the migration process has a bug.

Q: Azure Key Vault uses RSA-OAEP for key wrapping in its Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) import flow. The BYOK specification requires the customer to wrap their key with a Microsoft-provided RSA-2048 or RSA-3072 transport key. What PQC change would make this import ceremony quantum-safe?
  A) Increase the Microsoft transport key size to RSA-8192
  B) Replace the RSA transport key with an ML-KEM-1024 public key in the BYOK import specification, requiring the customer HSM to perform ML-KEM encapsulation for key transport
  C) Add an additional AES-256-GCM encryption layer around the RSA-wrapped key material
  D) Use TLS 1.3 with X25519MLKEM768 for the BYOK upload HTTP request, protecting the RSA-wrapped payload in transit
Answer: B
Explanation: The BYOK ceremony's fundamental vulnerability is RSA-OAEP transport wrapping: if an adversary captures the BYOK import request, they can later decrypt the wrapped customer key using a CRQC, gaining access to all data encrypted under that key hierarchy. Replacing the RSA transport key with ML-KEM-1024 makes the import ceremony post-quantum: the customer HSM performs CKM_ML_KEM_ENCAPSULATE to wrap the customer key, and even a CRQC cannot unwrap it.

Q: A cloud-native application runs 200 microservices on Kubernetes. Each service uses Vault Agent Sidecar to retrieve secrets. The Vault server uses ECDH P-256 for transit key wrapping. During a PQC migration audit, the team identifies that Vault Agent's OIDC auth method uses JWK RS256 signature verification. What is the complete PQC hardening checklist (in dependency order)?
  A) Update Vault TLS -> Rotate transit keys to ML-KEM-768 -> Update OIDC JWK signing to ML-DSA-65
  B) Update OIDC JWK signing to ML-DSA-65 -> Update Vault TLS to ML-DSA-65 -> Rotate all transit keys to ML-KEM-768 -> Restart Vault Agents
  C) Update Vault TLS to X25519MLKEM768 hybrid -> Rotate transit DEKs to AES-512 -> Update OIDC to ES256
  D) Enable Vault Sentinel policies to enforce ML-KEM usage -> Then rotate keys
Answer: B
Explanation: The correct dependency order is: (1) Migrate OIDC token signing to ML-DSA-65 first -- this hardens the authentication path that Vault Agents use to obtain vault tokens. (2) Upgrade Vault TLS to ML-DSA-65 certificates -- protects key material in transit. (3) Rotate all transit keys to ML-KEM-768 KEK wrapping -- this is the bulk operation; all 200 services' secrets must be re-wrapped. (4) Restart Vault Agents to pick up new token audiences. OIDC must come first because it's the trust anchor for agent authentication.

Q: What is the primary challenge that ML-DSA-65 certificates pose for NGFW TLS inspection (break-and-inspect) proxies?
  A) ML-DSA-65 certificates are incompatible with TLS 1.3 cipher suites
  B) Certificate sizes increase from approximately 1KB (RSA/ECDSA) to 5-6KB (ML-DSA-65), requiring buffer and memory capacity upgrades in inspection appliances
  C) TLS inspection becomes legally prohibited when ML-DSA-65 is used
  D) ML-DSA-65 requires a quantum co-processor for certificate validation, unavailable in current NGFWs
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 public keys are 1,952 bytes and signatures are 3,293 bytes, compared to ECDSA P-256's 64-byte public key and 64-byte signature. A full certificate chain with two ML-DSA-65 certs (leaf + intermediate) can reach 12-15KB versus 2-3KB for ECDSA. NGFW inspection appliances that buffer entire certificate chains for validation need capacity upgrades. Hardware SSL offload ASICs designed for RSA/ECDSA key sizes also require replacement or firmware updates.

Q: A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) inspects TLS traffic. After enabling PQC hybrid cipher suites (X25519MLKEM768), DPI throughput drops 35%. What is the MOST likely combined cause?
  A) PQC cipher suites use CBC mode, which is CPU-intensive for hardware ASICs
  B) Larger ML-KEM key exchange messages (1,568 bytes total) and larger ML-DSA certificate chains (5-15KB) increase the data volume processed per TLS handshake; hardware SSL offload ASICs designed for RSA/ECDSA cannot accelerate ML-KEM or ML-DSA in software fallback
  C) PQC algorithms use a proprietary TLS extension that bypasses hardware acceleration entirely
  D) The NGFW vendor's PQC implementation is unoptimized beta code with debug logging overhead
Answer: B
Explanation: The throughput impact has two components: (1) Larger TLS handshakes due to ML-KEM ciphertext (1,088 bytes for ML-KEM-768) and ML-DSA certificates (~6KB per cert). (2) Hardware SSL offload ASICs -- designed to accelerate RSA/ECDSA operations -- cannot accelerate lattice-based algorithms. PQC processing falls back to general-purpose CPU cores, reducing total inspection capacity. This is an architectural constraint, not a software bug.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: What does Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) mean in practice?
  A) All network traffic is encrypted with AES-256 by default
  B) No device or user is trusted by default regardless of network location; access requires continuous verification of identity, device health, and context for every request
  C) All internal network traffic must pass through a quantum-safe VPN
  D) Zero knowledge proofs replace passwords in network authentication
Answer: B
Explanation: ZTNA replaces the traditional perimeter model ('trust everything inside the firewall') with continuous verification. Each access request is evaluated against identity, device posture, application policy, and context -- regardless of whether the request originates from inside or outside the corporate network. PQC impacts ZTNA primarily through the cryptographic underpinning of identity verification (certificates, tokens) and device attestation.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: A Palo Alto Networks NGFW running PAN-OS 11.x performs SSL Inspection using a forward proxy. To maintain inspection capability after clients adopt ML-KEM key exchange, which component requires a PQC certificate upgrade?
  A) The firewall's management interface certificate (HTTPS admin access)
  B) The SSL Inspection forward proxy CA certificate, which the firewall uses to re-sign intercepted connections -- it must be upgraded to an ML-DSA-65 CA to issue valid ML-DSA-signed re-signed certificates to clients
  C) Client-side browser trust store certificates
  D) The upstream server certificates
Answer: B
Explanation: When a NGFW performs SSL forward proxy inspection, it intercepts the TLS session, decrypts the traffic, inspects it, then re-encrypts and forwards it to the client with a firewall-signed certificate. For clients that verify ML-DSA signatures, the firewall's re-signing CA must itself use ML-DSA-65 to produce valid certificate signatures. If the firewall still uses an RSA CA for re-signing while clients enforce ML-DSA-only, inspection will fail with certificate validation errors.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: A Cisco Firepower NGFW uses custom hardware TLS offload ASICs rated for RSA-4096 and ECDSA P-384. After network-wide PQC adoption, what is the expected SSL inspection behavior for ML-KEM connections?
  A) Hardware offload continues transparently -- modern ASICs support all IANA-registered algorithms
  B) Hardware TLS offload is bypassed for ML-KEM connections; the ASIC falls back to general-purpose CPU processing for ML-KEM key exchange, significantly reducing the number of concurrent TLS sessions the appliance can inspect
  C) ML-KEM connections are automatically passed through without inspection as a security bypass
  D) The ASIC can be field-upgraded via firmware to support ML-KEM with no performance impact
Answer: B
Explanation: Current-generation TLS offload ASICs are hardwired for RSA and ECDSA operations. Lattice-based algorithms (ML-KEM) require different mathematical primitives (Module Learning With Errors polynomial multiplication) that are not accelerated by these ASICs. The result is a software fallback that runs at 5-20% of hardware-accelerated throughput for RSA, depending on core count and ASIC overhead. Cisco has announced next-generation ASICs with ML-KEM acceleration for late 2026+.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: An IDS/IPS rule engine needs to be updated for PQC traffic. Which new detection rule is MOST valuable for identifying legitimate PQC key exchange versus potential TLS-based covert channels?
  A) Block all TLS ClientHello messages larger than 2KB to prevent ML-KEM enumeration attacks
  B) Alert on TLS ClientHello messages containing the IANA-registered X25519MLKEM768 group (0x11EC) or ML-KEM-768 (0x6399) in supported_groups, combined with matching client application (Chrome 124+, Firefox 127+, BoringSSL 2024+) to baseline legitimate PQC adoption
  C) Block all connections using TLS 1.3 extension type 0x002B (supported_versions) with PQC entries
  D) Alert on all key_share extensions larger than 500 bytes as potential buffer overflow attempts
Answer: B
Explanation: Legitimate PQC key exchange has identifiable fingerprints: IANA-assigned group IDs (0x11EC for X25519MLKEM768, 0x6399 for ML-KEM-768) in supported_groups, specific key_share sizes (1,568 bytes for X25519MLKEM768), and correlation with known PQC-capable client software. Correlating these signals allows the IDS to distinguish legitimate PQC adoption (which should be allowed and baselined) from anomalous oversized handshakes (which may warrant investigation).

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: Fortinet FortiOS 7.6 added initial PQC support. Which feature was prioritized in this release?
  A) Full ML-DSA-65 certificate validation for deep SSL inspection
  B) ML-KEM hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) support for IPsec VPN and SSL-VPN tunnels
  C) SLH-DSA-based IPS signature package signing
  D) ML-KEM support in the FortiGate management plane API only
Answer: B
Explanation: Fortinet's initial PQC priority was IPsec VPN key exchange hardening. The X25519MLKEM768 hybrid KEM protects VPN tunnel session keys from HNDL attacks without breaking interoperability with sites that haven't yet deployed PQC (the X25519 component ensures backward compatibility). Full ML-DSA certificate validation for SSL inspection is a more complex feature requiring ASIC changes and is targeted for FortiOS 8.x.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: In a Zero Trust architecture with micro-segmentation, east-west mTLS traffic between services uses ML-DSA-65 certificates. Which operational challenge is MOST significant compared to ECDSA P-256 mTLS?
  A) ML-DSA-65 mTLS is incompatible with service mesh implementations
  B) Certificate revocation checking latency increases due to ML-DSA OCSP response sizes being larger than ECDSA responses
  C) Service-to-service authentication latency increases because ML-DSA-65 signature verification is slower than ECDSA P-256 for high-frequency micro-calls
  D) Both B and C represent measurable operational impacts that require capacity planning adjustments
Answer: D
Explanation: Both impacts are real: (1) ML-DSA-65 OCSP responses include the 3,293-byte signature rather than a 64-byte ECDSA signature, increasing OCSP response sizes from ~2KB to ~5KB and adding network overhead in high-volume environments. (2) ML-DSA-65 verification requires approximately 0.3ms on modern CPUs vs 0.1ms for ECDSA P-256. For microservices making 10,000+ mTLS connections per second, this 3x slowdown requires horizontal scaling adjustment.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: For site-to-site IPsec VPN with Juniper SRX routers, which PQC changes are BOTH required for a complete quantum-safe migration?
  A) ML-KEM for IKEv2 key exchange only (authentication is already quantum-safe)
  B) ML-DSA for IKEv2 authentication only (key exchange AES-256 is already quantum-safe)
  C) Both ML-KEM (for IKEv2 KE payload per RFC 9370) and ML-DSA (for IKEv2 AUTH payload, replacing RSA/ECDSA certificates) are required for complete PQC IPsec
  D) ML-KEM for key exchange + AES-512 for ESP encryption replaces both RSA and ECDSA
Answer: C
Explanation: IPsec has two distinct crypto surfaces: (1) IKEv2 Key Exchange (KE payload) -- uses DH/ECDH for session key derivation, replaced by ML-KEM per RFC 9370 to defeat HNDL. (2) IKEv2 Authentication (AUTH payload) -- uses RSA or ECDSA certificates to authenticate VPN endpoints; replaced by ML-DSA-65 to prevent quantum-capable forgery of VPN identities. Both must be migrated: an attacker who harvests the KE payload can reconstruct session keys without authentication bypass, but one who compromises the AUTH certificates can impersonate VPN endpoints.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: Check Point's Smart-1 management server uses TLS for communication with Security Gateways. In a PQC migration, which component should be upgraded FIRST?
  A) The Security Gateway TLS inspection CA certificate
  B) The Smart-1 management server TLS certificate and CA, as it is the root of trust for all gateway management communications
  C) The remote access VPN certificates for end users
  D) The gateway cluster synchronization certificates
Answer: B
Explanation: The Smart-1 management server is the root of trust for the entire Check Point management infrastructure. All Security Gateways authenticate to Smart-1 using TLS. If an adversary harvests management plane TLS traffic, they can later recover policy configurations and credential material. Upgrading Smart-1's TLS to ML-DSA-65 first protects the most sensitive management channel before working outward to gateway TLS inspection and VPN certificates.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: A network architect designs a PQC-aware ZTNA architecture using a ZTNA proxy that terminates and re-originates TLS. To support both legacy (RSA/ECDSA) and PQC (ML-DSA-65) clients simultaneously, which architecture is MOST appropriate?
  A) Deploy a single ZTNA proxy with a unified ML-DSA-65 certificate; legacy clients that cannot validate ML-DSA will fail gracefully with a certificate error
  B) Deploy dual-root CA infrastructure: RSA/ECDSA root for legacy clients and ML-DSA-65 root for PQC clients; the ZTNA proxy serves the appropriate certificate chain based on TLS ClientHello capabilities
  C) Deploy separate proxy instances for legacy and PQC clients, split by DNS or BGP anycast
  D) Enable TLS-in-TLS tunneling for legacy clients to avoid certificate compatibility issues
Answer: B
Explanation: Dual-root CA infrastructure is the standard transition pattern. The ZTNA proxy inspects the TLS ClientHello's signature_algorithms extension: if the client advertises ml-dsa65 support, the proxy presents an ML-DSA-65 certificate chain. If not, it presents the RSA/ECDSA chain. This approach maintains compatibility with legacy clients while providing PQC protection for quantum-capable clients -- exactly the transition period behavior required.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) with PQC faces a TCP segmentation challenge. What is the most accurate description of the problem?
  A) ML-KEM ciphertext is encrypted at the IP layer, preventing DPI from parsing TCP segments
  B) X25519MLKEM768 key_share entries (1,600+ bytes) may span multiple TCP segments requiring DPI engines to reassemble fragmented TLS records before pattern-matching can occur, increasing memory and processing requirements
  C) TLS 1.3 record size limits (16KB max) prevent ML-DSA certificates from being transmitted
  D) ML-DSA handshake fragmentation requires a new TLS extension that legacy DPI engines do not recognize
Answer: B
Explanation: A TLS record carrying an X25519MLKEM768 key_share entry (1,568 bytes) plus TLS record overhead is approximately 1,600 bytes. Standard MTU is 1,500 bytes (Ethernet). This means the key_share entry itself may span two or more TCP segments. DPI engines that perform pattern matching on individual packets (not reassembled streams) will miss handshake signatures that span packet boundaries. Stream-based DPI reassembly (like Suricata's stream engine) handles this correctly, but packet-based inspection tools require updates.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: A SIEM analyst receives alerts about anomalously large TLS ClientHello messages (>3KB) from workstations in the engineering department. The analyst must distinguish PQC key exchange adoption from malicious TLS fingerprinting or exfiltration. Which combination of signals is MOST diagnostic?
  A) Source IP reputation + destination port 443 + ClientHello size
  B) ClientHello supported_groups extension containing IANA group 0x11EC (X25519MLKEM768) + client software version (Chrome 124+/Edge 124+/Firefox 127+) + normal destination (known SaaS/CDN) + consistent key_share size of exactly 1,600 bytes
  C) Block all ClientHellos >2KB as a precautionary measure
  D) Correlate with endpoint EDR to check if a PQC VPN client was recently installed
Answer: B
Explanation: Legitimate PQC key exchange has a highly specific fingerprint: IANA group 0x11EC (X25519MLKEM768) in supported_groups, key_share size of exactly 1,568 bytes (ML-KEM-768 ciphertext 1,088 + X25519 32 + framing = ~1,600 bytes), and originated from known PQC-capable browsers/clients connecting to known destinations. Malicious oversized ClientHellos would likely not align with these specific IANA identifiers or would show irregular sizes. This combination provides high-confidence disambiguation.

chunks.title: Quiz: network-security-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: network-security-pqc

Q: RFC 9370 defines 'Multiple Key Exchanges in IKEv2' for hybrid PQC+classical key exchange. Which statement accurately describes its operation?
  A) RFC 9370 replaces IKEv2 entirely with a new quantum-safe key agreement protocol
  B) RFC 9370 adds Additional Key Exchange (AKE) payloads to IKEv2, allowing a classical key exchange (ECDH) and a PQC key exchange (ML-KEM) to be combined: the session key is derived from BOTH exchanges, ensuring security if either is compromised
  C) RFC 9370 mandates ML-KEM-1024 for all IKEv2 negotiations
  D) RFC 9370 is an informational RFC describing deployment best practices but does not change IKEv2 on-wire format
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9370 extends IKEv2 with Additional Key Exchange (AKE) payloads that carry a second (or more) key exchange alongside the classical DH. The IKEv2 SKEYSEED derivation mixes all key exchange outputs using HMAC, resulting in a session key that is secure if any one of the contributing key exchanges is secure. This hybrid approach ensures: (1) No regression vs classical IKEv2 if ML-KEM is somehow broken; (2) Post-quantum security if ECDH is broken by a CRQC.

Q: An enterprise is selecting a NGFW platform to lead its PQC migration. Requirements: (1) ML-KEM TLS inspection by Q3 2026, (2) ML-DSA for management plane cert auth, (3) Hardware form factor, (4) Junos/PAN-OS/FortiOS ecosystem with ML-DSA management plane support. Which vendor best matches all four requirements based on public roadmaps as of early 2026?
  A) SonicWall NSa Series (roadmap TBD 2027+)
  B) pfSense CE with OPNsense (community-driven, no committed enterprise roadmap)
  C) Palo Alto Networks NGFW with PAN-OS 11.x (ML-KEM TLS inspection beta Q2 2026) + PAN-OS 12 (ML-DSA management plane Q4 2026)
  D) Juniper SRX with Junos 25.x (ML-KEM IKEv2 2025) + ML-DSA management plane 2026
Answer: C
Explanation: Palo Alto Networks has the most mature PQC NGFW roadmap as of early 2026: PAN-OS 11.x introduced ML-KEM hybrid TLS key exchange support (preview), with full ML-KEM TLS inspection targeted for Q2-Q3 2026. ML-DSA management plane certificate authentication is planned for PAN-OS 12 (Q4 2026). Juniper SRX's Junos PQC roadmap is strong for IPsec (ML-KEM IKEv2 shipped in 24.x) but management plane ML-DSA support is later. SonicWall and pfSense have no committed enterprise PQC timelines.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: What is Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)?
  A) A feature that encrypts database network traffic between client and server
  B) A database encryption feature that automatically encrypts data files and transaction logs at rest without requiring application changes
  C) An encryption standard for individual database column values only
  D) A method for encrypting SQL query parameters before transmission
Answer: B
Explanation: TDE encrypts the physical storage layer: data files (.mdf, .ndf), log files (.ldf), and backups. Encryption and decryption happen automatically at the database engine level, making it transparent to applications -- no code changes are required. TDE uses a hierarchical key structure: a Data Encryption Key (DEK) encrypted with a certificate or asymmetric key, which is protected by the database master key or an external KMS.

Q: In current TDE implementations, which component is MOST vulnerable to a quantum attack?
  A) The AES-256-GCM data encryption key (DEK) -- Grover's algorithm halves its security to 128 bits
  B) The RSA or ECDH-based mechanism that wraps and protects the DEK, which Shor's algorithm can break to expose the DEK
  C) The SHA-256 hash in the transaction log integrity check
  D) The TLS channel between application and database server
Answer: B
Explanation: TDE uses a two-layer architecture: the DEK (AES-256-GCM) encrypts the actual data, and a certificate/asymmetric key wraps the DEK. AES-256-GCM with 128-bit post-quantum security (after Grover) remains computationally infeasible to break. The vulnerability is in the DEK wrapping: RSA-OAEP or ECDH key derivation for the DEK protection is broken by Shor's algorithm. An adversary who harvests the encrypted DEK today can decrypt it in the future to expose all TDE-protected data.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: What does HYOK (Hold Your Own Key) mean in the context of database encryption?
  A) The database encryption key is automatically rotated by the cloud provider
  B) The customer maintains exclusive control of encryption keys in their own HSM or data center; the cloud provider never has access to the keys
  C) The database uses a hybrid encryption scheme combining classical and PQC algorithms
  D) A backup key retention policy requiring keys to be held for 7 years
Answer: B
Explanation: HYOK extends BYOK: in BYOK, the customer generates keys but the cloud provider may temporarily process the key material during import. In HYOK, the cloud provider performs cryptographic operations using the customer's key without ever accessing the plaintext key -- typically via a protocol where the cloud service sends data to the customer HSM for decryption and receives only the result. This eliminates cloud-provider key exposure but introduces latency for every database decryption operation.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: SQL Server TDE protects the Database Encryption Key (DEK) using a certificate stored in the master database. The certificate uses RSA-2048. What is the correct PQC migration for the SQL Server TDE key hierarchy?
  A) Increase the SQL Server TDE certificate key size from RSA-2048 to RSA-4096
  B) Replace the TDE certificate with an ML-DSA-65 certificate; the AES-256-CTR DEK itself remains quantum-safe and does not require algorithm change
  C) Migrate all TDE-encrypted databases to Always Encrypted (column-level)
  D) Enable SQL Server Database Encryption Key rotation using AES-512 algorithm
Answer: B
Explanation: SQL Server TDE's crypto weakness is in the certificate key: RSA-2048 is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. The AES-256 DEK is already post-quantum resistant (128-bit security after Grover). The migration is: (1) Create a new ML-DSA-65 certificate in master, (2) Alter the Database Encryption Key to be protected by the new ML-DSA-65 certificate, (3) Allow SQL Server to re-wrap the DEK under the new certificate (this is fast -- only the DEK wrapper changes, not the 50TB of data).

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: Oracle Advanced Security TDE uses a Master Encryption Key (MEK) stored in Oracle Wallet (PKCS#12). The MEK wraps all Tablespace Encryption Keys (TEKs). What is the most feasible PQC migration for Oracle TDE?
  A) Increase the Oracle Wallet RSA key size to RSA-8192
  B) Migrate the MEK from Oracle Wallet to Oracle Key Vault (OKV), configure OKV to use an external ML-KEM-768-capable HSM for MEK wrapping, eliminating the RSA dependency in the key hierarchy
  C) Re-encrypt all Oracle tablespaces with AES-512 as a post-quantum upgrade
  D) Use Oracle's Transparent Sensitive Data Protection (TSDP) instead of TDE
Answer: B
Explanation: Oracle Wallet PKCS#12 uses RSA for the MEK protection. The migration path via OKV provides: (1) Centralized key management with HSM backing, (2) ML-KEM-768 capable HSMs (nShield, Thales Luna, AWS CloudHSM) can provide PQC-resistant MEK wrapping, (3) OKV's REST API supports plugin-based KMS integration. Re-encrypting tablespaces with AES-512 is not a real option (no Oracle TDE supports AES-512) and would require full offline re-encryption of all data.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: MongoDB's Queryable Encryption (QE) allows encrypted field queries using Structured Encryption. The Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE) library uses ECDH P-256 for the Key Encryption Key (KEK) wrapping. What change is required for PQC?
  A) Disable Queryable Encryption and switch to application-level AES-256 column encryption
  B) Replace the ECDH P-256 KEK wrapping in CSFLE with ML-KEM-768 once MongoDB adds PQC key providers (targeting MongoDB 8.x)
  C) Upgrade the MongoDB Atlas cluster to M200 tier for PQC hardware acceleration
  D) Use the mongocrypt library's key rotation API to rotate CSFLE data keys to AES-512
Answer: B
Explanation: MongoDB CSFLE uses ECDH P-256 for KEK derivation (in the local key provider) or RSA/ECDH in cloud KMS providers. Shor's algorithm breaks ECDH P-256. The migration path is to switch the CSFLE key provider to an ML-KEM-768-based KMS once MongoDB's libmongocrypt adds PQC KMS provider support. The encrypted field values (AES-256-GCM) do not need to change; only the key wrapping layer requires migration.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: Column-Level Encryption (CLE) in SQL Server uses symmetric keys (SymKey) protected by asymmetric keys (AsymKey) or certificates. After migrating the protecting AsymKey from RSA-2048 to ML-DSA-65, what additional operation is REQUIRED to complete the CLE migration?
  A) Re-index all encrypted columns to rebuild full-text search indexes
  B) Re-encrypt all protected SymKeys under the new ML-DSA-65 AsymKey, and optionally rotate the AES-256 SymKey data itself
  C) Enable Always Encrypted to replace the legacy CLE implementation
  D) Add a new EncryptByKey() call in all stored procedures to re-encrypt data
Answer: B
Explanation: CLE has two layers: (1) SymKey (AES-256) encrypts the actual column values -- this is already quantum-safe. (2) AsymKey (RSA-2048) encrypts the SymKey -- this is quantum-vulnerable. After creating a new ML-DSA-65 AsymKey, you must re-encrypt each SymKey under the new AsymKey using ALTER SYMMETRIC KEY. If multiple SymKeys are protected by the same AsymKey, each must be re-encrypted. The column values themselves do not change.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: An organization uses Azure SQL Database with HYOK (Customer-Managed Key) TDE stored in an on-premises Thales Luna HSM. Despite the key never leaving the HSM, what is the residual HNDL risk?
  A) None -- the key is in an HSM and never exposed to any network
  B) The Azure SQL TDE protocol sends the DEK to the customer HSM for decryption via HTTPS; an adversary who intercepts these HTTPS requests today can store the encrypted DEK and decrypt it later if they compromise the RSA/ECDH transport wrapping
  C) The Thales Luna HSM's PKCS#11 interface is accessible over the network and can be replayed
  D) HSMs are not quantum-resistant regardless of key type
Answer: B
Explanation: HYOK reduces key exposure but does not eliminate HNDL risk entirely. The protocol works as: Azure SQL sends the AES-256 DEK (encrypted with the customer's RSA public key) to the customer HSM for decryption; the HSM returns the plaintext DEK; Azure SQL uses the DEK for the database operation. An adversary intercepting the HTTPS request between Azure and the HSM captures the RSA-encrypted DEK. They cannot decrypt it today, but with a CRQC they can. Migrating the HSM-Azure transport to ML-KEM-768 eliminates this vector.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: PostgreSQL does not natively support TDE (as of 2026). For a PQC-compliant PostgreSQL deployment requiring encryption at rest with BYOK, what is the most practical architecture?
  A) Use the pgcrypto extension with ML-DSA for column-level authenticated encryption
  B) Implement filesystem-level encryption (dm-crypt/LUKS2) with an AES-256-XTS volume key, where the LUKS2 master key is protected by an ML-KEM-768-capable external KMS
  C) Deploy PostgreSQL in AMD SEV-SNP to provide hardware memory encryption as a TDE substitute
  D) Wait for PostgreSQL 18's native TDE with built-in ML-KEM support (planned for 2027)
Answer: B
Explanation: LUKS2 is the practical interim solution: AES-256-XTS encrypts the block device containing PostgreSQL data files. LUKS2 keyslots can be bound to an external KMS using the clevis/tang framework or custom KMS integration. The LUKS2 master key is wrapped by the KMS using ML-KEM-768. This provides BYOK semantics with PQC-resistant key wrapping. SEV-SNP addresses memory encryption (not storage at rest). pgcrypto ML-DSA would be signing, not encryption. PostgreSQL native TDE has been planned for many versions and has no committed ML-KEM date.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: A database team performs an online TDE migration on a 100TB SQL Server database. What is the PRIMARY operational risk during the migration?
  A) SQL Server automatically acquires exclusive table locks, causing application downtime during re-encryption
  B) TDE migration generates continuous I/O at near-full disk bandwidth and produces large transaction log growth, requiring careful capacity planning and rate limiting during business hours
  C) SQL Server cannot perform TDE migration on databases larger than 50TB without a licensing upgrade
  D) TDE migration requires the database to be in single-user mode for 4-6 hours
Answer: B
Explanation: SQL Server TDE migration is an online operation: it does not lock tables or prevent application access. However, the database engine re-encrypts all data pages in the background, generating sequential read and write I/O across all data files. For a 100TB database, this represents significant I/O load over 4-12 hours (depending on I/O throughput). Transaction logs grow proportionally during the migration. The operational risks are storage capacity exhaustion (log files) and I/O saturation causing application performance degradation.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: SQL Server Always Encrypted uses Column Master Keys (CMK) stored in external key stores (Azure Key Vault, Windows Certificate Store, HSM). The current CMK is RSA-2048 in Azure Key Vault. What is the migration path to ML-DSA-65?
  A) Generate a new RSA-4096 CMK as an interim step, then wait for SQL Server to add ML-DSA-65 native support
  B) Rotate the CMK using SSMS Always Encrypted Wizard: create a new ML-DSA-65 CMK in Azure Key Vault (when supported), rotate Column Encryption Keys (CEKs) to be protected by the new CMK, verify all encrypted columns, remove the old RSA CMK
  C) Export all Always Encrypted column data, decrypt locally, re-encrypt with new CEKs protected by ML-DSA-65 CMK
  D) Disable Always Encrypted, create a new SQL Server instance with ML-DSA-65 CMK, migrate data using bcp
Answer: B
Explanation: SQL Server provides a built-in CMK rotation workflow that eliminates the need for data re-encryption. The process: (1) Create new ML-DSA-65 CMK in Azure Key Vault (when AKV adds ML-DSA support, roadmap 2026). (2) In SSMS: Always Encrypted > Rotate CMK -- SQL Server generates new CEK values encrypted under the new CMK alongside old CEK values. (3) Applications using the old CMK continue to work during rotation. (4) After all applications have updated their CMK references, revoke the old RSA CMK. The actual column data (AES-256-GCM) never changes.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: A database encryption team is migrating 10,000 TDE certificates from RSA-2048 to ML-DSA-65. What is the approximate increase in certificate storage for the public key material?
  A) 2x increase -- ML-DSA-65 public key (1,952 bytes) is approximately twice RSA-2048 public key (256 bytes)
  B) Approximately 6x increase -- ML-DSA-65 public key (1,952 bytes) vs RSA-2048 public key (256 bytes) represents a 7.6x increase in public key size; combined with the larger signature (3,293 bytes vs 256 bytes), the total certificate size increases from ~1.2KB (RSA-2048 cert) to ~7KB (ML-DSA-65 cert), approximately 6x
  C) No significant increase -- certificates are a negligible fraction of total database storage
  D) 50x increase -- ML-DSA-65 private key is 50x larger than RSA-2048
Answer: B
Explanation: RSA-2048 certificate: ~256B public key + ~256B signature + overhead = ~1.2KB. ML-DSA-65 certificate: 1,952B public key + 3,293B signature + overhead = ~6-7KB. The per-certificate increase is approximately 5-6x. For 10,000 certificates, storage grows from ~12MB to ~70MB -- a manageable increase for a certificate store, though certificate revocation list (CRL) sizes also grow proportionally.
