Q: A financial institution requires PCI DSS 4.0 compliance for its Oracle database containing cardholder data. The current encryption uses Oracle TDE with AES-256 DEKs protected by RSA-2048 Oracle Wallet keys. For full quantum safety, which combination is required?
  A) Enable AES-256-GCM for all DEKs (already done) -- no further changes needed
  B) Migrate Oracle Wallet RSA-2048 key to ML-KEM-768 wrapping via OKV + external HSM; upgrade TLS between Oracle application servers and DB to use ML-DSA-65 certificates; document the migration in the PCI DSS crypto inventory for auditors
  C) Increase Oracle Wallet key to RSA-4096 to exceed PCI DSS minimum requirements
  D) Enable Oracle Database Vault to add access control on top of TDE
Answer: B
Explanation: PCI DSS 4.0 requires organizations to maintain a cryptographic inventory and have a migration plan for algorithms that will become vulnerable. For Oracle TDE PQC compliance: (1) The DEK wrapping mechanism (RSA-2048 in Oracle Wallet) is the primary vulnerability -- migrate via OKV to ML-KEM-768 HSM backing. (2) Application-to-database TLS uses ECDSA certificates that need ML-DSA-65 replacement. (3) The PCI DSS auditors require documentation of the migration in the cryptographic inventory per PCI DSS v4.0 Requirement 12.3.3.

chunks.content:

Q: A global bank uses Snowflake with Tri-Secret Secure (TSS), combining Snowflake's internal key and a customer-managed key in AWS KMS. When the AWS KMS key is RSA-2048-protected, what is the HNDL exposure?
  A) None -- Tri-Secret Secure adds a layer of protection that eliminates quantum vulnerability
  B) The KMS key wrapping material (RSA-2048 protecting the customer CMK) is exposed to HNDL: a harvested KMS API call containing the RSA-wrapped CMK can be decrypted by a CRQC, bypassing Tri-Secret Secure entirely
  C) TSS quantum vulnerability is limited to metadata only, not cardholder data
  D) Snowflake's internal key component in TSS is quantum-safe, providing 50% protection
Answer: B
Explanation: Tri-Secret Secure XORs two key components: Snowflake's internal key and the customer CMK. The customer CMK is protected by AWS KMS using RSA-2048 wrapping. If an adversary harvests AWS KMS API traffic (specifically the GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext and Decrypt calls), they capture RSA-encrypted key material. A CRQC recovers the customer CMK from this harvested material, breaking the TSS protection entirely. The migration path is to upgrade the AWS KMS customer CMK to ML-KEM-768 backing.

chunks.title: Quiz: database-encryption-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: database-encryption-pqc

Q: A database migration team performs a pg_dump/pg_restore of a 5TB PostgreSQL database that uses pgcrypto column-level PGP encryption. The target environment uses PQC keys. What is the SAFEST migration sequence that maintains data availability throughout?
  A) Stop all writes -> pg_dump -> decrypt all 50M encrypted rows -> re-encrypt with PQC keys -> pg_restore (16+ hour downtime)
  B) Deploy the new PQC-configured PostgreSQL instance -> Set up logical replication from old to new -> Migrate encrypted column values in batches (online decrypt/re-encrypt with PQC keys) -> Verify consistency -> Cut over DNS -> Stop replication -> Remove old instance
  C) Run parallel queries against both instances during a 2-week validation period
  D) Export encrypted ciphertext directly without decryption and re-wrap the PGP session keys using ML-KEM
Answer: B
Explanation: Logical replication + online batch re-encryption is the safest approach: (1) New PostgreSQL is provisioned with PQC-capable crypto configuration. (2) Logical replication (pglogical or built-in) syncs all new writes to the new instance in real time. (3) Background batch job decrypts pgcrypto columns in the old schema and re-encrypts with PQC keys in the new schema. (4) After all rows are migrated, DNS cut-over switches traffic to the new instance. (5) Replication lag is drained, replication stopped. This approach provides near-zero downtime and allows rollback if issues arise.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: What is an Identity Provider (IdP)?
  A) A cryptographic hardware module that generates and stores identity certificates
  B) A system that creates and manages identity information and provides authentication services to relying applications (Service Providers)
  C) A network appliance that enforces role-based access control policies
  D) A certificate authority that issues SSL/TLS certificates for web applications
Answer: B
Explanation: An IdP (Identity Provider) is the system of record for user identities. It authenticates users and issues identity assertions (SAML assertions, OIDC ID tokens, JWT access tokens) to Service Providers (SPs). Examples: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), PingFederate, ForgeRock, Keycloak. PQC migration of the IdP is high-impact because it protects all authentication assertions issued to all downstream SPs.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: JWT (JSON Web Token) uses RS256 (RSA-2048 with SHA-256) for signing. Why is RS256 quantum-vulnerable?
  A) SHA-256 is vulnerable to Grover's algorithm, which reduces its security from 256 bits to 128 bits
  B) RSA-2048 is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a CRQC, enabling derivation of the private signing key from the public key, allowing an attacker to forge authentication tokens
  C) JWT compact serialization exposes the signature to classical birthday attacks
  D) RS256 uses PKCS#1 v1.5 padding which is vulnerable to quantum timing attacks
Answer: B
Explanation: RSA-2048's security relies on the hardness of integer factorization. Shor's algorithm solves integer factorization in polynomial time on a quantum computer. An adversary with a CRQC who captures JWT tokens signed with RS256 can recover the IdP's RSA private signing key from the public key embedded in the JWKS endpoint. With the private key, they can forge valid JWTs for any user, granting unauthorized access to all applications trusting that IdP.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: When migrating SAML 2.0 assertion signing from RSA-SHA256 to a NIST FIPS-approved PQC algorithm, which algorithm is correct?
  A) ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203) -- the approved post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism
  B) ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) -- the approved post-quantum digital signature algorithm
  C) SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f (FIPS 205) -- stateless hash-based signatures
  D) HKDF-SHA-3 -- a key derivation function for SAML token binding
Answer: B
Explanation: SAML 2.0 assertions use XML Digital Signatures (xmldsig) with RSA-SHA256. The replacement algorithm must be a digital signature algorithm (not a KEM). ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, formerly Dilithium2) is the NIST-approved post-quantum signature algorithm replacing RSA and ECDSA. ML-KEM is a key encapsulation mechanism (for encryption/key exchange, not signing). SLH-DSA is an alternative PQC signature algorithm but with much larger signature sizes (7,856 bytes vs 3,293 bytes for ML-DSA-65).

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: Microsoft Active Directory uses PKINIT for certificate-based Kerberos pre-authentication (smart card logon). The client certificate uses RSA-2048. What is the quantum threat to PKINIT authentication?
  A) Grover's algorithm reduces Kerberos AES-256 session key security to 128 bits, making ticket forgery trivial
  B) A CRQC can recover the RSA private key from the client's PKINIT certificate, enabling an attacker to generate valid Kerberos pre-authentication requests and obtain Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) for any user
  C) PKINIT is deprecated in Windows Server 2022 and is no longer a relevant attack surface
  D) PKINIT only affects smart card logon and does not impact service account security
Answer: B
Explanation: PKINIT (RFC 4556) allows Kerberos clients to authenticate using public-key certificates instead of passwords. The KDC verifies the client's certificate and issues a TGT. If an adversary recovers the RSA private key from the certificate (via Shor's algorithm applied to captured PKINIT AS-REQ messages), they can impersonate any user who has a smart card certificate. The AES-256 session key (item A) is quantum-reduced to 128-bit security -- still computationally infeasible to break.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: A SAML 2.0 IdP migrates to ML-DSA-65 assertion signing. Service Provider (SP) metadata must be updated to include the new signing certificate. Which SAML metadata element contains the IdP signing certificate?
  A) <saml:Issuer> element in the IdP EntityDescriptor
  B) <md:KeyDescriptor use='signing'> element in the IdP EntityDescriptor, which contains the X.509 certificate used by SPs to validate assertion signatures
  C) <ds:SignatureValue> in the SAML AuthnRequest
  D) <samlp:StatusCode> in the SAML Response
Answer: B
Explanation: SAML metadata (EntityDescriptor) for an IdP contains a <md:KeyDescriptor use='signing'> element with the base64-encoded X.509 certificate. SPs extract the public key from this certificate to verify incoming assertion signatures. When migrating to ML-DSA-65, the IdP metadata must be updated with the new ML-DSA-65 certificate. SPs must accept and validate the updated metadata (either via federation registries or bilateral exchange) before the IdP switches to ML-DSA-65 signing.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) uses RS256 for JWT token signing. What is Microsoft's stated PQC migration approach for Entra ID token signing as of 2025-2026?
  A) Entra ID will maintain RS256 permanently -- Microsoft confirmed RSA-2048 is safe until 2040
  B) Microsoft is testing ML-DSA-65 for Entra ID JWT signing in a limited preview, with gradual rollout planned for 2026 as part of the broader Azure PQC program
  C) Entra ID is migrating to ES256 (ECDSA P-256) as a permanent replacement for RS256
  D) Microsoft will adopt ML-KEM-768 for token signing in Entra ID's 2026 release
Answer: B
Explanation: Microsoft's post-quantum roadmap includes Entra ID as a priority workload. ML-DSA is the designated FIPS 204 replacement for RSA/ECDSA in token signing scenarios. Microsoft's Azure PQC program (announced at Build 2025) includes JWKS endpoint migration to publish ML-DSA-65 public keys alongside RSA keys during transition. ES256 (answer C) is not a PQC algorithm. ML-KEM (answer D) is a key exchange algorithm, not a signing algorithm.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: When migrating PingFederate to ML-DSA-65 SAML assertion signing, what is the CORRECT procedure to maintain federation partner connectivity during transition?
  A) Rotate the signing certificate to ML-DSA-65 immediately and notify all SP partners to update their metadata simultaneously in a maintenance window
  B) Add the new ML-DSA-65 signing certificate to PingFederate alongside the existing RSA certificate (dual-signing), distribute updated metadata to all SP partners, wait for partner confirmation, then deprecate the RSA certificate
  C) Deploy a parallel PingFederate instance with ML-DSA-65 and migrate SPs one by one
  D) Update SP trust anchors first, then rotate the PingFederate signing certificate
Answer: B
Explanation: Dual-certificate rotation is the standard SAML migration pattern: (1) Generate new ML-DSA-65 signing key in PingFederate. (2) Configure PingFederate to include both RSA and ML-DSA-65 certificates in its metadata KeyDescriptor elements. (3) Distribute updated metadata to all SP partners via federation registries or bilateral exchange. (4) Wait for SP partner acknowledgment and confirmation that they have imported the new certificate. (5) Switch PingFederate to sign exclusively with ML-DSA-65. (6) Remove the RSA certificate after all SPs confirm successful validation.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: OpenID Connect (OIDC) uses a JWKS endpoint (/.well-known/jwks.json) to publish the IdP's JWT signing keys. What change is required to support ML-DSA-65 token signing?
  A) Add 'crv': 'ML-DSA-65' to the existing RSA JWK entry in the JWKS endpoint
  B) Publish a new JWK entry with 'kty': 'OKP' and 'crv': 'ML-DSA' (per draft-ietf-jose-fully-specified-algorithms) alongside existing RSA/EC JWK entries for backward compatibility
  C) Replace the JWKS endpoint with a PKCS#11 HSM API endpoint
  D) Add 'alg': 'ML-DSA-65' as an additional claim in the JWT header alongside 'alg': 'RS256'
Answer: B
Explanation: The JOSE/JWT PQC draft (draft-ietf-jose-fully-specified-algorithms + draft-ietf-cose-dilithium) defines JWK representation for ML-DSA: key type 'OKP' with algorithm-specific parameters for the public key. The JWKS endpoint should publish BOTH the existing RSA/ECDSA key and the new ML-DSA key during transition: clients that understand ML-DSA-65 will use the new key; legacy clients use the RSA key. The JWT header 'alg' field is set to the IANA-registered ML-DSA algorithm identifier.

chunks.content:

Q: A Zero Trust Architecture requires device attestation using ECDSA P-256 device certificates. After migrating device certificates to ML-DSA-65, what is the most significant operational impact on mobile devices?
  A) Mobile devices cannot support ML-DSA-65 due to hardware security module constraints
  B) Authentication latency increases and battery consumption rises because ML-DSA-65 signature generation and verification involve larger key material (private key: 4,032 bytes, signature: 3,293 bytes) compared to ECDSA P-256 (private key: 32 bytes, signature: 64 bytes)
  C) ML-DSA-65 device certificates are incompatible with Apple's Secure Enclave and Google's Titan chip
  D) ML-DSA-65 certificates cannot be used for device attestation -- only for server authentication
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 operations are computationally more expensive than ECDSA P-256 on constrained hardware: (1) Signing: ML-DSA-65 signing takes approximately 2ms on a modern mobile CPU vs 0.5ms for ECDSA P-256. (2) Larger key material increases storage requirements in the device's secure storage. (3) Each authentication exchange transmits 3,293 bytes of signature data vs 64 bytes for ECDSA. For high-frequency device authentication scenarios (zero trust continuous verification), this overhead requires battery and latency budgets to be adjusted.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: Keycloak 25.x supports integration with PKCS#11 HSMs via Java's SunPKCS11 provider. To enable ML-DSA-65 token signing in Keycloak, what configuration is required?
  A) Set realm token signing algorithm to 'ML-DSA' in the Keycloak admin console
  B) Configure Keycloak with a PKCS#11 HSM supporting CKM_ML_DSA, add the ML-DSA-65 JWK signing key to the realm's Keys settings, and register the JOSE algorithm identifier in Keycloak's algorithm registry
  C) Enable ML-DSA in Keycloak's SSL configuration file (keycloak.conf ssl-keystore-type=ML-DSA)
  D) Deploy a custom Keycloak SPI that overrides the default RS256 signing with ML-DSA-65 only
Answer: B
Explanation: Keycloak's signing key configuration flows through: (1) An HSM (PKCS#11) or software provider that can generate/use ML-DSA-65 keys. (2) The realm's Keys settings (Admin Console: Realm Settings > Keys > Add Provider > PKCS11), where Keycloak registers the ML-DSA-65 key as a signing key. (3) The algorithm identifier must be registered so Keycloak can set the JWT 'alg' header correctly. A custom SPI (option D) would work for a pure software approach but the PKCS#11 path is more secure and production-appropriate.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: CyberArk's Privileged Access Management (PAM) Vault uses RSA-2048 to protect the vault master encryption key. In a comprehensive PQC audit, which PAM component has the HIGHEST HNDL risk?
  A) The CyberArk PVWA web application TLS certificate (rotatable via standard PKI operations)
  B) The vault master encryption key backup and Disaster Recovery key material, which is encrypted with RSA-2048 and stored offline; if this backup is harvested and the RSA key later compromised by a CRQC, all privileged credentials it contains are exposed
  C) The CyberArk Central Policy Manager (CPM) SSH key for managed account rotation
  D) The CyberArk PTA (Privileged Threat Analytics) TLS channel
Answer: B
Explanation: Disaster Recovery key backups represent the highest HNDL risk because: (1) They are intended for long-term storage (often years or decades). (2) They contain the master key protecting ALL privileged credentials. (3) RSA-2048 encryption of the backup material is vulnerable to future quantum decryption. (4) Unlike TLS certificates (which are short-lived), DR backups are designed to outlast the current security posture. Migrating DR backup encryption to ML-KEM-768-wrapped AES-256 is a critical PQC priority for CyberArk deployments.

chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: An enterprise migrates its SAML 2.0 IdP to ML-DSA-65 signing. Three of twelve SP partners report metadata validation failures after receiving the updated IdP metadata. What is the MOST likely cause?
  A) The ML-DSA-65 certificate exceeds the SP's maximum metadata file size
  B) The SP SAML libraries do not support ML-DSA-65 certificate parsing -- specifically, the X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo OID for ML-DSA-65 (2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.17) is not recognized by older SAML libraries
  C) The ML-DSA-65 certificate uses a non-standard certificate profile incompatible with the SP's SAML metadata schema
  D) The federation registry rejected the metadata update due to an expired registration token
Answer: B
Explanation: The most common cause of SP metadata failures during PQC IdP migration is library support: SAML libraries built before 2024 typically do not recognize ML-DSA-65 OIDs in X.509 certificates. The SubjectPublicKeyInfo algorithm OID (2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.17 for id-ml-dsa-65) is unrecognized, causing certificate parsing to fail entirely. The SP must upgrade its SAML library (e.g., OpenSAML, Spring Security SAML, Apache Santuario) to a version that includes ML-DSA support before federation with the migrated IdP is possible.

chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: When migrating enterprise SSO from RS256 to ML-DSA-65 JWT signing, what is the impact on access token sizes for a typical API access token with standard claims (sub, iat, exp, aud, scope, roles)?
  A) No change -- JWT signature is not transmitted in the token body
  B) Token size increases from approximately 450 bytes (RS256: 256-byte signature base64url-encoded) to approximately 3,700-4,000 bytes (ML-DSA-65: 3,293-byte signature base64url-encoded) -- an 8x increase in signature size
  C) Token size doubles from 450 bytes to approximately 900 bytes
  D) Token size increases 20x from 450 bytes to approximately 9,000 bytes
Answer: B
Explanation: RS256 JWT structure: header (~50 bytes) + payload (~150 bytes) + signature (256 bytes -> 342 bytes base64url) ~ 542 bytes total. ML-DSA-65 JWT structure: header (~60 bytes) + payload (~150 bytes) + signature (3,293 bytes -> 4,391 bytes base64url) ~ 4,601 bytes total. The token size increases approximately 8.5x. This has operational impacts: cookie size limits (4KB), HTTP header size limits (8KB in some load balancers), and URL length limits for bearer tokens passed as query parameters must all be re-evaluated.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:

Q: HashiCorp Vault 1.16+ supports ML-DSA-65 for JWT/OIDC authentication method verification. An architect wants to use Vault as an OIDC provider for Kubernetes service account authentication, replacing the default Kubernetes RSA-2048 service account key. What is the benefit of Vault-issued ML-DSA-65 JWKS for Kubernetes workload identity?
  A) Eliminates the Kubernetes API server as a dependency for service account token validation
  B) Vault's ML-DSA-65 JWKS endpoint provides quantum-safe JWT signing for service account tokens, protecting workload identity assertions from HNDL attacks on the token signing key
  C) Allows Kubernetes pods to authenticate without network connectivity
  D) Reduces Kubernetes API server load by 50% by offloading token validation to Vault
Answer: B
Explanation: Kubernetes service account tokens are JWTs signed by the Kubernetes API server's RSA/ECDSA key. If this signing key is harvested (via etcd backup, API server audit logs, or network capture) and later compromised by a CRQC, all service account tokens ever issued can be forged. Vault as an OIDC provider with ML-DSA-65 signing replaces the RSA signing key with a quantum-safe alternative. The Kubernetes API server is configured to use Vault's JWKS endpoint for token validation, providing HNDL protection for workload identity assertions.

chunks.title: Quiz: iam-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: iam-pqc

Q: An IAM architect plans a phased zero trust identity migration to PQC. What is the correct ordering based on cryptographic trust chain dependencies?
  A) Migrate device attestation certificates -> Rotate IdP signing keys -> Update root CA -> Enable PQC MFA
  B) Update OIDC/SAML SP trust anchors -> Rotate IdP signing certificates -> Migrate device certificates
  C) Migrate root CA to ML-DSA-65 -> Issue new device and service certificates -> Migrate IdP signing keys to ML-DSA-65 -> Update SP trust anchors -> Enable PQC device attestation -> Enforce ML-DSA-only policy
  D) Enable PQC MFA attestation first -> Then migrate token signing -> Then update root CA
Answer: C
Explanation: The PKI trust chain dictates the migration order: (1) Root CA first -- all downstream certificates derive trust from the root. Migrating the root to ML-DSA-65 enables issuance of quantum-safe device, service, and IdP certificates. (2) Issue new device and service certificates from the PQC root. (3) Migrate IdP signing keys -- now backed by the PQC certificate chain. (4) Update SP trust anchors to recognize the ML-DSA-65 IdP certificate. (5) Enable PQC device attestation using ML-DSA device certificates. (6) Enforce ML-DSA-only after all clients and SPs confirm support.

chunks.title: Quiz: secure-boot-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: secure-boot-pqc

Q: What is the root of trust in the UEFI Secure Boot key hierarchy?
  A) Platform Key (PK)
  B) Key Exchange Key (KEK)
  C) Signature Database (db)
  D) Revocation Database (dbx)
Answer: A
Explanation: The Platform Key (PK) is the top-level certificate in UEFI Secure Boot that signs KEKs. It is set by the OEM at manufacturing time and establishes the entire chain of trust. All other Secure Boot keys are subordinate to the PK.

Q: In UEFI Secure Boot, the Signature Database (db) stores hashes and certificates of trusted bootloaders and OS kernels.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: The db database contains certificates and hashes of trusted EFI binaries. UEFI firmware verifies each binary against db before execution. The dbx (revocation database) contains forbidden signatures.

Q: Which PQC algorithm is recommended for UEFI Secure Boot firmware signing during the transition period?
  A) ML-KEM-768
  B) SLH-DSA-128s
  C) ML-DSA-65
  D) XMSS-SHA2-256
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, security level 3) is recommended for UEFI firmware signing. It provides 128-bit post-quantum security with reasonably sized signatures (3,309 bytes). SLH-DSA has larger signatures unsuitable for firmware; ML-KEM is a KEM not a signature scheme.

chunks.title: Quiz: secure-boot-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: secure-boot-pqc

Q: What is the primary quantum security concern with TPM 2.0 remote attestation using TPM Quote?
  A) The SHA-256 PCR extend operations are broken by quantum computers
  B) The AIK (Attestation Identity Key) uses RSA or ECDSA which is vulnerable to HNDL attacks
  C) The PCR log format uses 128-bit SHA-1 hashes
  D) TPM 2.0 cannot be upgraded via firmware update
Answer: B
Explanation: The TPM Quote signs PCR values using an Attestation Identity Key (AIK) with RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256. These signatures are quantum-vulnerable to HNDL attacks — an adversary recording attestation tokens today can verify authenticity after CRQC. The SHA-256 PCR extend operations are quantum-safe.

Q: DICE (Device Identifier Composition Engine) key derivation using HKDF-SHA-256 is already quantum-safe and does not require PQC migration.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: HKDF-SHA-256 is used in DICE to derive Compound Device Identifiers (CDI) from UDS and firmware measurements. SHA-256 provides 128-bit post-quantum security against Grover's algorithm. The quantum-vulnerable component in DICE is the signing algorithm (ECDSA P-256) used to sign device certificates — not the key derivation itself.

chunks.title: Quiz: secure-boot-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: secure-boot-pqc

Q: What is 'Measured Boot' and how does it differ from Secure Boot?
  A) Measured Boot encrypts boot components; Secure Boot signs them
  B) Measured Boot records what ran via TPM PCR extensions; Secure Boot enforces policy by blocking unsigned code
  C) Measured Boot only applies to Linux; Secure Boot is Windows-specific
  D) Measured Boot uses symmetric keys; Secure Boot uses asymmetric keys
Answer: B
Explanation: Secure Boot enforces a whitelist policy — it blocks execution of unsigned or untrusted EFI binaries. Measured Boot passively records all boot components by extending their hashes into TPM PCRs, creating an auditable log for remote attestation. The two mechanisms complement each other.

Q: What does Intel Boot Guard protect against?
  A) Network-based firmware tampering after OS load
  B) Unauthorized modification of the initial UEFI firmware before execution, using keys fused into the CPU
  C) Brute-force attacks on TPM PINs
  D) Key extraction from the Secure Boot db database
Answer: B
Explanation: Intel Boot Guard uses RSA-2048 keys fused into CPU management engine flash at manufacturing to verify the authenticity of initial UEFI firmware (IBB) before execution. It provides hardware-rooted protection against bootkit attacks that would modify the BIOS/UEFI image on the SPI flash.

chunks.title: Quiz: secure-boot-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: secure-boot-pqc

Q: Replacing a UEFI Platform Key (PK) with a PQC alternative requires physical presence at the machine or a signature from the existing PK.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: PK replacement requires either physical presence (pressing a button or entering UEFI setup) or a valid signature from the current PK. This security requirement prevents remote PK replacement attacks. For large-scale PK migration to ML-DSA, organizations must plan for either physical access or a multi-step process: sign the new ML-DSA PK with the current RSA PK during a maintenance window.

Q: In the DICE attestation model, what determines the Compound Device Identifier (CDI)?
  A) The device serial number and manufacturing date
  B) The TPM endorsement key hierarchy
  C) A combination of the Unique Device Secret (UDS) and a hash of the current firmware
  D) The UEFI Secure Boot db certificate fingerprint
Answer: C
Explanation: DICE derives CDI = HKDF(UDS, H(firmware)), where UDS is a hardware-secret unique per device and H(firmware) is a measurement of the current firmware image. This means CDI changes when firmware changes, ensuring any certificate derived from CDI is bound to both the specific device AND its current firmware state.

chunks.title: Quiz: secure-boot-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: secure-boot-pqc

Q: Why might ML-DSA-65 signatures cause compatibility issues in UEFI firmware update packages?
  A) ML-DSA-65 uses a non-standard ASN.1 encoding
  B) ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes which may exceed fixed-size signature fields in legacy UEFI capsule formats
  C) UEFI only supports RSA and cannot be updated to support new algorithms
  D) ML-DSA-65 requires TPM hardware acceleration to verify
Answer: B
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 produces 3,309-byte signatures compared to RSA-2048's 256 bytes. Some UEFI capsule update formats have fixed-size signature header fields designed for RSA signatures. During the PQC transition, dual-signing (ECDSA + ML-DSA) is recommended until UEFI 2.11 or later formats with flexible signature fields are deployed.

Q: The Platform Key (PK) in UEFI Secure Boot is typically set by the user during first-time setup.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: The Platform Key is typically enrolled by the OEM (original equipment manufacturer) during manufacturing. End users can change the PK but this requires physical presence or the current PK's signature. Pre-installed OEM PKs are RSA-2048 or RSA-4096 certificates from the hardware vendor.

Q: What is the FIDO Device Onboarding (FDO) protocol's PQC migration target algorithm?
  A) SLH-DSA-128s
  B) ML-KEM-512
  C) ML-DSA-65
  D) XMSS-SHA2-256
Answer: C
Explanation: The FIDO Alliance FDO specification v1.2 adds ML-DSA-65 support for device attestation certificates. FDO is used for zero-touch device provisioning and onboarding. The OEM must provision ML-DSA-65 device attestation certificates at manufacture; the rendezvous and owner onboarding servers must be updated to verify ML-DSA-65 certificates.

chunks.title: Quiz: secure-boot-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: secure-boot-pqc

Q: For a DICE-based attestation chain, which component requires PQC migration to eliminate quantum vulnerability?
  A) The HKDF-SHA-256 key derivation used to compute CDI
  B) The SHA-256 firmware measurement hash
  C) The signing algorithm used to create layer certificates (currently ECDSA P-256)
  D) The storage format of the Unique Device Secret (UDS)
Answer: C
Explanation: In DICE, key derivation (HKDF-SHA-256) and firmware measurement (SHA-256) are already quantum-safe. The quantum-vulnerable component is the signing algorithm for DICE layer certificates — currently ECDSA P-256. Migration to ML-DSA-44 (for constrained devices) or ML-DSA-65 for the certificate signing operations eliminates this vulnerability.

Q: TPM PCR (Platform Configuration Register) values can be directly written by privileged software to set specific measurements.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: TPM PCRs are write-once registers that can only be 'extended', not directly written. The extend operation computes PCR_new = SHA-256(PCR_old || new_value), making it impossible to forge a specific PCR value without knowing the complete sequence of measurements that led to it. This tamper-evident design is fundamental to TPM attestation security.

Q: Which PCR register typically stores the Secure Boot policy state in UEFI?
  A) PCR[0]
  B) PCR[4]
  C) PCR[7]
  D) PCR[11]
Answer: C
Explanation: PCR[7] is the standard TPM PCR for UEFI Secure Boot policy state, including the Secure Boot enabled/disabled status and the KEK, db, and dbx certificate hashes. This allows remote attestation verifiers to confirm that Secure Boot was enforced during boot. PCR[0] holds core firmware measurements; PCR[4] holds bootloader code.

chunks.title: Quiz: os-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: os-pqc

Q: What command updates the system-wide crypto policy on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) to enforce stronger settings?
  A) openssl config --set FUTURE
  B) update-crypto-policies --set FUTURE
  C) systemctl restart crypto-policy
  D) setsebool -P crypto_policy on
Answer: B
Explanation: The update-crypto-policies command controls system-wide cryptographic policies on RHEL/Fedora. The FUTURE policy disables SHA-1, RSA-2048, and TLS 1.0/1.1. This policy flows to OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, Kerberos, and Java through symlinks in /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/.

Q: OpenSSL 3.5 and later includes ML-KEM and ML-DSA support in the default provider without requiring the third-party oqsprovider.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: OpenSSL 3.5 (released 2025) includes ML-KEM-512/768/1024 and ML-DSA-44/65/87 in its default provider, implementing FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 respectively. Earlier OpenSSL 3.x versions required the separate oqs-provider from the Open Quantum Safe project to access these algorithms.

Q: Which command generates a new ML-DSA-65 SSH host key using OpenSSH 9.0+?
  A) ssh-keygen -t ecdsa -b 521 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa65_key
  B) ssh-keygen -t mldsa65 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa65_key
  C) openssl genpkey -algorithm mldsa65 -out /etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa65_key
  D) ssh-add -t mldsa65 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa65_key
Answer: B
Explanation: OpenSSH 9.0+ supports ML-DSA-65 via the -t mldsa65 type parameter. The generated key pair is stored at the specified path; the public key is appended with .pub. The private key uses the OpenSSH private key format. After generating, add HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_mldsa65_key to sshd_config.

Q: On Windows, which registry path controls TLS key exchange algorithm support in SChannel?
  A) HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Cryptography
  B) HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\KeyExchangeAlgorithms
  C) HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings\Ciphers
  D) HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\TLS
Answer: B
Explanation: The SChannel key exchange algorithm support is configured at HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\KeyExchangeAlgorithms. ML-KEM-768 hybrid key exchange support was added in Windows 11 24H2 and can be enabled via this registry path or Group Policy under Computer Configuration -> Administrative Templates -> Network -> SSL Configuration Settings.

Q: FIPS 140-3 mode on Linux disables TLS 1.0 and 1.1 in addition to enforcing approved algorithms.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: Enabling FIPS mode (via dracut-fips kernel parameter + update-crypto-policies --set FIPS) enforces FIPS 140-3 approved algorithms and also disables non-compliant protocol versions including TLS 1.0 and 1.1. It also disables SHA-1, MD5, RC4, and 3DES. Applications must support TLS 1.2 or higher to function in FIPS mode.

chunks.title: Quiz: os-pqc

Q: What is the purpose of the GnuTLS priority string 'NORMAL:+MLKEM768'?
  A) It sets the minimum TLS version to 1.3 with MLKEM768 as the only cipher
  B) It adds ML-KEM-768 hybrid key exchange to the normal GnuTLS algorithm set
  C) It replaces all ECDHE key exchanges with ML-KEM-768
  D) It configures GnuTLS to use only quantum-safe algorithms
Answer: B
Explanation: The ':+MLKEM768' suffix in a GnuTLS priority string adds ML-KEM-768 hybrid key exchange to the existing algorithm set defined by NORMAL. It does not remove classical algorithms — both ML-KEM hybrid and classical ECDHE key exchange remain available, allowing backward compatibility while enabling PQC for clients that support it.

Q: What is the key difference between the OpenSSL FIPS Provider and the default OpenSSL provider for PQC algorithms?
  A) The FIPS Provider supports more PQC algorithms than the default provider
  B) Only FIPS-validated implementations (CMVP-certified) in the FIPS Provider can be used in compliance contexts; the default provider lacks this certification
  C) The default provider uses software; the FIPS Provider requires an HSM
  D) The FIPS Provider includes oqsprovider; the default provider does not
Answer: B
Explanation: The OpenSSL FIPS Provider is a separately compiled module that has been validated by NIST CMVP. Using FIPS-validated implementations is required for US federal systems and some regulated industries. The default OpenSSL provider may contain the same algorithm implementations but lacks CMVP validation. As of 2026, OpenSSL FIPS Provider 3.0.9 (CMVP #4282) includes ML-KEM-768/1024.

chunks.title: Quiz: os-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: os-pqc

Q: On Linux, enabling FIPS mode requires only a configuration file change and does not require a kernel parameter or system restart.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: Enabling FIPS mode on Linux requires: (1) installing the dracut-fips package, (2) adding 'fips=1' to the kernel boot parameter, and (3) updating the GRUB configuration and rebooting. On RHEL, update-crypto-policies --set FIPS alone is insufficient — it must be combined with the dracut-fips kernel parameter for full FIPS 140-3 compliance.

Q: Which SSH host key algorithm provides the smallest signature size, making it suitable for bandwidth-constrained environments?
  A) RSA-4096 (rsa-sha2-512)
  B) ECDSA P-256 (ecdsa-sha2-nistp256)
  C) Ed25519
  D) ML-DSA-65 (ssh-mldsa65)
Answer: C
Explanation: Ed25519 produces 64-byte signatures, making it the most compact current SSH host key algorithm. RSA-4096 produces 512-byte signatures, ECDSA P-256 produces 64 bytes but uses a weaker curve, and ML-DSA-65 produces approximately 3,309-byte signatures. For PQC migration, ML-DSA-65 is necessary for quantum safety but comes with a significant signature size increase.

chunks.title: Quiz: os-pqc

Q: What does the OpenSSL 'provider' architecture in version 3.x enable that was not possible in OpenSSL 1.x?
  A) Hardware acceleration for RSA
  B) Pluggable algorithm implementations without patching the core library, enabling PQC algorithm addition via third-party providers
  C) Support for TLS 1.3
  D) Multi-threading for cryptographic operations
Answer: B
Explanation: OpenSSL 3.x introduced a provider architecture where algorithm implementations are dynamically loadable plugins. This allows adding PQC algorithms via the oqsprovider (or built into OpenSSL 3.5+ default provider) without patching or recompiling the core library. In OpenSSL 1.x, adding a new algorithm required patching the engine interface, which was more invasive.

Q: CNG (Cryptography API: Next Generation) on Windows supports ML-DSA key operations in Windows 11 as of 2026.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: As of 2026, CNG does not include ML-DSA support. Windows 11 24H2 added ML-KEM-768 hybrid key exchange in TLS (via SChannel), but ML-DSA certificate signing and verification requires a CNG provider update. Microsoft has this on the roadmap for Windows 12 / Server 2028. Third-party CNG KSP providers from HSM vendors may offer ML-DSA before native Windows support.

Q: In the APT package management system (Debian/Ubuntu), where are repository signing public keys stored?
  A) /etc/apt/trusted.gpg
  B) /etc/ssl/certs/
  C) /etc/apt/keyrings/
  D) /var/cache/apt/keys/
Answer: C
Explanation: Modern Debian/Ubuntu systems store repository signing keys in /etc/apt/keyrings/ as separate keyring files referenced by the signed-by option in sources.list entries. This provides per-repository key isolation compared to the older /etc/apt/trusted.gpg file which shared all keys. PQC migration: add ML-DSA-65 public key files to /etc/apt/keyrings/ alongside existing GPG keys.

Q: Which component of the APT repository trust chain is MOST quantum-vulnerable?
  A) The SHA-256 checksums of individual .deb packages in Packages.gz
  B) The GPG signature on the InRelease metadata file
  C) The HTTPS TLS certificate of the repository server
  D) The SHA-512 hash of the Sources.gz file
Answer: B
Explanation: APT repository trust relies on the GPG signature on the InRelease file, which is signed with RSA-4096 or ECDSA. This signature is the quantum-vulnerable component — a CRQC could forge it to distribute malicious packages. SHA-256 checksums are quantum-safe. The HTTPS certificate should also be migrated to PQC but the InRelease GPG signature is the primary trust anchor.

chunks.title: Quiz: os-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: os-pqc

Q: The system-wide crypto policy on RHEL/Fedora automatically applies to all applications that use OpenSSL, GnuTLS, and Java without requiring individual application configuration.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: Red Hat's crypto-policies system configures all major cryptographic libraries through symlinks in /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/. The policy applies to OpenSSL (via openssl.cnf), GnuTLS (via config file), NSS (via pkcs11.txt), Kerberos (via krb5.conf), and Java (via java.security). Applications that use these libraries inherit the policy without changes, though some applications (like Firefox) use their own bundled NSS.

Q: What is the primary challenge with adding ML-DSA-65 support to RPM package signing?
  A) RPM uses SHA-1 hashes that are incompatible with ML-DSA
  B) GPG (used by RPM) does not yet have standardized ML-DSA algorithm identifiers, requiring alternative signing approaches
  C) ML-DSA signatures cannot be embedded in RPM headers
  D) ML-DSA-65 key generation requires hardware TPM acceleration
Answer: B
Explanation: RPM package signing uses GPG (GnuPG), which uses the OpenPGP standard. As of 2026, OpenPGP RFC 9580 does not yet include ML-DSA algorithm identifiers, though standardization is in progress. Interim approaches include detached ML-DSA signatures stored alongside RPMs, or using a patched libgcrypt with experimental PQC support. The rpm v4.19+ pluggable backend architecture supports future ML-DSA integration.

chunks.title: Quiz: automotive-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: automotive-pqc

Q: What is the maximum payload size of a CAN 2.0B frame?
  A) 8 bytes
  B) 64 bytes
  C) 254 bytes
  D) 1500 bytes
Answer: A
Explanation: CAN 2.0B frames carry only 8 bytes of payload — far too small for any PQC signature. ML-DSA-44 produces a 2,420-byte signature, which is 302x larger than the entire CAN payload. In-vehicle authentication on CAN buses must rely on symmetric methods like AES-CMAC (via AUTOSAR SecOC).

Q: Which in-vehicle bus protocol has the best PQC feasibility due to its standard 1500-byte MTU?
  A) CAN FD
  B) FlexRay
  C) LIN
  D) Automotive Ethernet
Answer: D
Explanation: Automotive Ethernet (100BASE-T1/1000BASE-T1) uses standard Ethernet frames with a 1,500-byte MTU and supports MACsec, TLS/DTLS, and IPsec. An ML-KEM-768 encapsulation (1,088 bytes) fits in a single Ethernet frame, making it the preferred transport for PQC migration in vehicles.

Q: UWB (Ultra-Wideband) secure ranging in digital car keys uses AES-128 symmetric crypto that is already quantum-safe.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: UWB ranging in the CCC Digital Key 3.0 protocol uses AES-128 STS (Scrambled Timestamp Sequence) for anti-relay protection. Since this is symmetric cryptography, it is not vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. PQC migration is only needed for the initial key agreement and certificate-based authentication steps, which use ECDH and ECDSA.

chunks.title: Quiz: automotive-pqc
chunks.content:

Q: What ASIL level applies to electronic braking (ABS/ESC) systems?
  A) ASIL A
  B) ASIL B
  C) ASIL C
  D) ASIL D
Answer: D
Explanation: Electronic braking is classified as ASIL D — the highest automotive safety integrity level, requiring 99%+ diagnostic coverage, dual-channel or fail-operational redundancy, and the strictest crypto verification timing budgets (<15ms). PQC migration for ASIL-D functions requires dual-path verification: PQC primary plus classical backup.

Q: Which PQC signature algorithm is recommended for airbag crash sensor data authentication due to its 0.05ms verification time?
  A) ML-DSA-44
  B) FN-DSA-512
  C) LMS (H10/W4)
  D) SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s
Answer: C
Explanation: LMS (Leighton-Micali Signature) has the fastest verification at approximately 0.05ms on an automotive-grade SoC, making it ideal for the airbag's extremely tight 5ms verification budget. ML-DSA-44 at 0.3ms also fits, but LMS provides the largest safety margin for this fail-safe critical function.

Q: In the CCC Digital Key 3.0 protocol, by approximately how much does the total protocol data size increase when migrating from classical (ECDSA/ECDH) to PQC (ML-DSA-44/ML-KEM-768)?
  A) 3x
  B) 10x
  C) 23x
  D) 50x
Answer: C
Explanation: The classical CCC Digital Key protocol uses approximately 1,474 bytes total across pairing, authentication, and key sharing phases. The PQC equivalent using ML-DSA-44 and ML-KEM-768 requires approximately 33,504 bytes — a roughly 22.7x increase. This has significant implications for NFC transport, which requires fragmentation across many APDUs.

chunks.title: Quiz: automotive-pqc
chunks.content:

Q: CAN FD's 64-byte payload is sufficient to carry an ML-DSA-44 signature without fragmentation.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: CAN FD frames carry a maximum payload of 64 bytes. ML-DSA-44 signatures are 2,420 bytes — nearly 38x larger than the CAN FD payload. PQC signatures cannot be transmitted over CAN FD without application-layer fragmentation. The upcoming CAN XL standard (ISO 11898-2:2024) supports up to 2,048-byte payloads, which may improve feasibility.

Q: Which transport profile is preferred for PQC-enabled digital car key authentication?
  A) NFC (ISO 14443)
  B) BLE 5.0+
  C) UWB (IEEE 802.15.4z)
  D) Wi-Fi Direct
Answer: B
Explanation: BLE 5.0+ supports large payloads via L2CAP CoC segmentation (up to 512 bytes per segment), allowing PQC key exchange to fit natively without APDU fragmentation. NFC is problematic (256-byte max APDU requires 5+ APDUs for ML-KEM-768). UWB uses symmetric crypto and relies on BLE for initial key agreement.

Q: For OTA firmware signing, which PQC algorithm produces the most compact signatures at 666 bytes?
  A) ML-DSA-44
  B) ML-DSA-65
  C) FN-DSA-512
  D) LMS (H10/W4)
Answer: C
Explanation: FN-DSA-512 (FN-DSA, FIPS 206) produces 666-byte signatures — the most compact among PQC signature algorithms. For comparison, ML-DSA-44 produces 2,420-byte signatures (3.6x larger) and ML-DSA-65 produces 3,309-byte signatures. FN-DSA-512's compact size makes it attractive for bandwidth-constrained OTA campaigns across millions of vehicles.

Q: What is the typical road life of a commercial truck that determines its post-quantum vulnerability window?
  A) 8 years
  B) 12 years
  C) 20 years
  D) 30 years
Answer: C
Explanation: Commercial trucks have a typical road life of 20 years. If a truck enters service in 2025 and a CRQC arrives by 2035, the truck would operate for 10 years in a post-quantum vulnerable state (2035–2045). This long vulnerability window makes PQC migration planning especially critical for commercial vehicle fleets.

Q: What is the maximum verification time budget for ASIL-D braking functions that PQC algorithms must satisfy?
  A) 100ms
  B) 50ms
  C) 15ms
  D) 5ms
Answer: C
Explanation: ASIL-D requires the strictest crypto verification timing at <15ms with dual-channel or fail-operational redundancy. Braking specifically has a 10ms budget, while the general ASIL-D requirement is <15ms. ML-DSA-44 verification at approximately 0.3ms meets this budget, but fail-operational design requires dual-path architecture (PQC primary + classical backup).

Q: The NSA CNSA 2.0 directive requires all firmware and software signing to use PQC algorithms (LMS/XMSS/ML-DSA) by 2030.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: NSA CNSA 2.0 establishes 2030 as the deadline for transitioning all firmware and software signing to PQC algorithms — specifically LMS, XMSS, or ML-DSA. Full PQC transition across all cryptographic operations is targeted for 2033. These timelines directly affect automotive OTA infrastructure and ECU firmware signing.

Q: For a 10-million vehicle OTA campaign using ML-DSA-44, approximately how much total signature overhead is added per vehicle across 32 signatures per firmware package?
  A) 3.1 KB
  B) 22.2 KB
  C) 78.9 KB
  D) 107.8 KB
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-44 produces 2,420-byte signatures. With 32 signatures per firmware package (one per firmware segment) plus a 1,312-byte public key, the total overhead is approximately 78.9 KB per vehicle. This is a 25.4x increase over ECDSA P-256 (3.1 KB) but negligible compared to the firmware itself (hundreds of MB).

Q: Which vehicle lifecycle phase involves V2X pseudonym certificate batch enrollment and ECU identity key pair injection?
  A) Road Life (In Service)
  B) End of Life & Decommission
  C) Production & Provisioning
  D) OTA Update Campaign
Answer: C
Explanation: Production & Provisioning is when factory HSMs (FIPS 140-3 Level 3) generate OEM root keys, Key Injection Facilities inject per-ECU keys, and V2X Certificate Authorities sign pseudonym certificates in bulk. Starting in 2027+, this phase must dual-provision both classical and PQC root keys for crypto-agility.

Q: What is the primary quantum threat to V2X (Vehicle-to-Everything) communication?
  A) Jamming of V2X radio signals
  B) Forgery of IEEE 1609.2 ECDSA certificates enabling fake safety alerts
  C) Denial of service against roadside units
  D) Eavesdropping on unencrypted BSM broadcasts
Answer: B
Explanation: V2X communication relies on ECDSA P-256 signatures per IEEE 1609.2 for authenticating Basic Safety Messages (BSMs). A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could forge these signatures, enabling attackers to inject fake safety alerts, create ghost vehicles, or manipulate traffic signals — with potentially fatal consequences for connected vehicles.

Q: Which quantum threat to encrypted data is already occurring today — before any quantum computer can break encryption?
  A) Q-Day arrival
  B) Board liability exposure
  C) Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) data collection
  D) Cyber insurance premium increases
Answer: C
Explanation: HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) is the immediate threat: adversaries are actively intercepting and storing encrypted communications today with the intent to decrypt them once a CRQC becomes available. This threat is classified as critical severity because it is already happening, regardless of how far away Q-Day is.

Q: Under CNSA 2.0 guidelines what is the deadline for migrating software and firmware signing to PQC algorithms?
  A) 2027
  B) 2030
  C) 2033
  D) 2035
Answer: B
Explanation: CNSA 2.0 sets 2030 as the deadline for PQC-compliant software and firmware signing as well as networking protocols. Web and cloud services follow in 2033. Full deprecation of classical algorithms occurs by 2035. These deadlines apply to National Security Systems (NSS) and serve as the benchmark for broader enterprise planning.

Q: The SEC Cyber Disclosure Rule (effective December 2023) requires organizations to disclose material cybersecurity risks. What is the maximum window to report a material quantum-related risk incident?
  A) 30 calendar days
  B) 10 business days
  C) 4 business days
  D) 1 business day
Answer: C
Explanation: The SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Rule requires publicly traded companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents within 4 business days of determining materiality. If a CRQC compromise of sensitive data is deemed material to investors, it triggers this mandatory disclosure timeline. This creates direct board liability for unaddressed quantum exposure.

Q: True or False: NIST finalized the first post-quantum cryptography standards in August 2024.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024, marking the completion of the 8-year PQC standardization process. NIST IR 8547 accompanied these standards with migration guidance.

Q: In the executive self-assessment framework what score threshold indicates a HIGH quantum risk posture requiring immediate escalation to the board?
  A) Above 30%
  B) Above 40%
  C) Above 55%
  D) Above 70%
Answer: D
Explanation: The self-assessment uses 9 weighted criteria summing to 100%. A score above 70% indicates HIGH quantum risk requiring immediate board escalation and budget authorization. Scores between 40% and 70% indicate MEDIUM risk requiring a formal migration roadmap. Below 40% indicates LOW risk with monitoring-only actions appropriate.

Q: Which KPI best measures an organization's real-time exposure to HNDL attacks on data in transit?
  A) Board Awareness frequency
  B) Crypto Inventory Coverage percentage
  C) HNDL Exposure measured in years of data sensitivity
  D) Vendor PQC Readiness score
Answer: C
Explanation: HNDL Exposure — measured as the number of years of data sensitivity remaining — is the most direct KPI for current HNDL risk. If an organization transmits data with a 15-year confidentiality requirement and quantum computers are expected within 10 years, the HNDL gap is already open. The target KPI threshold is HNDL Exposure below 5 years.

Q: Which of the six threat categories in the executive quantum risk framework carries MEDIUM severity?
  A) Competitive disadvantage from quantum-aware competitors
  B) HNDL data collection by nation-state adversaries
  C) Regulatory compliance deadline exposure
  D) Board liability for undisclosed material risk
Answer: A
Explanation: Competitive disadvantage is rated MEDIUM severity — significant but less immediately actionable than HNDL (critical) or regulatory deadlines (critical). Cyber insurance rate impacts are also MEDIUM. HNDL and regulatory deadline exposure are both CRITICAL. Board liability and vendor supply chain risk are both HIGH.

Q: True or False: The 30-day action phase of a PQC action plan focuses on completing the full enterprise-wide cryptographic migration.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. The 30-day action phase focuses on strategic planning and scoping: commissioning a PQC risk assessment, defining scope, reviewing HNDL exposure windows, and assessing vendor PQC roadmaps. The immediate phase covers emergency actions like requesting a crypto inventory. The 90-day phase launches governance and business case. The 6-month phase executes the first production migrations.

Q: What does the Vendor PQC Readiness KPI measure and what is its target threshold?
  A) The percentage of software vendors who have attended PQC training; target 50%
  B) The fraction of critical third-party vendors with a published PQC roadmap; target above 80%
  C) The number of vendors supplying FIPS-validated HSMs; target 100%
  D) The percentage of vendor contracts containing quantum-safe SLAs; target 60%
Answer: B
Explanation: Vendor PQC Readiness tracks the fraction of critical third-party vendors who have either published a credible PQC migration roadmap or offer a FIPS-validated PQC product. The target is above 80%. Vendors without a roadmap represent supply-chain risk because a critical dependency that cannot support PQC algorithms blocks the organization's own migration.

Q: CNSA 2.0 mandates full deprecation of classical public-key algorithms across all NSS systems by which year?
  A) 2030
  B) 2033
  C) 2035
  D) 2040
Answer: C
Explanation: CNSA 2.0 sets 2035 as the hard deadline for complete deprecation of classical public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, DH) in National Security Systems. The phased schedule is: 2030 for software/firmware signing and networking, 2033 for web/cloud/OS, and 2035 for full deprecation.

chunks.title: Quiz: dev-quantum-impact
chunks.content:

Q: How large is an ML-DSA-65 digital signature compared to a classical ECDSA P-256 signature?
  A) Approximately the same size (64-72 bytes)
  B) About 5x larger (320 bytes)
  C) About 52x larger (3309 bytes)
  D) About 500x larger (32000 bytes)
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204 security level 3) produces signatures of 3309 bytes. ECDSA P-256 produces 64-byte signatures. This 52x size increase directly impacts every system that stores, transmits, or verifies digital signatures: TLS handshakes, JWT tokens, code-signed artifacts, and certificate chains all grow substantially.

Q: What is the ciphertext size for ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation?
  A) 64 bytes
  B) 256 bytes
  C) 1088 bytes
  D) 4096 bytes
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203 security level 3) produces a 1088-byte ciphertext. Compared to a classical X25519 key exchange which involves 32-byte public keys, this is a 34x increase in key exchange data size.

Q: True or False: OpenSSL 3.x introduced a provider architecture that allows PQC algorithms to be added as pluggable modules without patching the core library.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. OpenSSL 3.x providers are dynamically loadable modules. The Open Quantum Safe project's oqs-provider adds ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and other PQC algorithms to any OpenSSL 3.x installation. OpenSSL 3.5+ includes ML-KEM and ML-DSA in the default provider natively.

chunks.title: Quiz: dev-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
