Q: Which TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange group combines X25519 with ML-KEM-768 for backward-compatible PQC protection?
  A) X25519Kyber768Draft00
  B) X25519MLKEM768
  C) P256MLKEM768
  D) ECDH-KEM-768
Answer: B
Explanation: X25519MLKEM768 is the IETF-standardized hybrid key exchange group combining classical X25519 with ML-KEM-768. It provides security as long as either algorithm remains unbroken. Browsers (Chrome, Edge) and servers (OpenSSL 3.5+, BoringSSL) deploy this group as the primary PQC-capable TLS 1.3 key exchange mechanism.

Q: What is the primary code-level pattern for implementing crypto agility in a library-independent application?
  A) Hardcode the algorithm in a central constants file for easy single-point changes
  B) Use direct calls to a specific PQC library throughout the codebase
  C) Introduce an abstraction layer (provider or strategy pattern) that maps algorithm names to implementations
  D) Use compile-time flags to select between classical and PQC implementations
Answer: C
Explanation: The provider or strategy pattern creates an abstraction layer between application code and cryptographic implementations. The application calls a named algorithm via the abstraction layer; the layer resolves it to the current best implementation. This allows swapping algorithms without modifying application business logic.

chunks.title: Quiz: dev-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: dev-quantum-impact

Q: True or False: JWT access tokens will remain the same size when migrating from RS256 to ML-DSA-65 signing because the header and payload do not change.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. The JWT signature grows from 256 bytes (RS256) to 3293 bytes (ML-DSA-65). A typical RS256 JWT of ~540 bytes becomes ~4600 bytes with ML-DSA-65. This exceeds many cookie size limits (4096 bytes) and HTTP header maximums in some load balancers, requiring architectural review.

Q: Which Java library provides PQC algorithm support including ML-KEM and ML-DSA and is widely used in enterprise Java applications?
  A) Java Standard Library (java.security)
  B) SunPKCS11 provider
  C) Bouncy Castle
  D) Apache Commons Crypto
Answer: C
Explanation: Bouncy Castle's Lightweight Cryptography API and JCA provider include full ML-KEM and ML-DSA support. It is the most mature PQC-capable Java cryptography library. The AWS-LC-Java library is an alternative for AWS workloads.

Q: What testing challenge is most common when integrating PQC algorithms into existing test suites?
  A) Unit tests fail due to non-deterministic key generation
  B) Buffer size assertions fail because PQC keys and signatures exceed the buffer limits tested against classical algorithm sizes
  C) PQC algorithms cannot be mocked in unit test environments
  D) Test execution time doubles due to quantum-safe key generation speed
Answer: B
Explanation: Existing test suites often hardcode expected sizes for keys, signatures, and ciphertexts based on classical algorithm dimensions. After PQC migration, assertions like assertEquals(64, signature.length) fail because ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3309 bytes.

chunks.title: Quiz: dev-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: dev-quantum-impact

Q: Which Rust crate provides ML-KEM and ML-DSA implementations aligned with the FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 specifications?
  A) ring
  B) openssl
  C) pqcrypto
  D) aws-lc-rs
Answer: D
Explanation: aws-lc-rs is a Rust wrapper around AWS-LC (Amazon's fork of BoringSSL) which includes FIPS 203 ML-KEM and FIPS 204 ML-DSA. The pqcrypto crate family also provides PQC bindings. The ring crate focuses on classical algorithms and does not include PQC.

Q: True or False: Migrating from ECDH to ML-KEM requires no changes to key storage because ML-KEM public keys are the same size as ECDH public keys.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. ML-KEM-768 public keys are 1184 bytes compared to a 32-byte X25519 public key — a 37x increase. Key storage databases, certificate formats, and key serialization code must all accommodate larger key material.

chunks.title: Quiz: arch-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: arch-quantum-impact

Q: What is a hybrid certificate in the context of PQC PKI migration?
  A) A certificate that works on both Windows and Linux platforms
  B) A certificate containing both a classical (ECDSA) and a PQC (ML-DSA) key and signature pair
  C) A certificate issued by both a root CA and a cross-signing CA simultaneously
  D) A certificate containing two ML-DSA keys at different security levels
Answer: B
Explanation: A hybrid certificate includes both a classical key/signature (e.g., ECDSA P-256) and a PQC key/signature (e.g., ML-DSA-65). Relying parties that understand PQC validate the ML-DSA signature; legacy clients validate the ECDSA signature. This backward-compatible design allows gradual PQC adoption without breaking existing clients.

Q: What is the approximate performance of ML-KEM-768 encapsulation on modern server hardware?
  A) ~50ms per operation
  B) ~5ms per operation
  C) ~0.1ms per operation
  D) ~0.001ms per operation
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-KEM-768 encapsulation runs at approximately 0.1ms (100 microseconds) on modern server hardware, making it suitable for high-throughput TLS handshake scenarios. ML-DSA-65 verification takes approximately 0.5ms.

Q: True or False: An ML-DSA certificate chain can be approximately 10 times larger than an equivalent ECDSA certificate chain.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. An ECDSA P-256 certificate is approximately 500-800 bytes. An ML-DSA-65 certificate is approximately 4-6KB due to the larger public key (1952 bytes) and signature (3309 bytes). A typical 3-certificate chain grows from ~2KB to ~15-20KB.

chunks.title: Quiz: arch-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: arch-quantum-impact

Q: What is a crypto-agile abstraction layer and what architectural problem does it solve?
  A) A load balancer that routes traffic to quantum-safe servers; solves network segmentation
  B) An intermediate interface layer between application code and cryptographic implementations; allows algorithm swapping without modifying business logic
  C) A hardware security module with multiple algorithm slots; solves key storage capacity
  D) A PKI policy document; solves algorithm selection governance
Answer: B
Explanation: A crypto-agile abstraction layer defines a stable API that application code calls, while the implementation behind it resolves the named algorithm to the current best library. When algorithm recommendations change, only the abstraction layer's implementation needs updating.

Q: How does the introduction of larger PQC key sizes affect HSM slot capacity planning?
  A) HSMs store PQC keys more efficiently due to structured lattice encoding
  B) HSMs fit fewer PQC keys per slot because ML-KEM and ML-DSA keys are significantly larger than classical keys
  C) PQC keys do not require HSM storage as they are always generated ephemerally
  D) HSM slot capacity is unaffected because keys are referenced by handle not stored by size
Answer: B
Explanation: HSM slot capacity is determined partly by key material size. An ML-DSA-65 private key is 4032 bytes compared to an ECDSA P-256 private key of 32 bytes — a 126x difference. Organizations with dense HSM deployments must audit slot capacity.

chunks.title: Quiz: arch-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: arch-quantum-impact

Q: True or False: FIPS 140-3 validated HSMs were widely available with ML-DSA support by 2024.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. FIPS 140-3 validation for ML-DSA and ML-KEM support in HSMs has been a significant constraint. Most HSM vendors began shipping ML-DSA-capable firmware in 2025, with CMVP validation processes lagging 12-18 months behind firmware release.

Q: In a cross-signed CA architecture for PQC migration what does the cross-signature accomplish?
  A) It allows the subordinate CA to issue certificates to end entities faster
  B) It enables a new PQC root CA to be trusted by relying parties through a signature from an established classical root CA
  C) It distributes the cryptographic load between two CA servers
  D) It merges two PKI hierarchies into a single root of trust
Answer: B
Explanation: Cross-signing enables trust bootstrapping: the new ML-DSA root CA is signed by the existing RSA root CA that is already in client trust stores. Clients that have updated root stores trust the PQC root directly; legacy clients follow the cross-signed path through the classical root.

chunks.title: Quiz: arch-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: arch-quantum-impact

Q: Certificate Transparency (CT) logs record all publicly trusted TLS certificates. What architectural challenge does PQC certificate migration create for CT infrastructure?
  A) CT logs cannot accept ML-DSA signatures because they use different ASN.1 encoding
  B) CT log entries grow significantly as ML-DSA certificates are submitted, requiring CT log operators to scale storage and bandwidth capacity
  C) CT logs stop working entirely once PQC certificates are submitted
  D) PQC certificates cannot be submitted to CT logs until FIPS 206 is finalized
Answer: B
Explanation: Certificate Transparency logs must store and serve every submitted certificate. As PQC certificates with ML-DSA signatures (3309 bytes per signature vs 64 bytes for ECDSA) are issued at scale, CT log storage and bandwidth requirements grow substantially.

Q: Which reference architecture pattern is recommended for applications that cannot be immediately updated to use PQC algorithms directly?
  A) Quantum-safe gateway proxy that terminates and re-encrypts traffic using PQC before forwarding to legacy application
  B) Delay migration until the application is rewritten
  C) Add a hardware firewall that strips PQC headers before they reach the legacy application
  D) Deploy a separate PQC-only server and redirect PQC clients to it
Answer: A
Explanation: A quantum-safe gateway proxy (TLS termination with PQC on the external face and classical TLS internally) allows legacy applications to remain unchanged while protecting external traffic. The proxy handles ML-KEM key exchange and ML-DSA certificate validation; the legacy app sees a classical TLS connection on the internal side.

chunks.title: Quiz: arch-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: arch-quantum-impact

Q: True or False: The security of hybrid cryptography holds as long as at least one of the combined algorithms remains unbroken.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. This is the fundamental security property of hybrid cryptography. If X25519 is broken by Shor's algorithm but ML-KEM-768 is secure, the hybrid scheme remains safe. Both algorithms must be broken simultaneously for the hybrid to fail.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: What operational challenge does migrating to ML-DSA certificates create for certificate renewal automation tools like cert-manager?
  A) cert-manager cannot parse ML-DSA certificate requests
  B) ML-DSA certificates have shorter default validity periods requiring more frequent renewals
  C) ML-DSA certificates are substantially larger, potentially causing API payload size errors and increased storage requirements in certificate management systems
  D) ML-DSA certificates require a separate ACME server, incompatible with existing Let's Encrypt infrastructure
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 certificates are approximately 6-8KB versus 2-3KB for ECDSA P-256 certificates. Certificate management systems storing thousands of certificates see meaningful storage growth. More critically, ingress controllers may need buffer size adjustments to handle larger TLS handshake payloads.

Q: True or False: Typical TLS handshake latency increases when migrating from ECDSA/X25519 to ML-DSA/X25519MLKEM768.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. TLS handshake latency typically increases from approximately 5ms to 12ms when migrating to PQC algorithms. The increase comes from larger certificate payloads, additional computation for ML-DSA verification, and ML-KEM-768 encapsulation overhead. Monitoring systems must adjust alerting baselines.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: When migrating IPsec VPN endpoints to PQC what IKEv2 extension enables quantum-safe key exchange?
  A) IKEv2 Quick Mode with ML-KEM
  B) Postquantum Preshared Keys (RFC 8784)
  C) IKEv2 with ECDH Group 31 (X25519)
  D) IKEv2 Mode-Config with PQC KEM
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 8784 defines Postquantum Preshared Keys (PPK) for IKEv2, providing a transition mechanism that adds a pre-shared key layer to the classical Diffie-Hellman exchange. The more complete solution is IKEv2 hybrid key exchange using ADDITIONAL_KEY_EXCHANGE (RFC 9370) which supports ML-KEM-768 directly.

Q: What is the recommended approach for migrating SSH host keys to PQC on a large server fleet?
  A) Rotate all SSH host keys simultaneously during a single maintenance window
  B) Generate PQC SSH host keys alongside existing classical host keys and advertise both in sshd_config until client compatibility is confirmed
  C) Remove classical SSH host keys immediately to force PQC adoption
  D) Use a configuration management system to disable SSH and use certificate-based auth only
Answer: B
Explanation: Dual host key configuration allows SSH clients to negotiate the algorithm they support. New clients capable of ML-DSA-65 will use the PQC host key; legacy clients fall back to Ed25519. This parallel operation allows gradual fleet migration without breaking connectivity.

Q: True or False: Container image signing with Sigstore Cosign will produce the same signature size after migrating from ECDSA to ML-DSA-65.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Cosign signatures stored in OCI registries grow substantially with ML-DSA-65. A classical ECDSA P-256 signature is 64 bytes; an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3309 bytes. CI/CD pipelines with strict payload size limits may require reconfiguration.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: A Prometheus alert fires when TLS handshake duration exceeds 8ms. After migrating to PQC what should the alert threshold be adjusted to?
  A) Keep it at 8ms — PQC migration should not increase handshake latency
  B) Increase to approximately 15ms to account for typical PQC handshake overhead
  C) Increase to 50ms because PQC is orders of magnitude slower than classical algorithms
  D) Remove the alert entirely as TLS latency monitoring is not useful post-migration
Answer: B
Explanation: Typical PQC TLS handshake latency increases from ~5ms to ~12ms due to larger certificate chains and PQC computation. Setting a threshold at approximately 15ms provides headroom for normal PQC-era variation while still alerting on genuine degradation.

Q: What is a crypto inventory and why is it the first step in PQC migration planning?
  A) A list of all software licenses for cryptographic products; required for compliance audits
  B) A complete mapping of all cryptographic algorithms in use across the infrastructure including where keys are stored and what data they protect; identifies migration scope and priority
  C) A hardware inventory of HSMs and TPMs; required for budget planning
  D) A vendor list of all cryptographic library suppliers; required for supply chain risk assessment
Answer: B
Explanation: A cryptographic inventory catalogs every algorithm in use, the systems where they appear, the key material involved, and the sensitivity of data they protect. Without this map, teams cannot prioritize migration or identify HNDL-exposed systems.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: True or False: Rolling back a failed PQC migration is straightforward because classical algorithm certificates and keys are still valid while both are deployed in parallel.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. A key advantage of deploying hybrid or dual-algorithm configurations during PQC migration is that rollback remains possible. If a PQC deployment causes compatibility issues, the classical algorithm configuration can be re-activated without service interruption.

Q: In a Kubernetes environment what resource most commonly needs updating to handle larger PQC TLS certificates?
  A) ConfigMap
  B) Service
  C) TLS Secret (kubernetes.io/tls type) and Ingress controller buffer configurations
  D) Namespace RBAC policy, because larger certificates require elevated permissions
Answer: C
Explanation: Kubernetes TLS secrets store certificate and key data that may exceed expectations sized for classical algorithms. More critically, ingress controllers (nginx, HAProxy, Envoy) have configurable proxy_buffer_size and proxy_buffers settings that may need increasing to handle PQC certificate chain sizes.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: What does the ADDITIONAL_KEY_EXCHANGE extension in IKEv2 (RFC 9370) enable for PQC VPN migration?
  A) It allows two VPN endpoints to negotiate two separate SA tunnels simultaneously
  B) It adds a second key exchange round to IKEv2 allowing ML-KEM-768 to be combined with classical ECDH in a single IKE negotiation
  C) It replaces the Diffie-Hellman group entirely with ML-KEM, requiring both endpoints to be PQC-capable
  D) It adds post-quantum certificate validation to IKEv2 authentication
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9370 (Multiple Key Exchanges in IKEv2) adds a mechanism to perform additional key exchange rounds beyond the initial IKE_SA_INIT exchange. This enables hybrid key exchange: IKE establishes an initial ECDH key exchange, then an additional ML-KEM-768 exchange adds a second layer of key material.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: Why does genomic research data require particular urgency in PQC migration compared to most enterprise data?
  A) Genomic databases use weaker encryption than financial systems
  B) Genomic data has an effectively permanent sensitivity horizon — an individual's DNA cannot be changed, making HNDL threats permanent and irreversible
  C) Genomic research data is publicly available and does not require encryption
  D) Genomic data files are too large for classical encryption algorithms
Answer: B
Explanation: Genomic data identifies individuals permanently. Unlike financial records where account numbers can be changed after a breach, DNA sequences are immutable identifiers tied to both the subject and their biological relatives. 50+ year confidentiality requirements are common in genomics and clinical trials.

Q: True or False: Research publications signed with ECDSA today face a long-term quantum integrity threat because the publication record is permanent.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. A digital signature on a research publication protects the integrity claim that the document has not been altered since signing. If a CRQC later allows signature forgery, adversaries could create fraudulent versions of foundational research papers with valid-looking classical signatures.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: What security property is most at risk when research institutions share data in federated learning collaborations using classical TLS?
  A) Data accuracy and completeness of the training dataset
  B) Long-term confidentiality of research contributions transmitted between institutions — susceptible to HNDL if adversaries record the exchanges
  C) The intellectual property rights to the trained model
  D) Compliance with IRB approval requirements
Answer: B
Explanation: Federated learning transmits model gradients and potentially sensitive derivative data between institutions over TLS. If an adversary records these exchanges today they can potentially reconstruct sensitive training data from the gradients after CRQC arrival.

Q: Clinical trial data is typically required to be retained for 25 years under ICH E6 GCP guidelines. What does this mean for the HNDL risk horizon?
  A) No additional action needed — 25-year retention periods predate quantum computing
  B) Classical encryption is sufficient because quantum computers will not exist within 25 years
  C) The full 25-year retention period falls within the HNDL risk window since CRQC estimates range from 2030-2040; data encrypted today may be decrypted before its retention period expires
  D) 25-year retention data should be deleted rather than encrypted
Answer: C
Explanation: ICH E6 Good Clinical Practice requires 25-year retention for clinical trial master files. With CRQC estimates ranging from 2030 to 2040, data encrypted today is at risk of quantum decryption well before the retention period expires.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: Federal funding agencies have begun including quantum-resilient security requirements in grants. What algorithm family do they specifically reference for data protection?
  A) RSA-4096 as the extended-lifetime standard
  B) AES-256 for all data protection with no PQC requirement
  C) NIST-standardized PQC algorithms (FIPS 203 ML-KEM and FIPS 204 ML-DSA) for protecting sensitive research data
  D) Elliptic-curve algorithms upgraded to P-521
Answer: C
Explanation: Federal funding agencies have aligned with NIST PQC standards post-August 2024. Grant cybersecurity requirements for federally funded research increasingly reference FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) for data protection and authentication.

Q: True or False: Code-based cryptography such as HQC derives its security from the hardness of decoding random linear codes — a problem believed hard for both classical and quantum computers.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Code-based cryptography relies on the syndrome decoding problem for random linear codes. This problem has resisted over 50 years of classical cryptanalysis and is not believed to be efficiently solvable by quantum computers. NIST selected HQC as the 5th PQC standard in March 2025.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: What is a lattice-based cryptographic algorithm and what makes its security assumptions conservative?
  A) An algorithm using physical silicon lattice structures for key generation; conservative because hardware is hard to clone
  B) An algorithm whose security reduces to the hardness of lattice problems (LWE/SIS); conservative because these problems are well-studied and believed hard for quantum computers
  C) An algorithm built on graph theory; conservative because NP-hard problems are assumed quantum-safe
  D) An algorithm based on hash functions organized in a lattice structure; conservative because hash security is well understood
Answer: B
Explanation: Lattice-based algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) rely on the Learning With Errors (LWE) and Short Integer Solution (SIS) problems on high-dimensional lattices. These problems have been studied for 25+ years with no known efficient quantum algorithm.

Q: Why are isogeny-based cryptographic schemes such as SIDH no longer considered viable PQC candidates?
  A) They are too slow for practical deployment
  B) A classical (non-quantum) attack published in 2022 completely broke the most efficient variants
  C) They were never formally submitted to the NIST PQC process
  D) They require quantum hardware to perform key generation
Answer: B
Explanation: In 2022, researchers Castryck and Decru published a classical polynomial-time attack that broke SIDH (Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman) and SIKE (a NIST candidate). The attack used auxiliary torsion point information to recover private keys classically. No quantum computer was needed.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: True or False: Hash-based signature schemes like SLH-DSA rely solely on hash function security — if the hash function is secure the signature scheme is secure regardless of quantum advances.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) is provably secure assuming only the collision resistance and preimage resistance of the underlying hash function (SHA-256 or SHAKE-256). Unlike lattice or code-based schemes, it does not rely on algebraic hardness assumptions.

Q: What is the primary challenge of 50-year data confidentiality requirements common in health and genetic research with respect to PQC migration?
  A) Modern computers cannot encrypt data with 50-year security guarantees
  B) Current PQC standards may themselves need to be replaced during a 50-year horizon, requiring cryptographic agility to be built into research data archives
  C) 50-year data must be stored offline and encryption cannot be applied
  D) HIPAA only requires 6-year data retention making 50-year encryption unnecessary
Answer: B
Explanation: 50-year confidentiality horizons extend well beyond the expected lifespan of any current cryptographic standard. Research data archives must implement crypto-agile storage: envelope encryption with version-tagged key identifiers that allow the outer encryption layer to be re-wrapped with updated algorithms as standards evolve.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: Which tool operates in passive mode — inspecting TLS handshakes on a SPAN port without injecting any packets?
  A) pqcscan
  B) SSLyze
  C) CryptoNext COMPASS
  D) Keysight CyPerf
Answer: C
Explanation: CryptoNext COMPASS (and pqc-flow) operate in passive mode on a SPAN/TAP port — zero packets are injected, making them safe for production and OT environments. pqcscan, SSLyze, and CyPerf are active tools that initiate connections.

Q: What is the key limitation of passive discovery tools compared to active scanners?
  A) They require expensive hardware appliances
  B) They can only analyze OT protocols
  C) They cannot validate whether a remote endpoint actively supports PQC — only what is currently in use
  D) They inject packets that may disrupt production traffic
Answer: C
Explanation: Passive tools can only detect algorithms in currently observed flows. If no connection is being made using ML-KEM, a passive probe will not detect ML-KEM support on that endpoint. Active scanners probe endpoints directly to discover their full PQC capability.

Q: According to VIAVI TeraVM benchmark data, what is the approximate IKEv2 SA setup time for pure PQC on a WAN link (50ms RTT) compared to classical?
  A) 3× slower (720ms vs 240ms)
  B) 53× slower (12,626ms vs 240ms)
  C) 2× slower (480ms vs 240ms)
  D) 10× slower (2,400ms vs 240ms)
Answer: B
Explanation: IKEv2 SA establishment rises from 240ms (classical DH) to 12,626ms (pure PQC, WAN) — a 53× increase. This is why hybrid IKEv2 (380ms, 1.6×) is the recommended migration path rather than jumping directly to pure PQC for VPN gateways.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: TCP fragmentation occurs when a TLS ClientHello exceeds approximately 1,400 bytes, adding one extra RTT to the handshake.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: Pure PQC ClientHellos (1,536 bytes) and composite certificates (17KB) exceed the typical TCP MSS of ~1,460 bytes. This causes TCP fragmentation, adding exactly one extra round-trip time to the TLS handshake — which is significant on WAN and satellite links.

Q: Why does classical fixed-vs-random TVLA fail for ML-KEM and ML-DSA side-channel analysis?
  A) Lattice algorithms run too fast for power measurement equipment
  B) The public key and ciphertext are structurally coupled, making fixed test vectors trivially distinguishable regardless of implementation quality
  C) Welch's t-test requires more than 10,000 traces to be effective
  D) TVLA only works for symmetric cryptography
Answer: B
Explanation: In ML-KEM/ML-DSA, a fixed ciphertext always uses the same secret polynomial because the public key and ciphertext are mathematically linked. This structural coupling means the fixed set is distinguishable from random even for a perfectly constant-time implementation. Instead, target NTT/INTT, polynomial multiplication, and modular reduction stages directly.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: What does CBOM stand for, and which tool generates it from source code repositories?
  A) Cryptographic Binary Object Model — generated by CBOMkit
  B) Cryptography Bill of Materials — generated by CBOMkit (IBM)
  C) Certificate Bundle of Materials — generated by pqcscan
  D) Crypto Baseline Operations Map — generated by PQC-LEO
Answer: B
Explanation: CBOM (Cryptography Bill of Materials) is standardized in CycloneDX 1.6. CBOMkit (open source, IBM-contributed) generates CBOM by scanning git repositories for cryptographic algorithm usage. It is the primary tool for code-level crypto inventory as the first step of PQC migration.

Q: RFC 9794 defines hybrid PQC design rules. Which of the following is a core requirement?
  A) Only the PQC component needs to complete — the classical component is optional for performance
  B) Both the classical and PQC components must complete successfully — no silent downgrade
  C) Hybrid schemes must always use X25519 as the classical component
  D) The shared secret must be the PQC ciphertext XORed with the classical shared secret
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9794 mandates that both components of a hybrid scheme complete successfully. The shared secret is derived as KDF(classical_secret || pqc_secret). If either component fails, the shared secret is invalid — no silent fallback to classical is permitted. This prevents downgrade attacks.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: Which TVLA threshold (|t| value) does NIST recommend as the standard cutoff for declaring statistically significant side-channel leakage?
  A) 2.0
  B) 3.0
  C) 4.5
  D) 6.0
Answer: C
Explanation: The NIST-standard TVLA threshold is |t| > 4.5. Values above this indicate statistically significant leakage requiring countermeasures. A stricter threshold of 3.0 is used in some high-security evaluations. Values below 4.5 indicate no detectable leakage at the tested confidence level.

Q: Which of the following is an open-source passive PQC network discovery tool?
  A) VIAVI Observer
  B) Keysight Inspector
  C) pqc-flow (CipherIQ)
  D) VIAVI TeraVM
Answer: C
Explanation: pqc-flow (CipherIQ) is an open-source passive analyzer that detects PQC in encrypted network traffic — TLS, SSH, QUIC — without storing payload content. VIAVI Observer, VIAVI TeraVM, and Keysight Inspector are commercial tools.

Q: When testing a pure PQC client (ML-KEM-768 only, no classical component) against Cloudflare, what result is expected?
  A) Full ML-KEM-768 negotiation — Cloudflare supports pure PQC clients
  B) Incompatible — Cloudflare requires hybrid (both classical + PQC) per RFC 9794 policy
  C) Partial — Cloudflare accepts pure PQC but disables QUIC
  D) Compatible — Cloudflare falls back to X25519+ML-KEM-768 automatically
Answer: B
Explanation: Cloudflare enforces RFC 9794's requirement for hybrid schemes with both components. Pure PQC clients that send only ML-KEM-768 without a classical component are rejected. This is a deliberate security policy to prevent downgrade attacks during the transition period.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: What is the primary use case for VIAVI TeraVM in PQC testing?
  A) Passive network monitoring on SPAN ports
  B) Performance benchmarking of VPN gateways under PQC load — emulating tens of thousands of concurrent users
  C) Source code scanning for cryptographic algorithm usage
  D) Side-channel power analysis of embedded devices
Answer: B
Explanation: VIAVI TeraVM is a cloud-enabled benchmarking platform specifically designed for PQC performance testing of VPN gateways and IPSec systems. It emulates realistic workloads and supports all NIST PQC standards, making it the leading commercial tool for pre-migration capacity planning.

Q: Which stage of ML-KEM's computation is most commonly identified as the primary leakage point in TVLA analysis?
  A) Randomness sampling (CBD sampling)
  B) Key serialization
  C) NTT (Number Theoretic Transform)
  D) Ciphertext compression
Answer: C
Explanation: The NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) is ML-KEM's core polynomial multiplication operation. It processes secret coefficients in a loop structure that creates key-dependent power patterns detectable with TVLA. Randomness sampling is typically not a leakage point as it handles public values.

Q: pqcscan is an open-source, Rust-based active TLS and SSH scanner that produces JSON and HTML report output.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: pqcscan (Anvil Secure) is indeed written in Rust for high performance, supports TLS and SSH scan modes, and outputs results in both JSON and HTML formats. It is BSD-licensed and available for Linux, macOS, and Windows. It is classified as an active scanner — it initiates connections to probe endpoints.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: In the recommended PQC test strategy for an OT/ICS environment, why must the inventory phase use passive-only tools?
  A) OT devices cannot handle TLS connections
  B) Active scanning tools are not licensed for OT environments
  C) Active probing can disrupt real-time safety systems and cause unplanned shutdowns
  D) OT networks use proprietary protocols that no active scanner supports
Answer: C
Explanation: OT/ICS environments run safety-critical systems with real-time constraints. Active scanning initiates unexpected connections that can trigger fault conditions, cause PLCs to enter safe-stop mode, or disrupt time-sensitive control loops. Passive-only discovery (CryptoNext COMPASS, pqc-flow in read-only mode) is mandatory for initial inventory of OT segments.

Q: What is the most significant performance overhead introduced by pure PQC certificates (ML-DSA + ML-KEM) compared to classical (ECDSA + ECDH)?
  A) Signing speed — ML-DSA signing is 100× slower than ECDSA
  B) Certificate size — pure PQC certificates (~17KB) force TCP fragmentation, adding an extra RTT
  C) Key generation time — ML-KEM key generation is 50× slower than ECDH
  D) Verification cost — ML-DSA verification requires more CPU than TLS record decryption
Answer: B
Explanation: Pure PQC certificates reach ~17KB vs 1.2KB for classical, causing TCP fragmentation in TLS handshakes (ClientHello + certificate chain exceeds MTU). This adds one extra RTT to every new connection — on WAN (50ms RTT) this is 50ms per connection, on satellite (600ms RTT) this is 600ms. The crypto computation overhead itself is under 1ms. This drives the recommendation to use hybrid schemes during the transition period.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)?
  A) A virtual machine for testing software
  B) A hardware-isolated secure area within a processor that protects code and data during execution
  C) An encrypted network tunnel
  D) A secure operating system
Answer: B
Explanation: A TEE is a hardware-enforced isolated execution environment within a CPU that protects the confidentiality and integrity of code and data loaded inside it. Even privileged software (OS, hypervisor) cannot access TEE-protected memory. Examples include Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, Arm CCA, and AWS Nitro Enclaves.

Q: What is remote attestation in the context of confidential computing?
  A) Logging into a remote server
  B) A cryptographic proof that code is running inside a genuine TEE with a specific software configuration
  C) Encrypting data before sending it to the cloud
  D) A backup verification process
Answer: B
Explanation: Remote attestation allows a relying party to verify that their workload is running inside an authentic TEE on genuine hardware, with the expected software loaded. The TEE generates a signed attestation report containing measurements (hashes) of the loaded code. The signature uses the TEE manufacturer's attestation key.

Q: True or False: Confidential computing protects data while it is being processed in memory, not just at rest or in transit.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Confidential computing addresses the third state of data protection: data in use. Traditional encryption protects data at rest (disk encryption) and in transit (TLS), but data must typically be decrypted for processing. TEEs keep data encrypted in memory and only decrypt it within the hardware-isolated enclave.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: Which Intel technology provides VM-level confidential computing with hardware memory encryption?
  A) Intel SGX
  B) Intel TDX
  C) Intel AMT
  D) Intel vPro
Answer: B
Explanation: Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) provides VM-level confidential computing, encrypting entire virtual machine memory and isolating VMs from the hypervisor. SGX provides application-level enclaves (smaller scope). TDX is designed for cloud workloads where full VM isolation is needed without modifying applications.

Q: What is AMD SEV-SNP?
  A) A network firewall technology
  B) AMD's confidential computing technology providing encrypted VM memory with integrity protection against hypervisor tampering
  C) A CPU overclocking feature
  D) A solid-state drive encryption standard
Answer: B
Explanation: AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization - Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) encrypts VM memory and adds integrity protection that prevents the hypervisor from modifying encrypted memory pages. SNP builds on earlier SEV and SEV-ES generations to provide the strongest protection against a compromised hypervisor.

Q: Why is confidential computing relevant to the PQC transition?
  A) TEEs replace the need for PQC algorithms
  B) TEE attestation keys and memory encryption use classical cryptography that is vulnerable to quantum attack
  C) Confidential computing is unrelated to quantum threats
  D) TEEs already use quantum-safe algorithms
Answer: B
Explanation: TEE attestation signatures typically use ECDSA or RSA, and memory encryption uses AES (quantum-safe for symmetric, but key agreement is classical). A CRQC could forge attestation reports by breaking the signing key, or compromise key provisioning. TEE vendors must migrate attestation to ML-DSA and key agreement to ML-KEM.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is Arm Confidential Compute Architecture (CCA)?
  A) A cloud service from Arm
  B) Arm's hardware architecture for isolating workloads in Realms, providing confidential computing for Arm-based processors
  C) A certificate authority protocol
  D) An ARM assembly instruction set
Answer: B
Explanation: Arm CCA introduces Realms — hardware-isolated execution environments for Arm v9 processors. Unlike Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP (x86), CCA targets mobile, edge, and server workloads on Arm silicon. Realms are managed by a Realm Management Monitor (RMM) that runs at a new privilege level (EL2-Realm).

Q: What is the Confidential Computing Consortium (CCC)?
  A) A quantum computing research lab
  B) A Linux Foundation project promoting standards and open-source frameworks for hardware-based TEE technologies
  C) A government regulatory body
  D) A cloud provider alliance
Answer: B
Explanation: The Confidential Computing Consortium (CCC) is a Linux Foundation project with members including Intel, AMD, Arm, Google, Microsoft, Red Hat, and others. It promotes the adoption of confidential computing through open-source projects (Enarx, Gramine, Open Enclave SDK), standards, and best practices.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is the primary quantum threat to TEE attestation?
  A) Quantum computers can break AES memory encryption
  B) A CRQC could forge attestation signatures by breaking the ECDSA/RSA attestation key, allowing fake TEE reports
  C) Quantum noise interferes with TEE hardware
  D) TEE memory becomes unstable near quantum computers
Answer: B
Explanation: TEE attestation relies on digital signatures (typically ECDSA P-256 or RSA) rooted in manufacturer-provisioned keys. A CRQC running Shor's algorithm could derive these private keys, enabling an attacker to forge attestation reports that falsely claim code is running in a genuine TEE. This would undermine the entire trust model of confidential computing.

Q: How could a TEE-HSM integration improve PQC key management?
  A) TEEs replace HSMs entirely
  B) TEEs can provide a secure execution environment for PQC operations when HSM firmware lacks PQC support, using the HSM for key storage and the TEE for PQC computation
  C) TEEs and HSMs are incompatible
  D) HSMs provide better TEE attestation
Answer: B
Explanation: TEE-HSM integration allows organizations to bridge the gap during PQC transition: the HSM provides tamper-resistant key storage (FIPS 140-3 certified), while the TEE provides a secure environment for PQC computations that the HSM firmware does not yet support. Keys can be securely transferred between HSM and TEE for PQC operations.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: True or False: AWS Nitro Enclaves use a dedicated Nitro Security Chip that is separate from the main CPU for attestation.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. AWS Nitro Enclaves run on dedicated hardware managed by the Nitro Security Chip, which is separate from the main CPU. This chip handles attestation, provides a hardware root of trust, and ensures the hypervisor cannot access enclave memory. The Nitro attestation document includes PCR measurements signed by the Nitro Security Chip.

Q: What is memory encryption in the context of confidential computing?
  A) Encrypting files stored on disk
  B) Hardware-level encryption of DRAM contents using per-VM or per-enclave keys so that physical memory access reveals no plaintext
  C) Using VPN for network traffic
  D) Compressing memory to save space
Answer: B
Explanation: Memory encryption in confidential computing uses hardware AES engines integrated into the memory controller. Each VM or enclave gets unique encryption keys managed by the CPU, ensuring that even physical memory dumps, cold boot attacks, or compromised hypervisors cannot read protected data. Intel TME/MKTME, AMD SME/SEV, and Arm MTE provide different implementations.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: Which of the following are valid use cases for confidential computing in PQC transition? (Select all that apply)
  A) Running PQC algorithms in a TEE when the underlying OS or hypervisor is not yet PQC-ready
  B) Protecting PQC key generation inside an enclave to prevent side-channel leakage
  C) Using TEE attestation as a replacement for PQC certificates
  D) Securely migrating classical keys to PQC keys within a hardware-isolated environment
Answer: A|B|D
Explanation: TEEs can bridge PQC gaps in the software stack, protect sensitive PQC key generation from side-channel attacks, and provide secure environments for key migration operations. However, TEE attestation does not replace PQC certificates — attestation verifies the execution environment, while certificates verify identity. Both must independently migrate to PQC algorithms.

Q: What does Google Confidential VMs use for memory encryption?
  A) Software-based encryption at the OS level
  B) AMD SEV or SEV-SNP hardware memory encryption
  C) Intel SGX enclaves exclusively
  D) Application-layer TLS
Answer: B
Explanation: Google Cloud Confidential VMs leverage AMD SEV (and SEV-SNP on newer hardware) to encrypt VM memory with hardware-managed keys. The hypervisor and other VMs cannot decrypt the protected VM's memory. This provides lift-and-shift confidential computing without requiring application modifications.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is the key difference between Intel SGX and Intel TDX?
  A) SGX is newer than TDX
  B) SGX protects individual application enclaves while TDX protects entire virtual machines
  C) TDX is for consumer devices and SGX is for servers
  D) They are identical technologies with different names
Answer: B
Explanation: Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions) creates small application-level enclaves with limited memory (originally ~128MB). Intel TDX (Trust Domain Extensions) provides VM-level isolation, encrypting the entire VM memory space. TDX is designed for cloud workloads requiring full VM confidentiality without application redesign.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What does EMV stand for in payment card technology?
  A) Electronic Mobile Verification
  B) Europay, Mastercard, and Visa
  C) Encrypted Message Validation
  D) Enhanced Multi-Vendor
Answer: B
Explanation: EMV stands for Europay, Mastercard, and Visa — the three companies that originally developed the chip card standard. EMV specifications define how chip cards, terminals, and payment networks interact to authenticate transactions. EMVCo now manages the standard with six member organizations.

Q: What cryptographic operations do payment cards perform during a chip transaction?
  A) Only symmetric encryption of the PIN
  B) Dynamic data authentication (DDA) using RSA signatures and symmetric session key derivation
  C) Quantum key distribution
  D) No cryptographic operations — the terminal handles everything
Answer: B
Explanation: EMV chip cards perform RSA-based dynamic data authentication (DDA/CDA) to prove card authenticity, and use symmetric key derivation for transaction-specific session keys. The card's RSA private key signs transaction data, and the terminal verifies it against the CA public key hierarchy. This RSA dependency is the primary PQC concern.

Q: True or False: Payment tokenization (replacing card numbers with tokens) is already quantum-safe because tokens are random values.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: Partially true but misleading. While token values themselves are random, the tokenization infrastructure relies on classical cryptography for: token provisioning (TLS with RSA/ECDH), token vault protection, and the binding between tokens and original PANs. These surrounding cryptographic operations must migrate to PQC.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What is the primary PQC challenge for EMV chip cards?
  A) Cards lack internet connectivity
  B) PQC signatures and keys are too large for the constrained storage and bandwidth of chip card hardware
  C) Chip cards already use quantum-safe algorithms
  D) Payment networks do not use public-key cryptography
Answer: B
Explanation: EMV chip cards have severely constrained resources: limited NVM storage (typically 80-256KB), slow processors, and narrow communication bandwidth with terminals. ML-DSA-65 signatures (3,309 bytes) are ~13x larger than RSA-2048 signatures (256 bytes), creating significant challenges for card storage, transaction speed, and contactless communication bandwidth.

Q: How many payment cards are estimated to be in circulation globally?
  A) About 500 million
  B) About 4-5 billion
  C) About 50 million
  D) About 100 billion
Answer: B
Explanation: There are approximately 4-5 billion payment cards in circulation globally. This massive installed base makes PQC migration for EMV an enormous logistical challenge — cards have a typical 3-5 year lifecycle, terminals must be upgraded, and the CA hierarchy (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) must transition. Full migration could take 8-12 years.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What role does the EMV CA (Certificate Authority) hierarchy play in payment security?
  A) It encrypts all transaction data
  B) It provides the trust chain for card authentication — the payment network CA signs issuer certificates, which sign individual card certificates
  C) It stores cardholder PINs
  D) It manages network routing
Answer: B
Explanation: The EMV CA hierarchy is a multi-level PKI: Payment Network Root CA (Visa, Mastercard) → Issuer CA → Card Certificate. During DDA/CDA, the terminal walks this chain to verify the card's authenticity. Migrating this hierarchy to PQC requires coordinated upgrades across networks, issuers, and terminals worldwide.

Q: What is the HNDL risk for payment transactions?
  A) There is no HNDL risk because transactions are real-time
  B) Recorded transaction authentication data could be used to forge cards if the CA signing keys are later broken by a CRQC
  C) Harvest Now Decrypt Later only applies to email
  D) Payment PINs could be decrypted offline
Answer: B
Explanation: While individual transaction data has limited replayability, the HNDL threat to payments focuses on the CA key hierarchy. If an adversary captures RSA-signed card certificates and later breaks the CA root key with a CRQC, they could forge new card certificates, potentially enabling card cloning at scale. This makes CA key migration urgent.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: Which payment network published a post-quantum cryptography readiness framework first?
  A) Mastercard
  B) Visa
  C) American Express
  D) UnionPay
Answer: B
Explanation: Visa has been an early leader in PQC readiness for payments, publishing research and participating in PQC standardization. Mastercard has also engaged through its cryptographic research team. Both networks are actively evaluating PQC algorithm suitability for their card authentication and tokenization infrastructure.

Q: What is the approximate size increase when replacing RSA-2048 DDA signatures with ML-DSA-65 on EMV cards?
  A) 2x larger (512 bytes)
  B) 5x larger (1280 bytes)
  C) 13x larger (3309 bytes)
  D) 100x larger
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes compared to RSA-2048 signatures at 256 bytes — approximately 13x larger. Combined with larger public keys (1,952 bytes vs 256 bytes for RSA-2048), this creates significant storage and bandwidth challenges for the constrained chip card environment, especially for contactless (NFC) transactions with limited communication windows.

Q: Which components of the payment ecosystem must be upgraded for PQC? (Select all that apply)
  A) Payment network root CA keys and certificates
  B) POS terminal firmware and certificate stores
  C) Card chip operating systems and key storage
  D) All of the above
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: PQC migration for payments requires a coordinated upgrade across the entire ecosystem: network CAs must issue PQC certificates, terminals must verify PQC signatures and store larger certificates, and new card chips must support PQC key generation and signing. This makes payment PQC migration one of the most complex migration challenges due to the massive scale and hardware constraints.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What is the impact of larger PQC signatures on contactless (NFC) payment transactions?
  A) No impact — NFC bandwidth is unlimited
  B) Larger signatures may exceed the contactless transaction time budget (typically 500ms), potentially causing timeouts
  C) NFC transactions do not use signatures
  D) PQC signatures are faster over NFC
Answer: B
Explanation: Contactless (tap) payments have strict time budgets (~500ms total) dictated by the ISO 14443 protocol. Transferring 3,309-byte ML-DSA signatures plus larger certificates over the relatively slow NFC interface (106-848 kbit/s) may exceed this budget, causing transaction failures. This is a key constraint driving research into smaller PQC signature schemes for payments.

Q: What is 3D Secure and why does it need PQC migration?
  A) A 3D printing security protocol
  B) An e-commerce authentication protocol that uses RSA/ECDSA for server authentication and message signing between merchants, issuers, and card networks
  C) A physical card security feature
  D) A contactless payment standard
Answer: B
Explanation: 3D Secure (3DS) authenticates online card-not-present transactions through a challenge flow between the cardholder, merchant, and issuer. It uses TLS (RSA/ECDH) for channel security and digital signatures for inter-party message authentication. Both the TLS layer and the signing mechanisms must migrate to PQC algorithms.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What approach might EMVCo take to address PQC signature size constraints on chip cards?
  A) Abandon chip card authentication entirely
  B) Explore hash-based signatures, algorithm compression techniques, or split authentication across online and offline paths
  C) Require all transactions to be online only
  D) Use quantum key distribution for each transaction
Answer: B
Explanation: EMVCo and payment networks are exploring multiple approaches: using smaller PQC signature schemes (if standardized), compressing certificate chains, moving more authentication online (where bandwidth is not as constrained), and potentially splitting authentication between offline (card-present) and online (network verification) paths to reduce on-card storage requirements.

Q: True or False: The symmetric key derivation used in EMV for session keys (e.g., AES-based) is already quantum-safe and does not need migration.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Symmetric key derivation (AES, 3DES-based) used for EMV session keys and transaction authorization codes is resistant to quantum attack. Grover's algorithm only halves the effective key length (AES-256 → ~128-bit security), which remains secure. The quantum vulnerability is in the public-key operations (RSA-based DDA/CDA and key exchange).

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What is the estimated timeline for full PQC migration across the global payment card ecosystem?
  A) 1-2 years
  B) 3-5 years
  C) 8-12+ years
  D) It will never be completed
Answer: C
Explanation: Full PQC migration for payments is estimated at 8-12+ years due to: the 3-5 year card replacement cycle (4+ billion cards), terminal upgrade logistics (tens of millions of POS terminals worldwide), coordinated CA hierarchy migration across multiple payment networks, and the need for backward compatibility during the transition period. Early planning and hybrid approaches are essential.

chunks.title: Assessment: Industry Selection
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 1: Industry Selection

The Industry Selection step determines which compliance frameworks, threat scenarios, and migration priorities are relevant to your organization. Different industries face varying levels of quantum risk — for example, Financial Services and Government/Defense face the highest urgency due to long-lived data and regulatory mandates.

chunks.title: Assessment: Country Selection
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 2: Country Selection

The Country Selection step identifies which national PQC mandates and deadlines apply. Countries like the United States (CNSA 2.0), France (ANSSI), and Germany (BSI) have specific PQC migration timelines. This selection also filters compliance frameworks to show only relevant regulations.

chunks.title: Assessment: Current Cryptographic Usage
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 3: Current Cryptographic Usage

The Current Cryptographic Usage step identifies which classical algorithms your organization uses (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, AES, SHA-2, etc.). This determines which PQC replacements are needed — RSA/ECDSA require ML-DSA or SLH-DSA for signatures, while ECDH requires ML-KEM for key exchange.

chunks.title: Assessment: Data Sensitivity
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 4: Data Sensitivity

Data Sensitivity drives urgency assessment. Organizations handling Top Secret, classified, financial, or health data face higher HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) risk because adversaries may already be collecting encrypted data for future quantum decryption. Multiple sensitivity levels can be selected — the highest level determines the risk score.

chunks.title: Assessment: Compliance Frameworks
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 5: Compliance Frameworks

The Compliance step identifies which regulatory frameworks apply to your organization (CNSA 2.0, NIST guidelines, ANSSI requirements, BSI recommendations, etc.). Frameworks are filtered by your selected industry and country. Each framework has different PQC adoption deadlines and requirements.

chunks.title: Assessment: Migration Status
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 6: Migration Status

The Migration Status step assesses how far along your organization is in the PQC transition: Not Started, Planning, Pilot/Testing, Partial Deployment, or Fully Migrated. Organizations in earlier stages receive higher urgency scores to encourage action.

chunks.title: Assessment: Use Cases
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 7: Use Cases

The Use Cases step identifies specific cryptographic applications in your organization: TLS/HTTPS, VPN/IPsec, email signing, code signing, PKI/certificates, IoT device authentication, database encryption, etc. Each use case maps to specific PQC algorithms and migration complexity.

chunks.title: Assessment: Data Retention
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 8: Data Retention

Data Retention periods directly impact HNDL risk exposure. Data that must remain confidential for 10+ years (e.g., health records, state secrets, financial archives) faces the highest quantum threat since quantum computers could decrypt it within its retention window. Multiple retention levels can be selected.

chunks.title: Assessment: Credential Lifetime
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 9: Credential Lifetime

The Credential Lifetime step assesses how long cryptographic credentials (certificates, keys, tokens) must remain valid in your organization. Long-lived credentials (5+ years) face elevated HNDL/HNFL risk — a certificate valid through 2030 may need to remain trustworthy even after a CRQC arrives. This step drives urgency for PKI migration, code signing transitions, and certificate authority upgrades.

chunks.title: Assessment: Organization Scale
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 10: Organization Scale

Organization Scale affects migration complexity and timeline. Large enterprises with thousands of endpoints, multiple data centers, and complex supply chains require longer migration timelines and more comprehensive crypto-agility frameworks than smaller organizations.

chunks.title: Assessment: Crypto Agility
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 11: Crypto Agility

Crypto Agility measures your organization's ability to quickly swap cryptographic algorithms. Organizations with centralized key management, automated certificate rotation, and modular crypto libraries can migrate faster. Low agility increases migration risk and timeline.

chunks.title: Assessment: Infrastructure Assessment
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 12: Infrastructure Assessment

The Infrastructure step evaluates which systems need PQC upgrades: HSMs, load balancers, firewalls, certificate authorities, databases, cloud services, IoT devices. Hardware-bound systems (HSMs, embedded devices) require longer migration timelines due to firmware/hardware replacement cycles.

chunks.title: Assessment: Target Timeline
chunks.content:
PQC Assessment Wizard — Step 13: Target Timeline

The Target Timeline step sets your organization's PQC migration deadline based on regulatory requirements, risk tolerance, and industry benchmarks. Country-aligned options show relevant national deadlines (e.g., CNSA 2.0 2030/2033 milestones, ANSSI 2025 hybrid requirement).

chunks.title: Getting Started for Developers
chunks.content:
Getting Started with PQC for Developers

Start with the PQC 101 module to understand the quantum threat and why migration matters. Then explore ML-KEM key generation in the Playground — you can generate real PQC keypairs in your browser. The TLS Basics module shows how ML-KEM integrates with TLS 1.3 handshakes. For hands-on practice, OpenSSL Studio provides a full WASM-based OpenSSL 3.6 terminal for generating PQC keys and certificates. The Algorithm Reference page compares all NIST-standardized algorithms with performance benchmarks.

chunks.title: Getting Started for Organizations
chunks.content:
Getting Started with PQC for Organizations

Begin with the Assessment wizard to evaluate your organization's quantum risk posture — it analyzes industry, data sensitivity, compliance requirements, and infrastructure to generate a prioritized migration plan. Review the Compliance page for regulatory frameworks (CNSA 2.0, ANSSI, BSI guidelines) and their deadlines. The Migrate Catalog lists PQC-ready products across 7 infrastructure layers, including HSMs, TLS libraries, and certificate authorities. The Threat Landscape page shows industry-specific quantum risks to help build the business case.

chunks.title: Getting Started for Learners
chunks.content:
Getting Started with PQC for Learners

The Learn section has 50 modules covering PQC fundamentals to advanced topics. Start with PQC 101 for an overview, then Quantum Threats to understand Shor's and Grover's algorithms. Key modules include: Hybrid Cryptography (transition strategy), Crypto Agility (algorithm flexibility), TLS Basics (web security), KMS & PQC, HSM & PQC Operations, Data & Asset Sensitivity, 5G Security, industry-specific modules (Healthcare, Automotive, Aerospace, Energy, EMV Payments), and an executive track (Governance, Business Case, Risk Management, Compliance Strategy, Migration Program). Each module includes interactive demonstrations and a Workshop tab for hands-on exercises. Test your knowledge with the Quiz covering 530 questions across 33 categories. The Glossary provides definitions for 100+ PQC terms.

chunks.title: PQC Playground — Interactive Crypto Workshop
chunks.content:
PQC Playground Overview

The PQC Playground (/playground) is a browser-based cryptographic workshop with 22 interactive tools, an interactive lab, and a full PKCS#11 HSM emulator. All operations run locally via WebAssembly — no data leaves the browser.

Four sub-routes:
1. /playground — Workshop grid: searchable catalog of 22 tools across 6 categories (HSM / PKCS#11, Entropy & Random, Certificates & Proofs, Protocol Simulations, Blockchain & Digital Assets, OpenSSL Studio). Persona-aware filtering with difficulty badges (beginner/intermediate/advanced). Each persona (Executive, Developer, Architect, Researcher, Ops, Curious) sees tailored tool recommendations.
2. /playground/interactive — Interactive lab with 7 tabs: keystore (key generation), data (hex editor), kem_ops (ML-KEM + X25519 ECDH), symmetric (AES/ChaCha), hashing (SHA/SHAKE), sign_verify (PQC + classical signing), logs (operation history with timing).
3. /playground/hsm — PKCS#11 v3.2 HSM playground via SoftHSMv3 WASM with 10 tabs: keystore, symmetric, key_wrap, hashing, sign_verify, key_agree, key_derive, mechanisms, acvp (NIST KAT vectors), logs. Supports C++, Rust, and Dual engine modes with parity cross-check.
4. /playground/:toolId — Individual tool detail pages with lazy-loaded components, breadcrumbs, and endorse/flag buttons.

Supported algorithms: ML-KEM-512/768/1024 (FIPS 203), ML-DSA-44/65/87 (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA all 12 parameter sets (FIPS 205), X25519, P-256, RSA-2048/4096, Ed25519, secp256k1, AES-128/256, ChaCha20. All generated keys are for educational purposes only.

URL deep-linking: ?tab= selects Interactive lab tab (kem_ops, sign_verify, symmetric, hashing, data, keystore, logs). ?algo= pre-selects an algorithm. Combine: /playground/interactive?tab=kem_ops&algo=ML-KEM-768.

chunks.title: Playground — Interactive Lab: KEM & Key Operations
chunks.content:
Interactive Lab — KEM Operations & Key Generation

The PQC Interactive lab at /playground/interactive?tab=kem_ops provides ML-KEM (FIPS 203) hands-on key encapsulation:

KEM Operations tab (?tab=kem_ops) — ML-KEM encapsulation/decapsulation workflow: generate keypair → encapsulate (creates ciphertext + shared secret from public key) → decapsulate (recovers shared secret from private key). Includes X25519 ECDH classical baseline panel for comparison. ML-KEM-768 ciphertext is 1,088 bytes vs X25519 at 32 bytes; shared secret always 32 bytes. Demonstrates quantum-safe key exchange end-to-end.

Keystore tab (?tab=keystore) — Generate keypairs for any supported algorithm (ML-KEM-512/768/1024, ML-DSA-44/65/87, SLH-DSA, X25519, P-256, RSA, Ed25519, secp256k1). Shows public/private key sizes and generation time. Key store persists across tabs within the session.

URL: /playground/interactive?tab=kem_ops&algo=ML-KEM-768 to pre-select ML-KEM-768 for KEM operations.

chunks.title: Playground — Interactive Lab: Sign, Verify & Symmetric
chunks.content:
Interactive Lab — Signing, Verification & Symmetric Crypto

Sign/Verify tab (?tab=sign_verify) — Sign messages with ML-DSA-44/65/87 (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA all 12 parameter sets (FIPS 205), ECDSA, RSA, or Ed25519 private keys; verify with corresponding public keys. Signature size comparison: ML-DSA-65 = 3,309 bytes, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s = 7,856 bytes, ECDSA P-256 = 64 bytes. LMS stateful-key warning banner included. Pre-select algorithm: /playground/interactive?tab=sign_verify&algo=ML-DSA-65

Symmetric tab (?tab=symmetric) — AES-128/256-GCM, AES-CBC, AES-CTR, AES-CMAC, ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypt/decrypt operations.

Hashing tab (?tab=hashing) — SHA-256, SHA-512, SHAKE128, SHAKE256 digest computation with hex output.

Data tab (?tab=data) — Hex editor for input data used in subsequent operations.

Logs tab (?tab=logs) — Full operation history with execution times and result status.

chunks.title: Playground — PKCS#11 v3.2 HSM Playground
chunks.content:
PKCS#11 HSM Playground

The HSM Playground at /playground/hsm emulates a PKCS#11 v3.2 hardware security module in the browser using SoftHSMv3 (a fork of SoftHSM2 compiled to WebAssembly). All operations use real PKCS#11 C_ interfaces — mirroring what applications do against hardware HSMs.

Engine modes: C++ (default), Rust, Dual (cross-check where one engine generates and the other verifies for parity validation).

10 tabs:
1. Keystore — Token initialization, HSM key table with generated keys
2. Symmetric — AES-GCM/CBC/CTR, ChaCha20 encrypt/decrypt via C_EncryptInit/C_Encrypt
3. Key Wrap — AES key wrap/unwrap, AES-GCM wrap, RSA-OAEP wrap via C_WrapKey/C_UnwrapKey
4. Hashing — SHA-256/384/512, SHA3 digests via C_DigestInit/C_Digest
5. Sign/Verify — ML-DSA-44/65/87 and SLH-DSA (all 12 FIPS 205 parameter sets) signing with pre-hash support (SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, SHA3-512, SHAKE-128, SHAKE-256, Pure). Classical RSA/ECDSA also available. Uses C_SignInit/C_Sign/C_VerifyInit/C_Verify.
6. Key Agreement — ML-KEM encap/decap (C_EncapsulateKey/C_DecapsulateKey), ECDH, X25519
7. Key Derivation — HKDF (SP 800-56C), PBKDF2 (BIP39 mnemonic to seed) via C_DeriveKey
8. Mechanisms — PKCS#11 mechanism introspection (C_GetMechanismList/C_GetMechanismInfo)
9. ACVP — NIST ACVP Known Answer Test (KAT) vectors for ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA
10. Logs — Full PKCS#11 operation log with C_ function calls, parameters, and timing

Key attributes follow PKCS#11 v3.2 CKA_* conventions: CKA_EXTRACTABLE, CKA_SENSITIVE, CKA_ENCRYPT, CKA_DECRYPT, CKA_WRAP, CKA_UNWRAP, CKA_SIGN, CKA_VERIFY configured via key templates at generation time.

chunks.title: OpenSSL Studio — Browser-Based WASM Terminal
chunks.content:
OpenSSL Studio Overview

OpenSSL Studio provides a full OpenSSL 3.6.1 terminal running in the browser via WebAssembly (WASM). It supports PQC algorithms through the OQS provider, enabling hands-on practice with post-quantum key generation, certificate creation, and cryptographic operations without installing anything. 14 command categories: genpkey, req, x509, enc, dgst, hash, rand, version, files, kem, pkcs12, lms, configutl, kdf. Supports command aliases for user-friendly URLs (keygen→genpkey, sign→dgst, cert→x509, etc.). Embeddable mode hides the page header when used inside workshop tools. All operations execute locally in the browser with SharedArrayBuffer support.

chunks.title: OpenSSL Studio — PQC Key Generation Commands
chunks.content:
PQC Key Generation with OpenSSL Studio

Generate PQC keys using modern OpenSSL 3.x commands:
- ML-KEM: openssl genpkey -algorithm mlkem768 -out mlkem768_key.pem
- ML-DSA: openssl genpkey -algorithm mldsa65 -out mldsa65_key.pem
- SLH-DSA: openssl genpkey -algorithm slhdsa-sha2-128s -out slhdsa_key.pem
- Extract public key: openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout -out pub.pem

Use genpkey (not genrsa/ecparam) — modern OpenSSL commands support all PQC algorithms through the OQS provider.

chunks.title: OpenSSL Studio — PQC Certificate Operations
chunks.content:
PQC Certificate Operations with OpenSSL Studio

Create PQC certificates and CSRs:
- Self-signed cert: openssl req -x509 -new -key mldsa65_key.pem -out cert.pem -days 365 -subj "/CN=PQC Test"
- CSR: openssl req -new -key mldsa65_key.pem -out csr.pem -subj "/CN=PQC Test"
- Verify cert: openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout
- Sign data: openssl pkeyutl -sign -inkey mldsa65_key.pem -in data.txt -out sig.bin
- Verify signature: openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey pub.pem -in data.txt -sigfile sig.bin

All certificates use ML-DSA-65 or other PQC algorithms for signing, demonstrating post-quantum PKI workflows.

chunks.title: Judo Belt Grading System — 7 Tiers with Threshold Gates
chunks.content:
Judo Belt Grading System

PQC Today uses a 7-tier judo belt ranking system to measure learning progress. Each belt requires both a minimum composite awareness score AND meeting specific threshold gates (quiz mastery, step completion, artifacts generated, time invested, and daily streak).

Composite Score Formula: Knowledge (40%) + Breadth (30%) + Practice (20%) + Time & Consistency (10%)
- Knowledge: quiz questions correctly answered (cumulative mastery across sessions)
- Breadth: learning module workshop steps completed
- Practice: cryptographic artifacts generated (keys × 8pts, certs × 7pts, CSRs × 5pts, exec docs × 5pts)
- Time & Consistency: total learning minutes (60%) + current daily streak (40%)

Belt Ranks:
- **White Belt** (0–14 pts): "Beginning the journey" — Quiz ≥0%, Steps ≥0%, Artifacts ≥0, Time ≥0min, Streak ≥0 days
- **Yellow Belt** (15–29 pts): "Learning the basics" — Quiz ≥15%, Steps ≥10%, Artifacts ≥0, Time ≥15min, Streak ≥0 days
- **Orange Belt** (30–44 pts): "Exploring foundations" — Quiz ≥30%, Steps ≥25%, Artifacts ≥2, Time ≥45min, Streak ≥0 days
- **Green Belt** (45–59 pts): "Solid fundamentals developing" — Quiz ≥45%, Steps ≥40%, Artifacts ≥3, Time ≥90min, Streak ≥3 days
- **Blue Belt** (60–74 pts): "Building depth consistently" — Quiz ≥60%, Steps ≥60%, Artifacts ≥5, Time ≥180min, Streak ≥4 days
- **Brown Belt** (75–87 pts): "Strong practitioner" — Quiz ≥75%, Steps ≥80%, Artifacts ≥7, Time ≥300min, Streak ≥5 days
- **Black Belt** (88–100 pts): "PQC mastery achieved" — Quiz ≥90%, Steps ≥95%, Artifacts ≥10, Time ≥600min, Streak ≥7 days

Threshold gating: A learner can have the score for Brown Belt but be held at Blue Belt if they haven't generated enough artifacts or maintained a sufficient streak. Unmet gates produce actionable feedback messages (e.g., "Need 2 more artifacts for Brown Belt").

The belt system is persona-scoped: only modules in the active persona's learning path count toward breadth. Quiz mastery is filtered to persona-relevant questions.

chunks.title: Assessment Report: Risk Score
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: Risk Score

A composite score from 0 to 100 that quantifies your organization’s quantum risk. Higher scores mean more urgent action is needed.

Wizard Inputs:
  - **Industry (Step 1)**: Determines category weights. For example, government and finance weight regulatory pressure higher, while telecom and energy weight migration complexity higher.
  - **Quantum Exposure inputs**: Algorithms (Step 3), Crypto Use Cases (Step 7), Data Retention (Step 8), Data Sensitivity (Step 4).
  - **Migration Complexity inputs**: Crypto Agility (Step 11), Infrastructure (Step 12), System Scale + Team Size (Step 10), Vendor Dependency (Step 13).
  - **Regulatory Pressure inputs**: Compliance Frameworks (Step 5), Industry (Step 1), Country (Step 2), Timeline Pressure (Step 13).
  - **Organizational Readiness inputs**: Migration Status (Step 6), Team Size (Step 10), Crypto Agility (Step 11), Vendor Dependency (Step 13).
  - **See Risk Breakdown section**: Full per-category weights and situational boosts are documented under the Risk Breakdown info panel.

Scoring Principles:
  • Composite = (QE × w1) + (MC × w2) + (RP × w3) + (OR × w4), where weights are industry-specific.
  • Situational boosts (up to +20%) apply for compounding risks: critical data with long retention and no migration started (HNDL), signing algorithms with long credential lifetime (HNFL), government with CNSA 2.0 obligations, or hardcoded crypto with legacy infrastructure.
  • Risk level thresholds: Low (0\u201325), Medium (26\u201355), High (56\u201375), Critical (76\u2013100).

chunks.title: Assessment Report: Key Findings
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: Key Findings

The 3\u20135 most critical insights automatically identified from your assessment: vulnerable algorithms, compliance gaps, HNDL/HNFL exposure, and migration blockers.

Wizard Inputs:
  - **Algorithms (Step 3)**: Identifies which of your algorithms are quantum-vulnerable.
  - **Compliance (Step 5)**: Flags frameworks with approaching PQC deadlines.
  - **Data Retention (Step 8) / Credential Lifetime (Step 9)**: Highlights HNDL or HNFL risk windows.
  - **Migration Status (Step 6)**: Flags if migration has not started.

chunks.title: Assessment Report: Risk Breakdown
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: Risk Breakdown

Shows your score across four risk categories, each computed from specific wizard inputs with industry-tuned weights.

Wizard Inputs:
  - **Quantum Exposure**: Algorithms (40%), Use Cases (25%), Data Retention (20%), Data Sensitivity (15%). Measures how exposed your data and operations are to quantum attacks.
  - **Migration Complexity**: Crypto Agility (40%), Infrastructure (30%), System Scale (15%), Vendor Dependency (15%). Measures effort to transition to PQC.
  - **Regulatory Pressure**: Compliance Frameworks (45%), Industry Regulation (30%), Country Urgency + Timeline Pressure (25%). Measures external pressure to migrate.
  - **Organizational Readiness**: Migration Status (40%), Team Capacity (25%), Crypto Agility (20%), Vendor Dependency (15%). Measures your organization’s current ability to execute.

Scoring Principles:
  • Each category is scored 0\u2013100 independently.
  • Category weights are industry-specific (e.g., Finance: QE=0.30, MC=0.25, RP=0.25, OR=0.20).
  • Category drivers (the text under each bar) explain what specifically is pulling each score up or down.

chunks.title: Assessment Report: Executive Summary
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: Executive Summary

A narrative summary of your key risks and recommended priorities, written in language tailored to your persona.

Wizard Inputs:
  - **All wizard inputs**: The narrative references your specific algorithms, compliance gaps, infrastructure, and migration status.

chunks.title: Assessment Report: Assessment Profile
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: Assessment Profile

Wizard Inputs:

chunks.title: Assessment Report: HNDL & HNFL Risk Windows
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: HNDL & HNFL Risk Windows

Calculates whether adversaries can harvest your encrypted data now and decrypt it later (HNDL), or forge your digital signatures retroactively (HNFL).

Wizard Inputs:
  - **Data Retention (Step 8)**: HNDL: how many years your data must stay confidential. Longer retention = larger risk window.
  - **Credential Lifetime (Step 9)**: HNFL: how many years your signed artifacts must remain trusted. Longer lifetime = larger risk window.
  - **Country (Step 2)**: Determines the estimated quantum threat year. Countries with earlier regulatory deadlines (e.g., US and France target 2030) use an accelerated horizon.
  - **Algorithms (Step 3)**: HNFL only applies when signing algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA) are present.
  - **Use Cases (Step 7)**: Use cases with high HNFL relevance (code signing, PKI, digital identity) are flagged.

Scoring Principles:
  • HNDL: At risk when (current year + retention years) > estimated quantum threat year.
  • HNFL: At risk when signing algorithms are present AND (current year + credential lifetime) > estimated quantum threat year.
  • Risk window = years of exposure beyond the quantum threat horizon.
  • “I don’t know” responses use conservative industry defaults (e.g., 75 years for government retention, 10 years for credential lifetime).

chunks.title: Assessment Report: Algorithm Migration Priority
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: Algorithm Migration Priority

Maps each classical algorithm you selected to its NIST-recommended post-quantum replacement, with urgency and effort estimates.

Wizard Inputs:
  - **Algorithms (Step 3)**: Each selected algorithm is looked up in the algorithm database to determine quantum vulnerability and recommended PQC replacement (e.g., RSA-2048 \u2192 ML-KEM, ECDSA \u2192 ML-DSA).
  - **Crypto Agility (Step 11)**: Affects effort estimate — hardcoded crypto means higher migration effort per algorithm.
  - **Infrastructure (Step 12)**: HSM and legacy systems increase migration complexity and effort scope.
  - **Compliance (Step 5)**: Frameworks with PQC mandates increase urgency for vulnerable algorithms.

Scoring Principles:
  • Urgency levels: Immediate (quantum-vulnerable + compliance deadline), Near-term (quantum-vulnerable, no immediate deadline), Long-term (not directly vulnerable).
  • Effort scope: Quick-win, Moderate, Major project, or Multi-year — based on crypto agility and infrastructure complexity.

chunks.title: Assessment Report: Compliance Impact
chunks.content:
Assessment Report Section: Compliance Impact

Wizard Inputs:
