- **5G SUCI — B→C transition no longer double-cleans**: `changeProfile('C')` now internally sets
  `pqcMode` to `'hybrid'`, so `onComplete` can call it once without a redundant `changeP…

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.85.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-07)
chunks.content:
Version 2.85.0 released 2026-04-07.

### Added

- **5G SUCI — Profile C visualization corrected**: The SUCI structure panel now correctly shows
  the hybrid Profile C output format — the scheme output starts with the ML-KEM ciphertext, not
  an ephemeral key. The abbreviated SUCI string and description both reflect the actual
  `kemCiphertext ‖ msinCiphertext ‖ macTag` layout per 3GPP TS 23.003.

- **Library — 3 new records with proper titles and download links**:
  - _Study of Post Quantum Status of Widely Used Protocols_ (Cisco Research, arXiv 2603.28728, Mar 2026) — PQC migration survey across TLS, IPsec, BGP, DNSSEC, SSH, QUIC, OpenID Connect, OpenVPN, and Signal.
  - _Securing Elliptic Curve Cryptocurrencies against Quantum Vulnerabilities_ (Google Quantum AI + Ethereum Foundation, Mar 2026) — new resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with a quantum computer; on-spend attack analysis.
  - _Protecting Subscriber Identifiers with SUCI_ (NIST CSWP 36A ipd, Aug 2024) — NIST guidance on enabling 5G subscriber identity concealment to prevent IMSI-catching.

- **5G SUCI — removed WIP badge**: The 5G SUCI Construction tool is now complete and no longer
  marked as Work in Progress in the Playground.

### Fixed

- **5G SUCI — HSM and OpenSSL cross-check now agree on key derivation**: The dual-engine
  comparison was previously using different ephemeral key bytes for the KDF — the HSM used its
  internal EC point while OpenSSL used an SPKI-wrapped version. The HSM key bytes are now synced
  into the shared state before derivation runs, so both engines produce matching output.

- **HSM — AES-GCM per-message encrypt/decrypt enabled on Rust engine**: The per-message AEAD
  functions (`C_MessageEncryptInit`, `C_EncryptMessage`, etc.) are now fully wired to the Rust
  WASM engine, which implements them in softhsmv3 v0.4.10. Previously they returned an error.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.84.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-07)
chunks.content:
Version 2.84.0 released 2026-04-07.

### Added

- **VPN Simulation — SKEYSEED key derivation step**: After the ML-KEM shared secret is verified,
  a new panel shows exactly how IKEv2 derives the session master key (SKEYSEED) — using
  `prf(Ni ‖ Nr, shared_secret)` with the actual KEM secret bytes displayed. Pure-PQC and hybrid
  modes each show their respective PRF inputs. References RFC 9370 and the ML-DSA IKEv2 draft.

- **VPN Simulation — IKE exchange phase labels on logs**: Each line in the charon.log panel is now
  tagged with its IKE exchange phase (SETUP / IKE_SA_INIT / IKE_INTERMEDIATE / IKE_AUTH). This
  makes it easy to see where ML-KEM fits into the handshake — encapsulation happens during
  IKE_INTERMEDIATE in hybrid mode, IKE_SA_INIT in pure-PQC mode.

- **VPN Simulation — payload size note**: A callout explains that PQC key exchange payloads are
  10–16× larger than classical ECDH (ML-KEM-768 public key: 1,184 bytes vs P-256: 64 bytes),
  and why IKEv2 uses the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange to handle the extra fragmentation load.

- **VPN Simulation — QKD toggle clarified**: The QKD PSK option now shows
  "(informational — not simulated)" so it is clear this is a display label, not an active feature.

### Fixed

- **5G SUCI — dual-engine comparison uses real HSM output**: The encrypted MSIN and MAC tag
  shown in the comparison panel now come directly from the HSM rather than the parallel
  OpenSSL computation, giving an accurate side-by-side result. The MAC tag is correctly
  truncated to 8 bytes per 3GPP TS 33.501.

- **5G SUCI Profile C — KEM ciphertext carried forward correctly**: The HSM-produced ML-KEM
  ciphertext is now stored in the shared state after the key encapsulation step, so downstream
  SUCI assembly and visualization use the real ciphertext.

- **Stateful Signatures — default message aligned across panels**: Both the XMSS key generation
  demo and the Stateful Signatures workshop now default to `"Hello, world!"`, making cross-engine
  verification work without any manual inp…

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.83.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-07)
chunks.content:
Version 2.83.0 released 2026-04-07.

### Added

- **VPN Simulation — full IKEv2 + ML-KEM-768 handshake working end-to-end**: The VPN simulator
  now completes a real PKCS#11-based ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation through the HSM, including
  key generation, encapsulation, shared secret extraction, and SKEYSEED derivation. This is the
  first full IKEv2 post-quantum handshake running entirely inside the browser HSM.

### Fixed

- **VPN Simulation — engine stability**: Switched back to the C++ HSM engine for VPN simulation
  after finding that the Rust WASM engine has compatibility issues in the browser's secure context
  that prevent it from running correctly in this scenario.

- **HSM — encapsulation bug fixed in softhsmv3**: A bug in the C++ HSM engine caused key
  encapsulation to return an error when reading standard key attributes. The WASM binary has been
  updated with the fix.

- **HSM — 8 additional Rust engine functions now active**: Pre-bound signature verification
  (`C_VerifySignatureInit/Final/Update`) and PKCS#11 v3.2 session functions that were previously
  disabled are now fully wired to the Rust engine.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.82.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-06)
chunks.content:
Version 2.82.0 released 2026-04-06.

### Added

- **5G SUCI — 3GPP TS 33.501 reference vectors modal**: A "Reference Vectors" button on the SUCI
  flow panel opens an expandable modal with the official 3GPP TS 33.501 Annex C.4 test vectors
  for Profile A (X25519) and Profile B (P-256) — including home network keys, ephemeral keys,
  scheme output breakdown (EphPub ‖ Ciphertext ‖ MAC), and copyable hex fields.
- **Profile C hybrid mode — full TR 33.841 §5.2.5.2 implementation**: Hybrid Profile C now
  generates two separate HN keypairs (ML-KEM-768 + X25519), derives Z_ecdh via ECDH and Z_kem
  via ML-KEM encapsulation, then combines them as `Z = SHA256(Z_ecdh ‖ Z_kem)` inside the HSM
  using `C_Digest`. Key derivation uses ANSI X9.63-KDF with SHA3-256 producing AES-256 + HMAC-SHA3-256 keys.
- **Stateful Signatures — cross-engine sign and verify**: The Stateful Signatures workshop can now
  sign on the Rust engine and verify on the C++ engine. Public key bytes are cached at generation
  time, imported into the C++ session via `C_CreateObject`, and verified with `C_VerifyInit` /
  `C_Verify`. Includes tamper-detection toggles (flip message / flip signature) and a live
  verification result indicator.
- **VPN Simulation — RSA-3072 certificate generation and inspection**: The VPN panel now generates
  a real RSA-3072 key pair via the HSM, constructs a TBS certificate using `@peculiar/asn1-x509`,
  signs it with `C_Sign` (SHA256withRSA), and shows a certificate inspector modal with full field
  breakdown. A warning badge notes that RSA-3072 is classical (not quantum-safe) per
  draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mldsa.

### Changed

- **5G SUCI — spec-correct ANSI X9.63-KDF replaces HKDF**: Key derivation now follows 3GPP TS
  33.501 §C.3.3 exactly — `block1 = SHA-256(Z ‖ 0x00000001 ‖ sharedInfo)`,
  `K_enc = block1[0:16]`, `K_mac = block1[16:] ‖ block2[0:16]`. HKDF was never in the 3GPP spec.
- **5G SUCI — AES-128-CTR with zero IV (was AES-GCM)**: MSIN encryption now uses AES-128-CTR per
  TS 33.501 §C.3.3 with a ze…

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.81.1 — Release Notes (2026-04-06)
chunks.content:
Version 2.81.1 released 2026-04-06.

### Fixed

- **VPN Simulation works on the live site**: The VPN simulation panel was showing "SharedArrayBuffer disabled" and blocking the simulation on the production deployment. Fixed by injecting the required Cross-Origin Isolation headers through the PWA service worker — the simulation now works in Chrome and Edge with no action required from users. (Safari is not affected; this was a Chrome/Edge-only production issue.)

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.81.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-06)
chunks.content:
Version 2.81.0 released 2026-04-06.

### Added

- **Download hybrid certificates**: Each certificate card in the Hybrid Cryptography workshop now has a download button alongside the copy button. Save the certificate as a `.pem` file or as a `.txt` file depending on the active view.

### Changed

- **5G SUCI flow matches the real spec**: The SUCI encryption and MAC steps now correctly reuse key material derived in the HKDF step, matching 3GPP TS 33.501. The key family label was corrected from "ML-KEM (Kyber)" to "ML-KEM (FIPS 203)".
- **Envelope Encryption — accurate sizes and wrap overhead**: The PQC column always shows correct ML-KEM reference sizes regardless of which key-encryption algorithm is selected. AES-KWP wrap overhead corrected to 48 bytes (per RFC 5649 §4.2).
- **Bitcoin Playground — pure HSM path**: The Bitcoin key derivation flow no longer relies on OpenSSL — all operations now run entirely through the in-browser PKCS#11 HSM.
- **Firmware Signing wizard**: The Firmware Signing step wizard now uses the same step-wizard UI pattern as other workshops for a consistent experience.
- **Key Derivation panel labels**: KBKDF entries now include the spec revision date ("SP 800-108 Rev1 (Aug 2022)"); PBKDF2 use-case description updated to "low-entropy key stretching".

### Data

- **RAG corpus regenerated**.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.80.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-05)
chunks.content:
Version 2.80.0 released 2026-04-05.

### Added

- **Algorithm region and status filters**: Filter PQC algorithms by geopolitical region (NIST/US, IETF/Global, BSI/ANSSI/Europe, ETSI, KpqC/Korea, CACR/China) or certification status (Certified, Candidate, To Be Checked). Region and Status columns added to the algorithm comparison table. Multivariate and Isogeny families added to the crypto-family filter.
- **Algorithm implementations**: A code icon on each algorithm card opens a list of open-source reference implementations and libraries, with direct links to Migrate catalog entries and Library references.
- **Work-in-progress badges on Playground tools**: Tools currently under development show an orange Wrench badge. WIP tools are hidden by default — use the new WIP filter to show or exclusively view them.
- **Migrate WIP filter**: Products currently under review are hidden by default in the Migrate catalog. A new WIP filter lets you include or exclusively show them.
- **XMSS deterministic keygen test**: A known-answer test (KAT) for XMSS-SHA2_10_256 verifies that key generation is fully reproducible — the same seed always produces the same key pair.

### Changed

- **VPN Simulation — isolated HSM slot management**: VPN slot initialization is now independent of other HSM panels, preventing conflicts when multiple Playground tools are open simultaneously.
- **Hybrid Encryption Demo**: Redesigned from a tab-based UI to a guided 5-step wizard for a clearer, more linear walkthrough.
- **SLH-DSA sign panel**: Streamlined interface — pre-hash mechanism labels, PKCS#11 log, and key inspector are now shown inline without extra navigation.

### Removed

- **Standalone SLH-DSA demo**: Removed a duplicate SLH-DSA demo that was redundant with the unified HSM Sign & Verify panel.

### Data

- New algorithm reference data with Region and Status fields.
- New algorithm implementations cross-reference.
- RAG corpus regenerated.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.79.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-05)
chunks.content:
Version 2.79.0 released 2026-04-05.

### Fixed

- **Stateful Signatures workshop — key generation no longer crashes**: LMS and XMSS key generation was hitting an internal error. Both now use the Rust WASM engine, which handles these algorithms correctly.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.78.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-05)
chunks.content:
Version 2.78.0 released 2026-04-05.

### Added

- **VPN simulation — all crypto through the in-browser HSM**: ECDH key exchange and random number generation during the IKEv2 handshake now run entirely through the in-browser SoftHSMv3 PKCS#11 module. OpenSSL is no longer used for IKE crypto — every cryptographic operation is visible in the PKCS#11 log.
- **Complete LMS/LMOTS parameter support**: Expanded from 9 to the full IANA registry — 20 LMS parameter sets and 16 LMOTS parameter sets, covering all SHA-256, SHA-256/24, SHAKE, and SHAKE/24 variants with correct signature size tables.

### Fixed

- **LMOTS W4 signature size lookups corrected**: The wrong constant value for the W4 Winternitz parameter was causing incorrect signature size calculations. Fixed to match the IANA registry.

### Data

- RAG corpus regenerated.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.77.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-05)
chunks.content:
Version 2.77.0 released 2026-04-05.

### Added

- **VPN Simulation with ML-KEM-768**: A complete IKEv2 handshake now runs entirely in your browser — no server required. Two Web Worker instances of strongSwan 6.0.5 (initiator and responder) negotiate a post-quantum secure tunnel using ML-KEM-768 key exchange, completing IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH across 4 packets. Watch every PKCS#11 call, packet exchange, and key agreement step in real time.
- **Configurable VPN pre-shared key**: Set your own PSK for both the client and server sides. A mismatch warning appears when the keys differ, mirroring what happens in a real IKEv2 deployment when authentication fails.
- **Stateful Hash-Based Signatures Workshop**: LMS, HSS, and XMSS key generation and signing now run through the in-browser PKCS#11 HSM. Remaining signature capacity is tracked live — H5 trees are limited to 32 signatures, matching the real-world constraint on stateful schemes.

### Fixed

- **VPN simulation no longer crashes on start**: Fixed a threading incompatibility in the strongSwan WASM build that caused an "Unreachable" crash in single-threaded Emscripten mode.

### Data

- **strongSwan product entry updated**: ML-DSA experimental support added with 5 verified source URLs. Validation status: VALIDATED.
- **RAG corpus regenerated**.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.76.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-02)
chunks.content:
Version 2.76.0 released 2026-04-02.

### Added

- **Collapsible Analysis section in the Gantt chart modal**: Clicking a Gantt bar now shows an "expand ▾ / collapse ▴" toggle when enrichment data is available. The collapsed state shows the main topic with mandate/urgency/sector badges; expanding reveals the full `TimelineAnalysisPanel` with all 8 enrichment dimensions. The panel resets to collapsed whenever a new bar is opened.

### Changed

- **Unified bookmark icon across all pages**: All "My" toggle buttons (Library, Compliance, Threats, Playground, Timeline, Migrate) now use `BookmarkCheck` (active) and `Bookmark` (inactive) from lucide-react, replacing the former `CheckSquare`/`Square` pattern for a consistent metaphor throughout the app.
- **Migrate catalog table cleanup**: Removed the redundant "My" and "Hide" columns from the table view. The Bookmark column now drives the "My" filter (same `useMigrateSelectionStore`), so bookmarking a product in the table immediately adds it to the My selection. chunks.title: PQC Today v2.75.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-02)
chunks.content:
Version 2.75.0 released 2026-04-02.

### Added

- **ACVP tests 23 & 24 — X25519/X448 ECDH round-trip**: The HSM ACVP compliance suite now covers Montgomery-curve Diffie-Hellman. Test 23 generates two X25519 keypairs, derives shared secrets from each side, and asserts they match. Test 24 does the same for X448. Both tests run on both the C++ and Rust engines in dual-mode (40 total assertions). A `extractMontgomeryPubKey` helper abstracts the engine difference: Rust stores raw bytes in `CKA_VALUE`; C++ stores a DER-wrapped point (`04 len raw`) in `CKA_EC_POINT`.
- **ACVP test 25 — X9.63 KDF with SHA3-256 / SHA3-512 (PKCS#11 v3.2 §5.2.12)**: Verifies `C_DeriveKey(CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE, CKD_SHA3_256_KDF)` and `C_DeriveKey(CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE, CKD_SHA3_512_KDF)` produce matching derived keys on both engines. Constants `CKD_SHA3_256_KDF = 0x0B` and `CKD_SHA3_512_KDF = 0x0D` are now exported from `softhsm/constants.ts`.
- **`hsm_pqcEncap` / `hsm_pqcDecap` wrappers (PKCS#11 v3.2 §6.3)**: String-variant API (`'ML-KEM-512' | 'ML-KEM-768' | 'ML-KEM-1024'`) over the existing `hsm_encapsulate` / `hsm_decapsulate` functions, for compatibility with the 5G SUCI Profile C UI layer.
- **`hsm_generateX25519KeyPair`**: PKCS#11 v3.2 compliant X25519 keypair generation via `CKM_EC_MONTGOMERY_KEY_PAIR_GEN` with `CKA_DERIVE=true` on the private key. Exported from `src/wasm/softhsm/classical.ts`.
- **`hsm_importECPrivateKey`**: Injects an EC private key scalar into the HSM via `C_CreateObject` for use in GSMA SUCI known-answer test injection. Supports P-256, P-384, P-521. Includes an inline warning documenting the `C_UnwrapKey` path that real hardware HSMs require.
- **`DerivedKeyProfile` interface + `buildDerivedKeyTemplate`**: Flexible PKCS#11 v3.2 attribute builder for `C_DeriveKey` templates. Replaces hardcoded `CKK_GENERIC_SECRET` templates in `hsm_ecdhDerive` and `hsm_ecdhCofactorDerive` — callers now pass a profile (`{ keyLen, derive, encrypt, decrypt, … }`) that maps 1-to-1 to `CKA_*` entries. Unspecified optional attributes a…

The browser URL also updates to include `?ref=` when the modal opens and clears when it closes, so the address bar is always shareable. Deep links open the modal automatically.
- **Share links for migrate products**: A share button appears in each expanded product row in the migration catalog table. Clicking it copies `/migrate?product=<name>::<category>&mode=table` to your clipboard. The URL updates to reflect the open row while browsing, and sharing the link re-opens the same row with the table view active and scrolled into view.
- **Share country timeline links**: A copy-link icon appears next to the country dropdown (desktop Gantt chart and mobile list) whenever a specific country is selected. Clicking it copies `/timeline?country=<Country>` to your clipboard — send it to a colleague to open the timeline pre-filtered to that country's roadmap.
- **Share buttons in all HSM Playground panels**: Every operational HSM panel (Hashing, Key Derivation, Key Agreement, Symmetric Crypto, Sign & Verify, Key Wrap) now has a share button in its header. Because the Playground already syncs `?tab=` and `?algo=` to the URL on every selection, sharing copies a fully-resolved deep link — e.g. `/playground?tab=hashing&algo=SHA3-256` — that lands a recipient directly on the right panel and algorithm.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.71.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-01)
chunks.content:
Version 2.71.0 released 2026-04-01.

### Added

- **SLH-DSA context string support (FIPS 205 §9.2)**: The SLH-DSA sign and verify operations in the HSM Playground now accept an optional context string — a short byte sequence that is cryptographically bound to the signature. A signature produced with context "A" will not verify with context "B", giving you a built-in domain-separation primitive for multi-protocol deployments.
- **SLH-DSA deterministic signing (FIPS 205 §10)**: A new "Deterministic" option in the SLH-DSA panel forces the HSM to derive its randomness from the key itself. Signing the same message twice with the same key produces identical signature bytes, making it easier to build reproducible test vectors and auditable log entries.
- **ACVP tests 21 & 22 — SLH-DSA context binding and deterministic mode**: The ACVP compliance test suite now covers the two new FIPS 205 capabilities. Test 21 verifies that context-bound signatures reject cross-context and no-context verification. Test 22 verifies that deterministic signing produces bit-identical signatures across two calls and that the result still verifies correctly. Both tests run on both the C++ and Rust engines in dual mode (44 total assertions).
- **Copy button on ACVP execution log**: A clipboard button in the ACVP log header lets you copy the full test output with one click — useful for attaching results to issue reports or compliance evidence packages.

### Fixed

- **SLH-DSA multi-message signing correctness**: The C++ HSM engine's message-API path (`C_MessageSignInit` / `C_SignMessage`) incorrectly lost session parameters (context string, deterministic flag) between the mandatory PKCS#11 size-query call and the actual signing call. Context binding and deterministic mode had no effect when using the message API. Parameters are now preserved across both steps.

chunks.content:
Q: How does the SUCI mechanism specifically address the security vulnerability known as 'IMSI catching' found in previous mobile generations?
A: SUCI addresses IMSI catching by encrypting the subscriber's permanent identity (SUPI/IMSI) before it is transmitted over the air interface. This prevents adversaries from intercepting and identifying subscribers, a flaw that plagued 2G, 3G, and 4G networks where identities were sent in plaintext.

chunks.title: Why is the MILENAGE algorithm used in 5G-AKA considered quantum-resistant despite the vulnerabilities of asymmetric cryptography?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is the MILENAGE algorithm used in 5G-AKA considered quantum-resistant despite the vulnerabilities of asymmetric cryptography?
A: MILENAGE relies on the symmetric AES-128 algorithm, which remains quantum-resistant because Grover's algorithm only reduces its effective key length to 64 bits rather than breaking it entirely. In contrast, the asymmetric ECDH used in SUCI concealment is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm.

chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary difference in cryptographic primitives between Profile A/B and Profile C regarding their vulnerability to quantum computers?
A: Profiles A and B use elliptic curve cryptography (X25519 and P-256 respectively), which are vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a quantum computer. Profile C uses the lattice-based ML-KEM algorithm, which is designed to be resistant to quantum attacks.

A: The operator must implement Profile C, which utilizes the ML-KEM (Kyber) algorithm. This migration replaces the quantum-vulnerable ECIES-based profiles (A and B) with a lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism to secure subscriber identities against future quantum threats.

A: The 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat implies that adversaries are currently recording encrypted SUCI traffic using vulnerable Profile A or B algorithms. A: SIM provisioning relies on symmetric encryption (AES) and key generation in factory HSMs, which remain quantum-resistant against Shor's algorithm. Conversely, SUCI concealment uses asymmetric ECDH for key agreement, making it vulnerable to quantum attacks unless migrated to Profile C (ML-KEM).

A: The 5G key hierarchy derives session-specific keys like KgNB from the anchor key KAUSF, which itself is derived from CK and IK generated by MILENAGE. A: Profile C uses ML-KEM with significantly larger public keys (1,184 bytes) compared to Profile A's X25519 (32 bytes), which increases bandwidth usage. A: Grover's algorithm halves the effective security margin of symmetric encryption, downgrading AES-128-XTS to an effective 64-bit security level. chunks.title: How does the 'Hold Your Own Key' (HYOK) architecture differ from 'Bring Your Own Key' (BYOK) regarding key exposure in cloud environments?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the 'Hold Your Own Key' (HYOK) architecture differ from 'Bring Your Own Key' (BYOK) regarding key exposure in cloud environments?
A: In HYOK, the customer's key never leaves the on-premises infrastructure, and the cloud database receives only encrypted Data Encryption Keys (DEKs). In contrast, BYOK involves uploading a wrapped Customer Master Key (CMK) to the cloud KMS, where it is briefly held unwrapped in HSM memory, creating residual exposure.

A: RFC 9794 standardizes the terminology for hybrid schemes, defining 'composite' as a single OID where both algorithms must verify, and 'non-composite' as parallel independent algorithms. It also establishes the 'PQ/T' naming convention.

chunks.title: Why is a hybrid approach recommended despite the existence of pure PQC algorithms?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is a hybrid approach recommended despite the existence of pure PQC algorithms?
A: A hybrid approach is recommended because PQC algorithms are newer and less battle-tested than classical ones, creating a fundamental dilemma. Waiting for full maturity exposes systems to HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) threats, while hybridization provides immediate defense in depth.

chunks.title: How does the 'Composite' certificate format differ from the 'Parallel (alt-sig)' format in terms of verification?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the 'Composite' certificate format differ from the 'Parallel (alt-sig)' format in terms of verification?
A: In the Composite format, a single OID identifies the algorithm pair, and both signatures must verify for the certificate to be valid. In contrast, the Parallel format uses a primary PQC signature with classical keys/signatures in X.509 extensions, maximizing backward compatibility.

Q: What is the impact of using X25519MLKEM768 on the size of the ClientHello message in TLS 1.3?
A: Integrating X25519MLKEM768 causes the ClientHello key_share extension to grow from 32 bytes to 1,216 bytes, representing a 38-fold increase. This expansion may push the ClientHello message beyond a single TCP packet, potentially affecting network performance.

Q: What is the primary advantage of using a single OID for composite signatures over parallel algorithms?
A: Using a single OID for composite signatures simplifies handling and prevents downgrade attacks by ensuring both algorithms must verify. This contrasts with parallel approaches where independent algorithms might be processed separately, potentially allowing an attacker to bypass one component.

Unlike Composite signatures that enforce dual verification via a single OID, parallel approaches could theoretically allow an attacker to bypass one algorithm if the implementation is flawed.

chunks.title: How does the verification process for an MTC inclusion proof work?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the verification process for an MTC inclusion proof work?
A: The relying party verifies a certificate by hashing it and then combining that hash with each sibling hash provided in the inclusion proof. This recomputation continues up the tree until a root hash is generated. The computed root is then checked against the signed root to confirm validity.

Q: What is the fundamental difference between 'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later' and 'Harvest Now, Forge Later' attacks?
A: 'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later' (HNDL) targets encrypted data, where adversaries store ciphertext today to decrypt it once quantum computers are available. In contrast, 'Harvest Now, Forge Later' (HNFL) targets digital signatures, allowing attackers to capture signed artifacts and forge new ones after recovering private keys with a CRQC.

This metric highlights the urgency for assets with long retention periods.

chunks.content:
Q: How does the structural coupling of public keys and ciphertexts in lattice-based PQC affect classical TVLA testing?
A: Classical TVLA (fixed-vs-random) fails for lattice-based PQC because the public keys and ciphertexts are structurally coupled, making fixed test vectors trivially distinguishable. This means standard side-channel assessment methods used for classical crypto cannot be directly applied to detect leakage in ML-KEM or ML-DSA.

A: RFC 9794 prohibits silent downgrade, meaning if either the classical or the PQC component of a hybrid scheme fails, the shared secret is considered invalid. Testing must validate that both components complete successfully to ensure the connection is secure.

Q: Combine knowledge of TCP fragmentation and algorithm sizes to explain why Pure PQC TLS is more viable than Pure PQC IKEv2.
A: Pure PQC TLS ClientHello (1,536B) causes fragmentation but remains manageable with a 40% latency increase. In contrast, Pure PQC IKEv2 involves much larger certificate chains (17.2KB), leading to severe fragmentation and a 5,000%+ latency spike, making it currently impractical for WAN.

Q: Develop a side-channel testing protocol that addresses the failure of classical TVLA for lattice crypto.
A: The protocol must abandon fixed-vs-random tests and instead focus on power/EM analysis of specific lattice operations: NTT, polynomial multiplication, and modular reduction. This targets the actual computational leakage points rather than the structurally coupled data structures.

A: Given that TCP overhead dominates crypto computation, the high RTT of satellite links will exacerbate the impact of TCP fragmentation caused by large PQC packets. The strategy must prioritize Hybrid PQC to minimize packet size and avoid the catastrophic latency spikes seen in Pure PQC IKEv2.

chunks.title: What fundamental physical principle distinguishes Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) security from Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)?
chunks.content:
Q: What fundamental physical principle distinguishes Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) security from Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)?
A: QKD derives its security from the laws of quantum physics, specifically the no-cloning theorem and the principle that measuring a quantum state inevitably disturbs it. In contrast, PQC relies on computationally hard mathematical problems that are resistant to quantum computer attacks.

chunks.content:
Q: Why is the sifted key in the BB84 protocol approximately 50% of the transmitted bits?
A: The sifted key is roughly 50% of the transmitted bits because Alice and Bob must discard all measurements where they used different bases. Since there are two conjugate bases chosen randomly, they only match about half the time.

chunks.title: What is the primary function of Shor's algorithm in the context of quantum threats to cryptography?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary function of Shor's algorithm in the context of quantum threats to cryptography?
A: Shor's algorithm solves integer factorization and discrete logarithm problems in polynomial time, effectively breaking RSA and ECC/DH cryptographic systems. It reduces the security of these algorithms by allowing a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) to derive private keys from public keys efficiently.

chunks.title: How does Grover's algorithm impact the security level of symmetric encryption algorithms like AES?
chunks.content:
Q: How does Grover's algorithm impact the security level of symmetric encryption algorithms like AES?
A: Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for searching unstructured databases, which effectively halves the security bits of symmetric keys. Consequently, AES-128 drops to 64-bit security (insufficient), while AES-256 retains 128-bit security and remains secure against quantum attacks.
Module: quantum-threats
References: KpqC-Competition-Results;FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205;NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: What is the approximate number of logical qubits required to break RSA-2048 using Shor's algorithm?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the approximate number of logical qubits required to break RSA-2048 using Shor's algorithm?
A: Breaking RSA-2048 using Shor's algorithm requires approximately 4,098 logical qubits. This metric highlights the significant hardware threshold needed for a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) to compromise current production-size keys.

chunks.title: What are the three distinct phases of a Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) attack?
chunks.content:
Q: What are the three distinct phases of a Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) attack?
A: The three phases of an HNDL attack are Harvest (intercepting encrypted traffic), Store (archiving the data cheaply), and Decrypt (using a CRQC to break the key exchange and recover symmetric keys). This model exploits the fact that adversaries can collect data today to decrypt it once quantum capabilities mature.
Module: quantum-threats

chunks.title: What is the definition of a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC)?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the definition of a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC)?
A: A CRQC is defined as a quantum computer powerful enough to run Shor's algorithm against production-size keys. It represents the threshold where current public-key cryptography like RSA and ECC becomes vulnerable to immediate compromise.
Module: quantum-threats
References: KpqC-Competition-Results;FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205;NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: How does the concept of superposition allow quantum computers to process information differently than classical computers?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the concept of superposition allow quantum computers to process information differently than classical computers?
A: Superposition allows qubits to exist in a combination of 0 and 1 simultaneously, whereas classical bits are strictly one or the other. When combined with entanglement, N qubits can process 2^N states in parallel, enabling exponential speedups for specific algorithms like Shor's.
Module: quantum-threats
References: KpqC-Competition-Results;FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205;NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: Why is AES-256 considered secure against Grover's algorithm while AES-128 is not?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is AES-256 considered secure against Grover's algorithm while AES-128 is not?
A: Grover's algorithm halves the effective security bits of symmetric keys; therefore, AES-128 drops to 64-bit security, which is insufficient for modern standards. In contrast, AES-256 retains 128-bit security after the quantum speedup, maintaining a robust security margin.
Module: quantum-threats
References: KpqC-Competition-Results;FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205;NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: What is the fundamental difference between the targets of HNDL and HNFL attacks?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the fundamental difference between the targets of HNDL and HNFL attacks?
A: HNDL attacks target encrypted traffic to recover session keys for past communications, whereas HNFL attacks target signed artifacts like firmware, certificates, and code-signing blobs. HNFL allows an adversary to forge signatures retroactively once a private key is recovered via Shor's algorithm.
Module: quantum-threats
References: KpqC-Competition-Results;FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205;NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: How does Mosca's Theorem determine the urgency of migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography?
chunks.content:
Q: How does Mosca's Theorem determine the urgency of migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography?
A: Mosca's Theorem states that if data must remain secure for X years, migration takes Y years, and a CRQC arrives in Z years, migration must start within Z - X - Y years. This formula highlights that organizations must begin migration before the CRQC arrives to protect long-term sensitive data.
Module: quantum-threats
References: KpqC-Competition-Results;FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205;NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: Why are root CA certificates and firmware signing considered high-priority targets for HNFL attacks?
chunks.content:
Q: Why are root CA certificates and firmware signing considered high-priority targets for HNFL attacks?
A: These artifacts are often publicly accessible and valid for long periods, making them ideal for 'Harvest Now' strategies. If an adversary captures these signed blobs today and waits for a CRQC, they can recover the private key and forge arbitrary signatures on any document or firmware retroactively.
Module: quantum-threats
References: KpqC-Competition-Results;FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205;NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: How do the timeline projections from NIST IR 8547 differ from the Global Risk Institute's estimates regarding CRQC arrival?
chunks.content:
Q: How do the timeline projections from NIST IR 8547 differ from the Global Risk Institute's estimates regarding CRQC arrival?
A: NIST IR 8547 sets regulatory planning horizons — deprecation by 2030 and disallowance by 2035 — based on a proactive transition schedule rather than a probability estimate. In contrast, the Global Risk Institute (2025 survey of 26 experts) provides a probabilistic estimate: 28–49% probability of a CRQC within 10 years (by 2036, up from 19–34% in 2024), rising to 51–70% by 2041. The majority of experts consider a CRQC by 2035 quite likely.

References: NIST IR 8547
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: If an organization needs to protect data for 10 years and estimates a 5-year migration time, when must they start migrating if a CRQC is expected in 2033?

chunks.content:
Q: What specific cryptographic properties form the basis of security for hash-based signatures like LMS and XMSS?
A: Hash-based signature security relies solely on the collision resistance and second-preimage resistance of the underlying hash function. Unlike other post-quantum schemes, these algorithms do not require new or unproven cryptographic hardness assumptions.

chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary consequence of signing two different messages with the same one-time signature (OTS) key in LMS or XMSS?
A: Signing two different messages with the same OTS key allows an attacker to compute enough of the private key to forge arbitrary signatures, resulting in a catastrophic break. This event necessitates the immediate revocation of the entire key pair.

chunks.content:

A: The Winternitz parameter W controls a trade-off where W=1 provides the fastest signing speed but results in the largest signature size, while W=8 yields the smallest signatures but is the slowest to sign. Changing this parameter has zero impact on the security level of the scheme.

chunks.title: Why is the Merkle tree root used as the public key in LMS and XMSS schemes?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is the Merkle tree root used as the public key in LMS and XMSS schemes?
A: In these schemes, each leaf of the Merkle tree contains the hash of a unique one-time signature (OTS) public key. The root of the tree serves as the overall public key because it cryptographically binds all the individual OTS keys together via the authentication path.

chunks.title: What is the primary architectural difference between LMS and HSS regarding signing capacity?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary architectural difference between LMS and HSS regarding signing capacity?
A: LMS utilizes a single Merkle tree with heights ranging from 5 to 25, supporting up to approximately 33 million signatures. HSS extends this by stacking up to 8 tree levels, enabling massive signing capacity far beyond the limits of a single LMS tree.

chunks.title: How does XMSS provide forward security compared to standard LMS implementations?
chunks.content:
Q: How does XMSS provide forward security compared to standard LMS implementations?
A: XMSS offers forward security, meaning that past signatures remain secure even if the current private key state is compromised. This property is achieved through its specific construction and tighter security proofs requiring only second-preimage resistance.

chunks.content:

A: The immediate risk is catastrophic key exhaustion and potential forgery, as the cloned state allows the same one-time key to be used for multiple signatures. This violates the fundamental security assumption of OTS schemes and requires full key revocation.

chunks.content:

A: The organization should configure the Winternitz parameter to W=8, as this setting produces the smallest signature sizes. While this results in slower signing speeds, it optimizes for the storage and bandwidth constraints of the embedded device.

chunks.title: What specific storage mechanism is recommended for managing the state of LMS/XMSS to prevent rollback attacks?
chunks.content:
Q: What specific storage mechanism is recommended for managing the state of LMS/XMSS to prevent rollback attacks?
A: Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) equipped with monotonic counters are the recommended deployment model. These devices ensure that state updates are atomic and persisted to non-volatile storage before signing, preventing state cloning or rollback.

A: A hybrid architecture could use SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for general-purpose signing where state management is risky, while reserving LMS/XMSS for high-frequency, low-latency firmware signing within a secure HSM environment. chunks.content:
Q: What are the five specific cipher suites supported in TLS 1.3 according to the module?
A: TLS 1.3 supports exactly five cipher suites: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256, and TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256. These suites specify only symmetric encryption and hash algorithms, as key exchange is negotiated separately.

chunks.content:
Q: Which FIPS standards correspond to the ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms mentioned in the module?

chunks.title: How does the HKDF key schedule in TLS 1.3 derive session keys from the initial shared secret?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the HKDF key schedule in TLS 1.3 derive session keys from the initial shared secret?
A: The HKDF key schedule uses Extract and Expand operations to derive all session keys. It progresses from an Early Secret (derived from PSK) to a Handshake Secret (from ECDHE/KEM), which produces client and server handshake traffic secrets, and finally to a Master Secret for application traffic.

chunks.content:
Q: Why is the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key exchange considered more secure than using classical ECDH alone?
A: The hybrid approach combines classical X25519 with post-quantum ML-KEM, ensuring security even if one of the algorithms is broken. This provides a defense-in-depth strategy against both current computational attacks and future quantum computer threats.

chunks.title: What is the primary trade-off when migrating from classical X25519 to pure PQC ML-KEM-768 in TLS handshakes?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary trade-off when migrating from classical X25519 to pure PQC ML-KEM-768 in TLS handshakes?
A: The primary trade-off is the significant increase in key size, with ML-KEM-768 public keys being approximately 1,184 bytes compared to 32 bytes for X25519. This larger size increases handshake overhead and bandwidth consumption during the connection establishment.

chunks.title: In a scenario where an adversary records TLS-encrypted traffic today, what specific threat does the HNDL concept describe?
chunks.content:
Q: In a scenario where an adversary records TLS-encrypted traffic today, what specific threat does the HNDL concept describe?
A: The HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) threat describes an adversary recording encrypted traffic now with the intent to decrypt it later once quantum computers are capable of breaking the classical ECDH key exchange. This would allow the recovery of symmetric session keys and the decryption of past communications.

chunks.content:
Q: Synthesize the relationship between TLS 1.3's removal of RSA key exchange and the necessity of PQC migration for forward secrecy.
A: TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange to mandate ephemeral ECDHE, ensuring forward secrecy where session keys cannot be recovered if long-term keys are compromised. However, since classical ECDH is vulnerable to quantum attacks, migrating to PQC algorithms like ML-KEM is necessary to maintain this forward secrecy against future quantum adversaries.

Q: Analyze how the integration of FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) into a TLS 1.3 handshake addresses both confidentiality and integrity.
A: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) provides post-quantum key encapsulation to establish a shared secret for symmetric encryption, ensuring confidentiality against quantum decryption. FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) provides post-quantum digital signatures for the CertificateVerify message, ensuring the integrity and authenticity of the handshake participants.

This standard was finalized on August 13, 2024, as part of the first wave of NIST post-quantum cryptography standards (alongside ML-KEM and ML-DSA). Q: What are the three primary hash functions supported by SLH-DSA in FIPS 205?
A: SLH-DSA supports SHA-256, SHA-512, and SHAKE256 as its underlying hash functions. The security of the scheme rests entirely on the collision resistance and second-preimage resistance of these specific hash functions. These functions are used to construct the WOTS+ and FORS components of the signature.

chunks.content:

A: The SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s parameter set produces a signature size of 7,856 bytes. This is the smallest signature size available in the FIPS 205 standard, corresponding to NIST Security Level 1. It achieves this small size by using fewer hypertree layers, which results in slower signing speeds.

chunks.title: Why is SLH-DSA considered 'stateless' compared to LMS or XMSS?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is SLH-DSA considered 'stateless' compared to LMS or XMSS?
A: SLH-DSA is stateless because it does not require the signer to track which keys have been used; each signing operation internally selects a fresh WOTS+ leaf using a pseudorandom index. In contrast, stateful schemes like LMS and XMSS require strict state management to prevent key reuse, which poses risks in distributed environments. This makes SLH-DSA safer for serverless and multi-instance deployments.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: How does the 's' (small) variant differ from the 'f' (fast) variant in SLH-DSA parameter sets?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the 's' (small) variant differ from the 'f' (fast) variant in SLH-DSA parameter sets?
A: The 's' variants use fewer hypertree layers (lower d), resulting in smaller signature sizes but requiring more hash rounds per layer, which slows down signing. Conversely, 'f' variants use more layers to achieve faster signing speeds at the cost of significantly larger signature sizes. This trade-off allows implementers to prioritize either bandwidth or performance based on their specific constraints.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: What is the role of the FORS (Forest of Random Subsets) component in the SLH-DSA architecture?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the role of the FORS (Forest of Random Subsets) component in the SLH-DSA architecture?
A: FORS acts as the few-time signature layer situated between the WOTS+ one-time signatures and the hypertree structure. It signs a k-subset of values using a-level hash trees, where the parameters k and a directly control the signature size and security against multi-target attacks. This layer allows the scheme to sign multiple messages without the state management required by pure one-time schemes.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: How does the hypertree architecture in SLH-DSA authenticate the public key?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the hypertree architecture in SLH-DSA authenticate the public key?
A: The hypertree consists of d layers of Merkle trees, where the bottom layer authenticates a FORS public key and higher layers each authenticate a WOTS+ public key. The root of the topmost tree serves as the final SLH-DSA public key. This multi-layered structure allows the scheme to derive a unique path for every signature without maintaining state.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: What is the purpose of context strings in FIPS 205 SLH-DSA signatures?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the purpose of context strings in FIPS 205 SLH-DSA signatures?
A: Context strings are optional byte strings bound into the signature to provide domain separation between different protocols or applications. If a signature is verified with a different context string than the one used during signing, the verification will fail with CKR_SIGNATURE_INVALID, even if the key and message are correct. This prevents signatures from being misused across different contexts.
Module: slh-dsa
References: FIPS 205

chunks.title: How does the deterministic signing mode in SLH-DSA affect the output?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the deterministic signing mode in SLH-DSA affect the output?
A: In deterministic mode, the random input (opt_rand) is set to a zero byte string, ensuring that identical inputs (secret key and message) always produce identical signatures. This is useful for audit trails and reproducibility but removes the protection against RNG failures that randomized signing provides. It is defined in FIPS 205 Section 10.
Module: slh-dsa
References: FIPS 205

chunks.title: If a developer needs to sign a message in a distributed serverless environment where state synchronization is impossible, which scheme should they choose?
chunks.content:
Q: If a developer needs to sign a message in a distributed serverless environment where state synchronization is impossible, which scheme should they choose?
A: The developer should choose SLH-DSA because it is stateless and requires no per-key state tracking. Unlike LMS or XMSS, which would fail or require complex synchronization in a serverless environment, SLH-DSA can safely operate across multiple instances. This makes it the ideal choice for distributed and serverless architectures.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: A system requires the smallest possible signature size for NIST Security Level 1. Which SLH-DSA parameter set should be selected?
chunks.content:
Q: A system requires the smallest possible signature size for NIST Security Level 1. Which SLH-DSA parameter set should be selected?
A: The system should select the SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s parameter set. This set provides the smallest signature size of 7,856 bytes while meeting NIST Security Level 1 requirements. It achieves this by using the 's' (small) variant with fewer hypertree layers, accepting slower signing speeds as a trade-off.
Module: slh-dsa
Algorithms: SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: An application requires high-speed signing for NIST Security Level 5 and can tolerate large signatures. Which parameter set is appropriate?
chunks.content:
Q: An application requires high-speed signing for NIST Security Level 5 and can tolerate large signatures. Which parameter set is appropriate?
A: The application should use the SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f parameter set. This set is optimized for fast signing at NIST Security Level 5 by using more hypertree layers (d=17). Although it produces the largest signature in the standard at 49,856 bytes, it meets the performance requirement.
Module: slh-dsa
Algorithms: SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: How should a developer configure the signing process to ensure that the same message always produces the same signature for audit purposes?
chunks.content:
Q: How should a developer configure the signing process to ensure that the same message always produces the same signature for audit purposes?
A: The developer must enable deterministic mode by setting the opt_rand parameter to a zero byte string. This configuration ensures that the signing operation is fully deterministic, producing identical signatures for identical inputs. This is explicitly defined in FIPS 205 Section 10.
Module: slh-dsa
References: FIPS 205

chunks.title: A protocol requires domain separation to prevent signature replay between two different services. How can SLH-DSA achieve this?
chunks.content:
Q: A protocol requires domain separation to prevent signature replay between two different services. How can SLH-DSA achieve this?
A: The protocol should utilize context strings as defined in FIPS 205 Section 9.2. By binding a unique context string to each service during the signing process, signatures generated for one service will fail verification in the other. This ensures that a valid signature for one context cannot be reused in another.
Module: slh-dsa
References: FIPS 205

chunks.title: Why might a government agency following BSI TR-02102 prefer the SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s parameter set?
chunks.content:
Q: Why might a government agency following BSI TR-02102 prefer the SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s parameter set?
A: BSI TR-02102 recommends the SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s parameter set for government use because it offers the smallest signature size (16,224 bytes) at NIST Security Level 3. This balance provides high security suitable for government data while minimizing bandwidth and storage costs compared to the 'f' variant.
Module: slh-dsa
References: BSI TR-02102-1;FIPS 205
Algorithms: SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s
Compliance: BSI;NIST

chunks.title: If a system must sign a pre-hashed message digest rather than a raw message, which SLH-DSA variant and mechanism should be used?
chunks.content:
Q: If a system must sign a pre-hashed message digest rather than a raw message, which SLH-DSA variant and mechanism should be used?
A: The system should use the HashSLH-DSA variant with the CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHA256 mechanism. This variant accepts an already-hashed message and embeds the pre-hash OID in the payload. Note that context strings are not permitted in HashSLH-DSA mode.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: How does the security of SLH-DSA differ from that of ML-KEM (FIPS 203) or ML-DSA (FIPS 204)?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the security of SLH-DSA differ from that of ML-KEM (FIPS 203) or ML-DSA (FIPS 204)?
A: SLH-DSA security relies entirely on the collision and second-preimage resistance of hash functions, making it independent of algebraic hardness assumptions. In contrast, ML-KEM and ML-DSA rely on the hardness of lattice problems. This fundamental difference makes SLH-DSA a valuable diversification strategy in a post-quantum portfolio.
Module: slh-dsa
References: FIPS 203;FIPS 204;FIPS 205
Algorithms: KEM

chunks.title: In a CNSA 2.0 compliant environment, how should an architect choose between LMS/XMSS and SLH-DSA for firmware signing?
chunks.content:
Q: In a CNSA 2.0 compliant environment, how should an architect choose between LMS/XMSS and SLH-DSA for firmware signing?
A: CNSA 2.0 mandates LMS or XMSS for firmware signing due to their smaller signature sizes and faster operations. However, it permits SLH-DSA as a stateless alternative if the deployment environment cannot support the state management required by LMS or XMSS. The choice depends on the trade-off between signature size and state management complexity.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: Compare the trade-offs of using SHA-2 versus SHAKE hash families in SLH-DSA parameter sets.
chunks.content:
Q: Compare the trade-offs of using SHA-2 versus SHAKE hash families in SLH-DSA parameter sets.
A: Both SHA-2 and SHAKE families offer parameter sets for NIST Levels 1, 3, and 5, but they differ in their underlying hash function properties and performance characteristics. SHAKE is an extendable-output function (XOF) which may offer different performance profiles compared to the fixed-output SHA-2 functions. The choice often depends on specific hardware acceleration availability for the chosen hash family.
Module: slh-dsa
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: How does the hypertree depth (d) influence the relationship between signature size and signing speed in SLH-DSA?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the hypertree depth (d) influence the relationship between signature size and signing speed in SLH-DSA?
A: A lower hypertree depth (d) results in fewer layers, which reduces the signature size but increases the number of hash rounds required per layer, slowing down signing. Conversely, a higher depth increases the signature size by adding more layers but reduces the work per layer, speeding up the signing process. This inverse relationship is the core of the 's' vs 'f' trade-off.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: Why is the pre-hash variant (HashSLH-DSA) restricted from using context strings?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is the pre-hash variant (HashSLH-DSA) restricted from using context strings?
A: HashSLH-DSA is restricted from using context strings because the pre-hash payload construction (M' = 0x01 || len(ctx) || ctx || OID_DER || H(M)) already embeds the context and OID directly into the message digest. Adding a separate context string would be redundant and could introduce ambiguity in the domain separation mechanism. This restriction is defined in FIPS 205 Section 11.
Module: slh-dsa
References: FIPS 205

chunks.title: How does the deterministic mode of SLH-DSA impact the security model regarding random number generator (RNG) failures?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the deterministic mode of SLH-DSA impact the security model regarding random number generator (RNG) failures?
A: Deterministic mode removes the reliance on a random number generator for the signing process, which eliminates the risk of RNG failures causing signature collisions or leaks. However, it also removes the protection that randomized signing offers against certain side-channel attacks that might exploit the randomness. This trade-off must be carefully considered in high-security environments.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: If a system migrates from a stateful hash-based scheme to SLH-DSA, what are the primary operational benefits and costs?
chunks.content:
Q: If a system migrates from a stateful hash-based scheme to SLH-DSA, what are the primary operational benefits and costs?
A: The primary operational benefit is the elimination of state management, which simplifies deployment in distributed, serverless, or multi-instance environments and removes the risk of state desynchronization. The primary cost is the increase in signature size and potentially slower signing speeds compared to stateful schemes like LMS or XMSS. This trade-off is often acceptable for the gain in operational simplicity and robustness.
Module: slh-dsa

chunks.title: What are the five pillars of the Cryptographic Maturity Model (CMM) in the crypto management modernization framework?
chunks.content:
Q: What are the five pillars of the Cryptographic Maturity Model (CMM) in the crypto management modernization framework?
A: The five pillars of the CMM are: (1) Inventory — knowing which certificates, libraries, software, and key material are in your estate; (2) Governance — documented policy and clear ownership (RACI); (3) Lifecycle / CLM — automating certificate and key renewal to meet the 47-day CA/B Forum cadence; (4) Observability — detecting policy drift or FIPS certificate revocation within the same business day; and (5) Assurance/FIPS — proving every library and HSM is backed by a current FIPS 140-3 validation.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST-FIPS140-3-IG-PQC;OMB-M-23-02

chunks.title: What are the four asset classes that must be included in a complete cryptographic inventory?
chunks.content:
Q: What are the four asset classes that must be included in a complete cryptographic inventory?
A: A complete cryptographic inventory must cover four asset classes: (1) Certificates & PKI — all TLS, code-signing, and CA certificates; (2) Crypto Libraries — the specific library versions and FIPS validation status used in each workload; (3) Application Software — applications with embedded cryptographic operations; and (4) Key Material — HSM-protected and software keys, including their rotation cadence and custody chain.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: OWASP-CycloneDX-CBOM-Guide;IBM-CBOM-Harishankar

chunks.title: What is the CA/B Forum Ballot SC-081v3 and what certificate validity reduction schedule does it mandate?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the CA/B Forum Ballot SC-081v3 and what certificate validity reduction schedule does it mandate?
A: CA/B Forum Ballot SC-081v3, adopted April 2025, mandates a phased reduction of publicly-trusted TLS certificate maximum validity: 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027, and 47 days from 15 March 2029. Domain control validation reuse is also capped at 10 days at the final stage. This forces organizations to fully automate certificate issuance and renewal via protocols like ACME (RFC 8555), EST (RFC 7030), or CMP (RFC 4210).
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: CAB-Forum-SC-081v3;IETF-RFC-8555;IETF-RFC-7030-EST;IETF-RFC-4210-CMP

chunks.title: What does OMB Memorandum M-23-02 require of US federal agencies regarding cryptographic inventory?
chunks.content:
Q: What does OMB Memorandum M-23-02 require of US federal agencies regarding cryptographic inventory?
A: OMB M-23-02 mandates that US federal agencies conduct annual cryptographic-inventory submissions through 2035, cataloguing all cryptographic systems and prioritizing migration to post-quantum algorithms. This makes CPM a compliance obligation for federal agencies, not just a best practice.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: OMB-M-23-02;NSA CNSA 2.0

chunks.title: What change did the September 2025 FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance update impose on already-validated PQC modules?
chunks.content:
Q: What change did the September 2025 FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance update impose on already-validated PQC modules?
A: The September 2025 FIPS 140-3 IG update retroactively imposed new Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) self-test requirements on modules already validated. This means a module that had completed CMVP validation prior to September 2025 may now need re-validation or an Implementation Guidance variance to remain compliant when supporting ML-KEM. Organizations must track IG updates as part of the CMM Assurance pillar.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST-FIPS-140-3-IG-Sep-2025-PQC;NIST-FIPS140-3-IG-PQC
Algorithms: ML-KEM-768

chunks.title: What is a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) and which standard defines its schema?
chunks.content:
Q: What is a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) and which standard defines its schema?
A: A CBOM is a structured inventory artifact that catalogues every cryptographic primitive, library, key type, and protocol version in use across an application or infrastructure estate — analogous to a software SBOM but focused on cryptographic components. The OWASP CycloneDX standard defines the CBOM schema, using JSON/XML with fields for algorithm family, key length, usage context, and FIPS validation status. A CBOM can be generated from SBOM pipelines or dedicated scanning tools.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: OWASP-CycloneDX-CBOM-Guide;IBM-CBOM-Harishankar;Keyfactor-Introducing-CBOM

chunks.title: What are the CNSA 2.0 preferred and exclusive adoption years for software signing in National Security Systems?
chunks.content:
Q: What are the CNSA 2.0 preferred and exclusive adoption years for software signing in National Security Systems?
A: NSA CNSA 2.0 sets preferred years (when agencies should prefer ML-DSA for software signing) and exclusive years (when only CNSA 2.0 algorithms are permitted) for National Security Systems. The exact years are product-category specific; the module uses 2030 (preferred) and 2033 (exclusive) as representative values for software signing. Organizations building software signing infrastructure for NSS should plan firmware and library upgrades to support ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87 before the preferred year.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NSA CNSA 2.0
Algorithms: ML-DSA-65

chunks.title: What is the difference between FIPS 140-3 status values "active", "active-pqc", "historical", and "revoked" for a crypto library?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the difference between FIPS 140-3 status values "active", "active-pqc", "historical", and "revoked" for a crypto library?
A: "Active" means the CMVP validation certificate is currently valid for the specific version and platform list. "Active-pqc" means active and the validated boundary explicitly includes FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms. "Historical" means the certificate has been superseded or sunset but is still permissible for existing deployments per SP 800-131B (not new procurements). "Revoked" means the certificate has been cancelled — often due to a discovered flaw — and may not be used in new federal procurements or for FIPS-required workloads.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST-CMVP-Validated-Modules;NIST-SP-800-140B

chunks.title: Why does OpenSSL 3.5 have a separate FIPS provider, and what is CMVP certificate #4985?
chunks.content:
Q: Why does OpenSSL 3.5 have a separate FIPS provider, and what is CMVP certificate #4985?
A: OpenSSL separates the FIPS-validated cryptographic boundary into a loadable "FIPS provider" module (fips.so / fips.dll) that has its own CMVP certificate — #4985 for OpenSSL 3.5. This separation means the FIPS provider can be validated independently of the overall OpenSSL version and allows non-FIPS algorithms to remain in the default provider. FIPS provider cert #4985 is issued to The OpenSSL Project and is the reference cert for deployments requiring OpenSSL FIPS compliance; PQC hybrid algorithms are available in the 3.5 provider.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST-CMVP-Validated-Modules;NIST-FIPS140-3-IG-PQC
Algorithms: ML-KEM-768;ML-DSA-65

chunks.title: What is SP 800-90B Entropy Source Validation (ESV) and why is it a separate CMVP track from FIPS 140-3?
chunks.content:
Q: What is SP 800-90B Entropy Source Validation (ESV) and why is it a separate CMVP track from FIPS 140-3?
A: NIST SP 800-90B defines requirements for entropy sources (hardware or software) that feed Deterministic Random Bit Generators (DRBGs). The ESV program validates the entropy source independently of the broader FIPS 140-3 module validation. It is a separate track because the entropy source may be a discrete hardware component (e.g., an HRNG chip) that is tested in isolation. PQC algorithms — especially ML-KEM encapsulation — demand higher-quality randomness (32 bytes of approved DRBG output), making ESV status increasingly important. Organizations should verify that HSMs and libraries carry both an active FIPS 140-3 cert and an active or in-process ESV certificate.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST-FIPS140-3-IG-PQC
Algorithms: ML-KEM-768

chunks.title: What is the HSM firmware CVE re-validation challenge and why does it take 6–18 months?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the HSM firmware CVE re-validation challenge and why does it take 6–18 months?
A: When a CVE is disclosed in an HSM firmware, the vendor must issue a patched firmware and submit it for CMVP re-validation. The re-validation process — lab testing, NIST review, and certificate issuance — typically runs 6–18 months from CVE disclosure (based on observed CMVP MIP queue times). During this window, the organization must choose between residual-risk acceptance (continuing to use the vulnerable-but-validated firmware), compensating controls, or emergency procurement of an alternate validated HSM. This window must be tracked explicitly in the CMM Assurance pillar.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST-CMVP-MIP-List;NIST-SP-800-140B

chunks.title: What maturity level in the CLM pillar is required to handle the 2029 CA/B Forum 47-day certificate validity mandate without manual toil?
chunks.content:
Q: What maturity level in the CLM pillar is required to handle the 2029 CA/B Forum 47-day certificate validity mandate without manual toil?
A: CLM Maturity Level 4 or 5 is required. At Level 4, end-to-end automation is in place across both public and internal CAs, covering issuance, renewal, and revocation without manual steps. Level 5 adds proactive revocation and drift alerting. An organization at Level 1 or 2 (manual renewal via spreadsheet or email reminders) cannot sustain ~213 daily renewals per 10,000 public TLS certificates at a 47-day cadence without unsustainable labor cost.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: CAB-Forum-SC-081v3;IETF-RFC-8555

chunks.title: Which EU regulations mandate demonstrable cryptographic governance, and what specific articles apply?
chunks.content:
Q: Which EU regulations mandate demonstrable cryptographic governance, and what specific articles apply?
A: Two EU regulations mandate cryptographic governance: DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) Article 9, which requires financial entities to maintain ICT risk management frameworks including cryptographic controls; and NIS2 (Network and Information Security Directive 2) Article 21, which mandates cybersecurity risk-management measures including encryption and cryptographic hygiene for operators of essential and important entities. Both regulations create audit obligations that a CBOM and CMM maturity framework directly satisfy.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: OMB-M-23-02

chunks.title: What is the role of the CISA "Strategy for Migrating to Automated PQC Discovery and Inventory Tools" (Sep 2024)?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the role of the CISA "Strategy for Migrating to Automated PQC Discovery and Inventory Tools" (Sep 2024)?
A: The CISA Sep 2024 strategy provides guidance for federal agencies and critical infrastructure operators on using automated tools for PQC cryptographic discovery and inventory. It emphasizes that manual spreadsheet-based tracking cannot scale to the scope of the transition and recommends CBOM-generating scanning tools integrated with CI/CD pipelines. The strategy is a key reference for CMM Inventory pillar maturity at Level 3 and above.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: US-CISA-ACDI-Strategy-2024;PQCC-Migration-Roadmap-2025

chunks.title: What is the No-Regret ROI model and why does it separate quantum-dependent and quantum-independent benefit streams?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the No-Regret ROI model and why does it separate quantum-dependent and quantum-independent benefit streams?
A: The No-Regret ROI model separates the business case for cryptographic management investment into: (A) quantum-independent benefits — cert-outage avoidance, CLM automation labor savings, FIPS drift remediation, library-CVE response acceleration, and M&A/time-to-market readiness — which pay off regardless of quantum timeline; and (B) quantum breach avoidance, which depends on a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer materializing within the planning horizon. This separation is "no-regret" because Scenario A benefits alone typically deliver positive ROI within 2–3 years, meaning the PQC migration program is justified even if quantum computers are delayed.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST IR 8547

chunks.title: How does RFC 8555 (ACME) relate to achieving 47-day certificate lifecycle automation?
chunks.content:
Q: How does RFC 8555 (ACME) relate to achieving 47-day certificate lifecycle automation?
A: RFC 8555 defines the ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) protocol, which enables fully automated certificate issuance and renewal with no human operator steps. An ACME client (e.g., certbot, cert-manager) communicates with an ACME server (e.g., Let's Encrypt, EJBCA, Venafi) to complete domain validation and receive a certificate — typically in seconds. Automating the entire lifecycle via ACME is the canonical solution for meeting the CA/B Forum 47-day TLS mandate across a large certificate estate, since manual renewal every 47 days is operationally unsustainable at scale.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: IETF-RFC-8555;CAB-Forum-SC-081v3;IETF-RFC-7030-EST

chunks.title: What does the CMM Observability pillar KPI "CMVP freshness ≤30 days" measure, and why is it important?
chunks.content:
Q: What does the CMM Observability pillar KPI "CMVP freshness ≤30 days" measure, and why is it important?
A: "CMVP freshness ≤30 days" measures how recently the organization has re-checked the NIST CMVP validated-modules list to confirm that every library and HSM in inventory still holds an active (not historical or revoked) certificate. It is important because CMVP status can change without notice — a library can move to "historical" when a newer version supersedes it, or to "revoked" after a flaw discovery. Organizations that only check CMVP annually may be unknowingly running historically-certified modules in workloads requiring active FIPS coverage.
Module: crypto-mgmt-modernization
References: NIST-CMVP-Validated-Modules;NIST-SP-800-140B

chunks.title: Protocol Support Matrix: SSH
chunks.content:
Protocol: SSH
Secure Shell — transport-layer security for remote login and tunneling.
PQC Standardization Status:
Pure KEM: draft (individual-draft)
  Stage note: Internet-Draft
  Note: ML-KEM-1024 required by CNSA 2.0 SSH profile from 2027 (Independent Submission track).
Hybrid KEM: rfc (rfc-published)
  Stage note: RFC 9941 published 2026-04; follow-on ML-KEM hybrid draft (draft-ietf-sshm-mlkem-hybrid-kex) now in RFC Editor Queue (EDIT)
Pure Signature: draft (individual-draft)
  Stage note: Internet-Drafts (individual)
Hybrid Signature: draft (individual-draft)
  Stage note: Internet-Draft (individual)
  Note: Composite ML-DSA+Ed25519 host-key authentication track; the CNSA 2.0 SSH profile (Independent Submission) also touches composite-sig host-key semantics.

Documents: RFC-4253, RFC-9941, draft-ietf-sshm-mlkem-hybrid-kex-10, draft-harrison-sshm-mlkem, draft-sfluhrer-ssh-mldsa, draft-josefsson-ssh-sphincs, draft-miller-sshm-mldsa65-ed25519-composite-sigs, draft-becker-cnsa2-ssh-profile-03
OSS Libraries: OpenSSH
Live Deployments:
  • OpenSSH: mlkem768x25519-sha256 default in OpenSSH 9.9 (since 2024-09)
  • GitHub SSH: sntrup761x25519-sha512 on github.com (from 2025-09-17) (since 2025-09)
  • AWS Transfer Family: ML-KEM SSH KEX policies for SFTP (TransferSecurityPolicy-2025-03) (since 2025-05)
Recommended for production PQC today. RFC 9941 published (April 2026), mlkem768x25519 shipped by default in OpenSSH 9.9, GitHub SSH, and AWS Transfer Family — the most deployment-ready PQC protocol today.

chunks.title: Protocol Support Matrix: TLS 1.2
chunks.content:
Protocol: TLS 1.2
Legacy transport-layer security — no PQC standardization path.
PQC Standardization Status:
Pure KEM: na (none)
  Stage note: No PQC track for TLS 1.2
  Note: IETF TLS WG has scoped all PQC work to TLS 1.3 only.
Hybrid KEM: na (none)
  Stage note: No PQC track for TLS 1.2
  Note: No IETF draft proposes hybrid PQC for TLS 1.2.
Pure Signature: na (none)
  Stage note: No PQC track for TLS 1.2
  Note: No PQC signature support planned for TLS 1.2.
Hybrid Signature: na (none)
  Stage note: No PQC track for TLS 1.2
  Note: No PQC signature support planned for TLS 1.2.

Documents: RFC-5246, RFC-9325
OSS Libraries: OpenSSL, BoringSSL
No live deployments: By design — the IETF TLS WG scoped all PQC work to TLS 1.3 only (TLS 1.2 BCP recommends migrating off TLS 1.2). Operators must migrate to TLS 1.3 to obtain any PQ posture; no path exists to retrofit PQ key exchange or signatures into TLS 1.2 transport.
Inherited by: DTLS 1.2, FIDO

chunks.title: Protocol Support Matrix: TLS 1.3
chunks.content:
Protocol: TLS 1.3
Modern transport-layer security with hybrid + pure PQC key exchange and PQ signatures.
PQC Standardization Status:
Pure KEM: draft (wg-document)
  Stage note: WG document
Hybrid KEM: draft (rfc-editor-queue)
  Stage note: RFC Ed Queue (EDIT) — draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem-04
  Note: X25519MLKEM768 hybrid group (IANA codepoint 4588) — already shipped in production while spec is in the RFC Editor queue.
Pure Signature: draft (ietf-last-call)
  Stage note: IETF Last Call (ends 2026-06-01) — draft-ietf-tls-mldsa-03
Hybrid Signature: draft (rfc-editor-queue)
  Stage note: LAMPS composite-sigs in RFC Ed Queue (EDIT); TLS dual-cert draft at I-D stage
  Note: Two work streams: dual-certificate negotiation in TLS WG (Internet-Draft) and composite signatures from LAMPS that TLS will profile after publication. TLS profiling pending LAMPS RFC publication.

Documents: RFC-8446, draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem-04, draft-ietf-tls-mlkem-07, draft-ietf-tls-mldsa-03, draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design-16, draft-yusef-tls-pqt-dual-certs
OSS Libraries: OpenSSL 3.5.0, AWS-LC, BoringSSL, rustls, oqs-provider
Live Deployments:
  • Cloudflare: X25519MLKEM768 default at the edge for all TLS 1.3 connections (since 2024-10)
  • Google Chrome: X25519MLKEM768 default for TLS 1.3 and QUIC in Chrome (since 2024-04)
  • AWS: ML-KEM hybrid TLS in KMS, ACM, Secrets Manager (non-FIPS endpoints) (since 2025-05)
  • Apple iOS / macOS: X25519MLKEM768 advertised in TLS 1.3 from iOS 26 / macOS 26 (since 2025-09)
  • Microsoft (Azure / Windows): SymCrypt ships ML-KEM + ML-DSA across Azure, Win11, Server 2025 (since 2025-11)
  • OpenSSL 3.5+: Default TLS keyshares offer X25519MLKEM768 (3.5 LTS) (since 2025-04)
  • F5 BIG-IP: X25519_ML-KEM-768 hybrid in TLS 1.3 (BIG-IP v17.5+) (since 2025)
  • Symantec SWG (Broadcom): X25519MLKEM768 hybrid KEX as first-to-market SWG PQ capability (since 2025)
Recommended for production PQC today. X25519MLKEM768 hybrid group already in production at Cloudflare, Google, and AWS; spec is in the RFC Editor queue (EDIT) — the de-facto standard for TLS PQC migration today.
Inherited by: DTLS 1.3, FIDO 2, MACsec

chunks.title: Protocol Support Matrix: X.509
chunks.content:
Protocol: X.509
PKI certificate format — algorithm OIDs for ML-DSA / ML-KEM / SLH-DSA + composite (hybrid) variants.
PQC Standardization Status:
Pure KEM: rfc (rfc-published)
  Stage note: RFC 9935 published 2026-03
  Note: Constraint: KEM certs are encryption-only — cannot self-sign, must be issued under a signature cert.
Hybrid KEM: draft (iesg-submitted)
  Stage note: Submitted to IESG (Mar 2026)
  Note: Composite mode pairs ML-KEM with RSA-OAEP / ECDH / X25519 / X448 classical KEMs.
Pure Signature: rfc (rfc-published)
  Stage note: RFC 9909 (SLH-DSA, Dec 2025) + RFC 9881 (ML-DSA, Oct 2025)

No live deployments: S/MIME PQ standards are very fresh (ML-DSA Oct 2025, SLH-DSA Jul 2025, ML-KEM Mar 2026) — typical standards-to-ship gap is 12–24 months. The quantum-safe consumer-email market migrated to OpenPGP (Proton Mail) and proprietary protocols (Tuta / TutaCrypt) rather than S/MIME; mainstream providers (Gmail / Outlook / Apple Mail) rely on TLS-in-transit + at-rest encryption and do not drive S/MIME at all. The procurement-cycle slots that will force S/MIME PQ deployment — CNSA 2.0 S/MIME profile (still draft) and X9 Financial PKI consumers — have not yet shipped a product. chunks.title: Protocol Support Matrix: DNSSEC
chunks.content:
Protocol: DNSSEC
DNS Security Extensions — sig-only protocol; PQ adoption blocked by signature size vs DNS MTU.
PQC Standardization Status:
Pure KEM: na (na)
  Stage note: DNSSEC is signature-only
  Note: DNSSEC is a signature-only protocol; no KEM dimension.
Hybrid KEM: na (na)
  Stage note: DNSSEC is signature-only
  Note: DNSSEC is a signature-only protocol; no KEM dimension.
Pure Signature: experimental (identified)
  Stage note: Problem flagged — no WG draft chartered
  Note: No IANA DNSKEY code point assigned yet. Constraint: ML-DSA (2.4–4.6 KB) and SLH-DSA (7.8–49.8 KB) signatures exceed the ~1232-byte DNS UDP limit — forces TCP fallback. No IETF WG currently addresses the IP fragmentation issue.
Hybrid Signature: experimental (identified)
  Stage note: Problem flagged — no WG draft chartered
  Note: Strategy draft enumerates candidates; no concrete hybrid mode. Same UDP fragmentation barrier as pure sig.

Documents: RFC-4034, RFC-9364, draft-fregly-dnsop-slh-dsa-mtl-dnssec-06, draft-sheth-pqc-dnssec-strategy-01
OSS Libraries: CoreDNS PQC DNSSEC, PowerDNS PQC DNSSEC, ISC BIND 9.21
No live deployments: No IANA DNSKEY algorithm code point has been assigned for any PQ scheme — definitionally cannot be in operational production. Signature sizes (ML-DSA 2.4–4.6 KB, SLH-DSA 7.8–49.8 KB) blow past the ~1232-byte DNS UDP limit, forcing TCP fallback. Resolver compatibility studies (SIDN Labs on .nl/.se/.nu zones) find roughly half of Internet resolvers fail when zones carry unknown algorithms. Verisign's Merkle Tree Ladder (MTL) mode draft and IETF 123/124 Hackathon work (BIND, NSD, CoreDNS extensions) are all lab/R&D — no live DNSSEC zone has been signed with PQ today. Verisign estimates the next root-zone algorithm rollover (mid-2030s) is the realistic deployment window.
